title: Peloton Launches First Foldable Treadmill, Adds More AI Features
snippet: The Tread Flex, one of three new models, is also the company’s least expensive treadmill at $2,200.
fullText:
Fitness enthusiasts who want to save both space and money, it’s your lucky day. Exercise company Peloton on Tuesday launched its first foldable — and least expensive — treadmill, capitalizing on a global running boom and rebuilding momentum from its pandemic-era success.

Peloton also launched two more treadmills, plus new AI tools for runners, walkers and hikers on its Peloton IQ platform. The new treadmills include the foldable Tread Flex ($2,200), Tread Vision ($3,500) and Tread Plus Vision ($6,700) and go on sale Oct. 1.

With marathons across the US enjoying a surge in competitors, Peloton CEO Peter Stern said in a press release that his company hopes to “connect with a much wider audience” through its new treadmill models and AI features.

Peloton, which combines internet-connected exercise machines with streaming and on-demand workout classes, has been on a bit of a roller-coaster ride since launching its first stationary bike in 2014. Revenues climbed quickly in the first few years, driven by online instructors who developed an enthusiastic following among home cyclists. Sales topped $4 billion in 2021 as the COVID pandemic ignited a home-fitness boom.

But after the pandemic ended and exercise enthusiasts went back outside and returned to gyms, Peloton struggled. Slumping revenues, mass layoffs and several safety recalls drove its stock price down from a peak of $151.72 per share in December 2020 to its current price of about $5 per share.

With people buying fewer machines after the pandemic, Peloton focused on selling app subscriptions, which you can use even without a bike or treadmill. For a monthly fee, you can access thousands of digital classes in cycling, running, yoga, Pilates, Barre and more.

App subscriptions now account for nearly 70% of the company’s revenue, up from 20% at the start of the pandemic. Peloton announced at its earnings call last month that fiscal year 2026 was its “first full year of net profitability.”

Folds to half the size

Peloton said the Tread Flex can fold to 50% of its floor footprint, a benefit for people with small apartments or workout rooms. The machine is better suited for walkers, hikers and people seeking lower-impact exercise than runners.

The Tread Flex’s price could be a major lure for fitness shoppers, says Anna Gragert, senior editor on CNET’s Health and Home team.

“That’s where Peloton could gain new users, by releasing its products at prices more people can afford,” Gragert said. “While Peloton might never return to its pandemic peak, I could see more people pay attention to its products based on price alone.”

The Tread Vision model — geared toward walkers, joggers, runners and strength trainers — features a 23.8-inch swivel screen with Sonos-tuned speakers and a camera integrated with Run Analysis, one of the new AI features in Peloton IQ.

The Tread Plus Vision is “built for high-mileage training and elite athletes,” the company says. The machine utilizes a slat-belt deck and a ball-bearing system and includes all the new AI features. It’s an upgraded version of the Tread Plus, which CNET rated as the best luxury treadmill for 2026.

CNET Senior Editor and Peloton loyalist Laura Michelle Davis liked the Tread Plus’s large screen, 15% incline and tread width exceeding 3 feet. But her main complaint was the machine’s bulky size and heavy weight, which made it impossible to fit in smaller spaces.

More AI for Peloton IQ

In addition to the new treadmills, Peloton members will have more AI tools at their disposal with Peloton IQ, the AI-powered software suite and personal training assistant that the company launched last October.

Run Analysis analyzes cadence, vertical oscillation and stride length to help runners increase efficiency. IQ Pace Targets enables runners to set speed targets and receive suggested speeds from the AI. Heart Rate Zone Workouts integrates heart rate data from smart watches or bands to personalize training targets.

Other new AI features include ReRuns, which lets members sync the inclines from their outdoor running routes via the Peloton app, and Sled Mode, which adds up to 300 pounds of resistance to your Tread for strength training.

Peloton also said people who use the Whoop biometric data app can integrate it into Peloton IQ. Customers have already been able to integrate Apple Health, Fitbit and Garmin Connect.

title: Xiaomi’s new 18 Pro phones improve on Samsung’s privacy display
snippet: Both 18 Pro phones feature rear displays, just like last year’s 17 Pro models. | Image: Xiaomi Xiaomi's new 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max launched in China today, and feature a more flexible take on the privacy display tech introduced this year on Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra. fullText:
Xiaomi’s new 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max launched in China today, and feature a more flexible take on the privacy display tech introduced this year on Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra. They combine it with returning rear screens, two 200-megapixel cameras, and both of Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips. A global launch is confirmed for later this year — especially welcome since last year’s 17 Pro phones skipped international markets.

The two 18 Pro phones look similar to the 17 Pros, with similar compact displays built around the rear cameras, capable of displaying notifications, taking selfies, playing simple games, and more.

The bigger changes are to the front screen, which is now equipped with hardware-level privacy features much like the S26 Ultra’s. Xiaomi’s implementation looks smarter than Samsung’s though: when you activate it for a specific app, it will not only turn on when that app is opened, but apply to notifications, floating windows, and split-screen views, without affecting the rest of the display. Location-based triggers allow you to set it to turn on when you reach work, or off when you come home, with smart triggers for when it detects locations like airports or elevators. It can also use the selfie camera to detect prying eyes and suggest activating the privacy mode.

1/3Xiaomi’s take on the privacy display can filter notifications by app. Image: Xiaomi

The two phones differ in size, with a 6.4-inch display on the Pro and 6.9 inches for the Pro Max. Battery varies accordingly: 7,000mAh or 8,500mAh respectively, using a high 32 percent silicon content. The other difference between the two is the chipset, with the Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite in the Pro and the Extreme version in the Pro Max, though differences between the two chips are slight.

Cameras are led by a 200-megapixel main camera using a large 1/1.28-inch-type sensor (the Light Fusion 960 in the Pro, and 960L in the Pro Max, though they seem similar). A 200-megapixel, 75mm telephoto joins it, the same on both phones, using Samsung’s 1/1.56-inch HP5 sensor and with a minimum focus distance of 12cm. A 50-megapixel ultrawide completes the trio.

Xiaomi’s launch follows similar announcements this week for the Vivo X500 and Oppo Find X10 flagships. The two 18 Pro phones start from ¥5,999 (about $900), and join the 18 Fold in Xiaomi’s new flagship lineup, but we’re still waiting for the regular Xiaomi 18 and the 18 Ultra, likely to appear next spring. An international launch for at least one 18 Pro phone will come later this year, though we’re still waiting to hear if the Fold will ever leave China.

title: Report: AI glasses shipments surged 263% in H1 2026 as Apple prepares to enter the market
snippet: Counterpoint Research says global AI glasses shipments surged 263% during the first half of 2026, with Meta comfortably leading the display-less segment amid growing privacy concerns. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Counterpoint Research says global AI glasses shipments surged 263% during the first half of 2026, with Meta comfortably leading the display-less segment amid growing privacy concerns. Here are the details.

While Meta’s first-generation smart glasses, launched with Ray-Ban, failed to gain much traction, its second-generation devices have been far more successful.

Earlier this year, Francesco Milleri, CEO of Ray-Ban owner EssilorLuxottica, said the two companies had sold more than 7 million AI glasses in 2025, putting a 10-million annual sales target within reach for the end of 2026.

Throughout the last year, Meta has largely had the display-less AI glasses market to itself, while most major rivals are still developing their own hardware.

Apple, for instance, is rumored to be developing its own display-less smart glasses to compete with Meta’s Ray-Bans, with a launch currently targeted for 2027. The glasses are expected to rely heavily on Siri and Apple Intelligence, with cameras, microphones, and speakers built into the frame, while a more advanced version with an AR display is reportedly still several years away.

In recent months, however, Meta’s camera-equipped smart glasses have faced increasing scrutiny, with the “perv glasses” label gaining traction as reports of non-consensual filming and harassment have drawn wider attention⁠.

That said, Counterpoint Research says Meta still accounted for 94% of global display-less AI glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, with its volumes growing 260% year over year. Xiaomi and Alibaba came in at 1% each, with other brands accounting for the remaining 4%.

North America reportedly accounted for 50% of total shipments of display-less AI glasses, with Western Europe accounting for 28%, Australia for 4.4%, followed by the Asia-Pacific region with 4%, Latin America with 3.8%, India with 3.7%, China with 3%, and the UAE with 2%.

Here’s Counterpoint on how it sees this market going forward:

“Despite near-term challenges, we expect the AI glasses market to maintain its strong growth trajectory as Meta, Google, Samsung and Apple intensify their investments and competition. The next phase of growth will be driven by agentic AI glasses offering more proactive, context-aware experiences, enabled by advancements in agent-integrated software, operating systems, voice interaction, and ultra-low-power sensing and computing technologies. These developments are expected to create new growth opportunities for component vendors in the AI glasses ecosystem. We also expect a wider range of AI glasses form factors to emerge to address privacy concerns associated with cameras, including camera-free AI audio glasses and AI glasses equipped with cameras primarily for contextual understanding rather than photo or video capture.”

Counterpoint’s report also detailed the AR & AI glasses segment, which they define as “AI glasses equipped with the necessary display(s) and optical components to enable an optical see-through experience.”

According to the report, shipments in this segment surged 449% year over year, with Rokid accounting for 41% of the market, followed by Meta at 37%, Even Realities at 11%, Alibaba at 7%, INMO at 2%, and other brands collectively accounting for the remaining 2%.

Region-wise, China accounted for 45% of total shipments in this market, followed by North America at 41% and the rest of the world at 14%.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro has a Privacy Display that does more than Galaxy S26 Ultra, launches this week [Video]
snippet: Xiaomi has confirmed support for the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display on the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Pro, and it apparently does a lot more than Samsung’s implementation of the feature. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi has confirmed support for the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display on the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Pro, and it apparently does a lot more than Samsung’s implementation of the feature.

The Privacy Display on Galaxy S26 Ultra is a hardware feature that can help hide the contents of your display from onlookers by physically altering how the light of the display shines outward. It’s a very clever feature which, despite some trade-offs, has been very well-received.

Now, it’s coming to a Xiaomi flagship.

In a teaser posted to Weibo, Xiaomi confirms that the Xiaomi 18 Pro will ship with a “smart privacy screen” that looks virtually identical to the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display. When activated, content is obfuscated at an angle, only allowing you as the person looking at the display straight-on to clearly see everything.

	

Similar to Samsung, Xiaomi looks to be allowing this to work in specific apps or on only certain parts of the display, like a notification, instead of being an all-or-nothing option. 

Notably, though, Xiaomi also shows the feature working on a floating app window, in split screen, and even on specific notifications on the lockscreen. While Samsung is working on improvements, Xiaomi seems to be delivering quite a bit more versatility right out of the gate.

You can see everything in action in the video below:

Xiaomi 18 Pro is officially set to debut on September 23 – just two days from now – with some key details already confirmed (via GSMArena) including battery sizes up to 8,500 mAh, another rear-facing display, and more.

title: Qualcomm launches two new smartphone chips with emphasis on AI
snippet: Qualcomm said that its new top chip can run 30B mixture-of-expert model locally.
fullText:
Qualcomm today announced two flagship smartphone processors, called Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with a focus on facilitating better AI-focused features.

At its annual Snapdragon Summit, Qualcomm said that the new chips can aid in improved personalization for AI agents. The chips have new sensing hubs that can run small models of up to 200 million parameters. With the new sensing hub, smartphones can run a personal scribe locally and differentiate between speakers. Plus, it can build memory based on your usage for better suggestions for automating tasks. The company said that it can run a complete voice-in and voice-out agent through the new chip.

The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 has a new accelerator element that’s designed to run models in a more efficient way. The high-end Extreme version can run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally. This means that while the overall model size is 30B, the model only activates a certain number of parameters for a particular task.

For comparison, at its Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple released a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, the most advanced of its third generation of foundation models.

The new Qualcomm CPU also provides pixel-level control for cameras to facilitate more pro-level experiences, along with improved stabilization and motion understanding. The Extreme version can support video recording at 8K 60fps and at 4K240 for ultra HD slow-motion. It also enables the new Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec for pro-level recording.

What’s more, both chips can use AI to boost vocals and reduce noise. Plus, it has Qualcomm’s new voice bubble tech, which isolates users’ noise during calls. 

At the event, Motorola announced its Motorola Signature 27 smartphone, powered by the Snapdragon Gen 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with general availability sometime this year. 

Qualcomm has been working on more than 40 AI devices, but there is still a belief that a lot of people will use their phones for AI rather than other dedicated devices. Nothing co-founder Carl Pei has hinted at this trend in the past, and more recently, new Apple CEO John Ternus reinforced the same line of thought during the iPhone Duo launch earlier this month.

title: Five AI safety sessions every founder should have on their TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 agenda
snippet: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, five sessions across the AI Stage and Real World AI Stage cover AI safety, featuring leaders from Anthropic, Nvidia, AWS, Waabi, and more. Register before September 25 to save up to $200.
fullText:
Would you trust an AI agent with access to your company’s systems? Put your employees in an autonomous vehicle? Deploy a robot that has to make sense of an unpredictable physical world?

These aren’t hypothetical questions for AI founders anymore. As AI moves out of demos and into businesses, vehicles, robots, and autonomous agents, safety and security become part of the product.

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, five sessions across the AI Stage and Real World AI Stage put those challenges front and center. From securing agents to getting enterprise AI into production, here’s where founders can dig into what it takes to build artificial intelligence (AI) that people and enterprises will actually trust and use.

Building the next generation of AI? Secure your pass to Disrupt and add these five AI safety sessions to your agenda. Save up to $200 on your pass before September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT. Get a second pass at 50% off.

Image Credits:Jeff Bottari / Flickr (opens in a new window)

1. What Anthropic Sees When Enterprises Actually Deploy Claude

Some enterprises are getting measurable value from AI. Others are still running pilots 18 months later. Why?

Anthropic Head of Applied AI Cat de Jong gets a close-up view. She works directly with enterprises putting Claude into critical workflows and sees where deployments succeed, where they stall, and what separates the two.

In “What Anthropic Sees When Enterprises Actually Deploy Claude,” de Jong will take the AI Stage to explore what happens when companies move from experimenting with AI to putting it into production. For founders trying to sell AI into the enterprise, her experience offers a firsthand look at why some deployments deliver real value while others remain stuck in pilot mode.

Want to know what separates AI pilots from deployments that deliver real business value? Hear what Anthropic is seeing firsthand. Register for Disrupt now to save up to $200 before September 25.

2. The Agent Security Problem Nobody Is Talking About

An AI agent that can take action can also create an entirely new set of security problems. What should it have access to? What should it be allowed to do? And what happens when application-level permissions aren’t enough?

In the AI Stage session “The Agent Security Problem Nobody Is Talking About,” Okta President of Products and Technology Ric Smith and NanoCo co-founder and CEO Gavriel Cohen will tackle agent security at the infrastructure level, including weaknesses in application-level permission models and architectural decisions founders need to consider when deploying agentic AI.

If agents are on your product roadmap, security belongs there, too. Get your ticket today to save up to $200 and add this session to your Disrupt agenda.

3. Securing the AI Enterprise: Why the Cloud Just Got a Lot More Complicated

Getting an AI product through the enterprise door takes more than an impressive demo.

Security, governance, and observability all become part of the conversation when companies consider putting AI into critical systems.

In the AI Stage session “Securing the AI Enterprise: Why the Cloud Just Got a Lot More Complicated,” AWS VP of Security Services Rudy Mitra; Luta Security CEO Katie Moussouris; and cybersecurity veteran Wendy Nather will examine the infrastructure that enterprises need as AI takes on more autonomous roles.

For founders building enterprise AI, this is a chance to hear what happens when innovation meets the security requirements of the organizations you want as customers.

Building AI for enterprise customers? Get closer to the security requirements that can stand between your product and deployment. Secure your pass to Disrupt before September 25 to save up to $200.

4. Building AI Systems When Failure Is Not an Option

AI that operates in the physical world raises the stakes. A mistake doesn’t stay on a screen; it can affect vehicles, aircraft, industrial systems, and critical missions.

On the Real World AI Stage, Shield AI Chief Technology Officer Nathan Michael; General Motors Director of Robotics Strategy Mikell Taylor; and Waabi founder and CEO Raquel Urtasun will bring perspectives from defense and autonomous systems to one of the toughest questions hard tech founders face: How do you know when an autonomous system is safe enough to deploy?

The conversation in “Building AI Systems When Failure Is Not an Option” will get into creating a safety culture, testing and validating AI, navigating regulatory hurdles, and building companies that can earn trust when the consequences of failure are physical.

When failure isn’t an option, testing can’t be an afterthought. See how leaders in autonomy are approaching safety at Disrupt. Explore your ticket options, and save up to $200 on your pass before September 25.

Image Credits:Kimberly White / Getty Images

5. Robots Are Waiting for Their ChatGPT Moment. Here Is What Is Standing in the Way

Robots have a data problem. They don’t have access to the massive pools of training data that helped accelerate advances in language models and self-driving vehicles.

That gap is one of the biggest obstacles to scaling physical AI. In the Real World AI session “Robots Are Waiting for Their ChatGPT Moment. Here Is What Is Standing in the Way,” Nvidia Inception Global Head of Physical AI Les Karpas will explore how data pipelines, simulation environments, and foundation models could help close it and what it will take to build, test, and deploy more capable and reliable robots.

For founders working in physical AI, the session tackles a big question: What will it take for robotics to reach its own ChatGPT moment and earn the trust needed to put those systems to work in the real world?

Get an inside look at what could help robotics clear its next big hurdle. Register for Disrupt today to save up to $200 before prices increase.

Five sessions. One question every AI founder needs to answer.

Can people trust what you’re building? These five conversations are part of 200+ sessions across six industry stages, roundtables, and breakouts at Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. More than 10,000 founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders are expected, along with 250+ speakers, 300+ exhibiting startups, and countless networking meetings.

You can build a smarter model, a more capable agent, or a robot that does something no one has done before. But getting customers to trust it enough to deploy it may be one of the hardest parts of bringing it to market.

Secure your pass to Disrupt now and save up to $200 before September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT. Save 50% on a second ticket. Hear how AI leaders are tackling the safety, security, and reliability challenges that can stand between breakthrough technology and real-world adoption.

title: TechCrunch Founder Summit’s agenda revealed: Unlock fundraising, hiring, and AI insights in Boston on November 4
snippet: Founders shouldn't have to learn the hardest lessons the hardest way. TechCrunch Founder Summit is designed to make the challenges of starting a company easier and the highs that much greater.
fullText:
On November 4, TechCrunch’s Founder Summit will bring a vital one-day crash course on startup building to Boston’s SoWa Power Station. Founders shouldn’t have to learn the hardest lessons the hardest way, and this event is designed to make the challenges of starting a company easier and the highs that much greater.

Instead of months of trial and error, you get direct access to the investors and founders who’ve already made the calls you’re now facing. We’re talking everything from fundraising and hiring to AI strategy, and topping your category.

Don’t take our word for it. Explore the full agenda of speakers and sessions we have planned for Founder Summit below, and lock in your spot at the event. All tickets are available for the lowest prices you’ll see, so now’s the best time to act.

The official TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda reveal

Without further ado, here’s the official agenda. Get to know each session and speaker on the event agenda page.

Image Credits:Halo Creative

The New Rules of Raising Capital 

Fundraising has never been easy, but the playbook keeps changing. Brian Devaney, partner at Underscore, will break down what investors are looking for now, how founders can stand out in a crowded market, and where founders often lose leverage without realizing it. Expect a candid look at today’s fundraising environment, from first checks to term sheets, and the mistakes that can make or break a round.

The CEO Job Never Gets Easier 

The title may stay the same, but the job changes with each stage of a company’s growth. HubSpot co-founder and Sequoia partner Brian Halligan will share the lessons he’s learned from building and advising startups through rapid growth, tough decisions, and constant reinvention.  

This session explores how founders can evolve as CEOs, avoid common leadership pitfalls, and build companies that can thrive well beyond the early days.

Built for AI From Day One 

Adding AI features is one thing. Building an AI-native company is something else entirely. Lior Div, co-founder and CEO of 7AI, will explore what changes when AI becomes the foundation of a startup rather than a product enhancement. From team structure and product development to operations and go-to-market strategy, this session examines what founders should rethink when building in the AI era.

Not Every Dollar Is Equal 

Raising capital is often framed as a milestone, but choosing the right investors can shape a company’s future long after the money arrives. After raising an $11 million round for Cogent Security, co-founder and CEO Vineet Edupuganti learned firsthand what separates helpful partners from costly distractions. This session explores how founders should evaluate investors, navigate trade-offs, and think beyond valuation when building their cap table.

How to Spot the ‘King of the Hill’ Company — Hidden Signals That Define Category Winners 

Innovation is needed to solve the world’s biggest challenges, but only certain companies can realistically become category-defining winners at industrial scale. In this session, TDK Ventures investment director Tina Tosukhowong unpacks the firm’s “King of the Hill” framework: the disciplined process that the best investors use to evaluate companies based on economics, scalability, and commercial timing.  

Through real-world examples, including Tina’s exploration of fission and fusion, attendees will learn actionable frameworks for evaluating startup readiness, mapping competitive landscapes, and identifying when timing, talent, and technology align.

Your Company Is Who You Hire 

Early hiring decisions can define a startup’s culture, speed, and ability to execute. Melissa Taunton, partner at NEA, will share lessons from working with founders as they build teams through periods of rapid growth and uncertainty.  

From identifying the right early hires to avoiding common recruiting mistakes, this session explores how founders can build organizations that are resilient, adaptable, and prepared for what comes next.

The Boston Founder Playbook 

Silicon Valley gets the headlines, but Chase Garbarino has been quietly building category-defining companies from Boston for over a decade. As co-founder and CEO of HqO, he has raised $200 million from investors and scaled to 30+ countries without ever needing to change geographies.  

He’ll break down the real advantages and disadvantages of building where the startup playbook wasn’t written, and what every founder outside a major hub should know.

Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale 

Every founder wants product-market fit, but knowing when you’ve actually found it is far more complicated. Kent Bennett, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, will unpack how founders can validate demand, build an MVP that answers the right questions, and avoid scaling before the fundamentals are in place.  

This session explores the signals that matter, the metrics that mislead, and the decisions that separate enduring companies from expensive experiments.

What happens beyond Founder Summit’s sessions 

The programming is a huge part of TechCrunch Founder Summit’s value, but it’s not the whole deal. You’ll also get the chance to mix and mingle with founders working through the same fundraising decisions and the same hiring calls as you, and then network with those who have already lived through those experiences. Or better yet … those who have funded those who have gone through the startup wringer.  

A day filled with discussions turns into months of action at TechCrunch Founder Summit, and we’re eager for you to join us and the rest of the Boston startup community on November 4. Register now to secure your ticket savings and join the ultimate founder’s bootcamp.

title: Ema raises $77M as AI starts eating into enterprise software and services
snippet: Ema has raised $140 million to date and has more than 50 enterprise customers, including Google and Microsoft.
fullText:
Ema, a startup that uses teams of AI agents to automate corporate processes across HR, IT, and finance, has raised $77 million in a new funding round as it aims to take on more of the work traditionally handled by enterprise software and IT services.

The Series B round was led by Bengaluru-based venture firm Creaegis, with existing investors Accel, Section 32, and Prosus increasing their stakes. The financing brings the startup’s total funding to $140 million and more than quadruples its valuation from its last funding round in 2024. (Ema declined to disclose its latest valuation.) The round consisted entirely of primary equity, with no debt or secondary transactions, the startup confirmed to TechCrunch.

The funding comes as AI is beginning to compete for dollars that businesses have traditionally spent on enterprise software and IT services. Startups, major AI labs, and established software companies are now fighting to capture that spending.

Founded in 2023 by former Google and Coinbase executive Surojit Chatterjee and ex-Okta executive Souvik Sen, Ema is looking to expand its position in that market. The startup deploys its technology, which it calls “AI employees” — systems that coordinate multiple AI agents. These help carry out multi-step business processes across a company’s existing applications, rather than handling a single task at a time.

Chatterjee sees that model eventually reducing companies’ reliance on traditional software products, including those sold as software-as-a-service (SaaS). Ema first “wraps” around an enterprise’s existing applications, he said, before customers can reduce their dependence on some of those products — and, in some cases, replace them altogether.

“Many of our customers are already on the way to replace [large SaaS applications] completely, removing dependency on them, because they are mostly becoming like a database,” Chatterjee said.

Benefiting from AI labs’ push

In recent months, major AI companies have also pushed deeper into the enterprise market where Ema operates. Anthropic has expanded efforts to bring Claude into companies’ core operations, including financial and legal work. Similarly, OpenAI has established teams of forward-deployed engineers who work alongside customers to put AI into production.

Chatterjee, however, does not see the frontier AI labs as direct competitors. He told TechCrunch that Ema’s software can draw on more than 150 models, including frontier and open source models, while the startup focuses on the domain knowledge, integrations, and orchestration needed to automate business processes end-to-end.

“Progress in frontier models is actually very beneficial to us,” Chatterjee stated.

Ema’s approach is already gaining traction. The startup has more than 50 active enterprise deals, as well as over 1 million active enterprise users, and has handled more than 5 million actions and queries. Its customers include NTT DATA, Hitachi, ADP, PwC, Google, KPMG, Wipro, and Microsoft.

Over the past two years, Ema said its revenue has grown 50-fold, while revenue bookings have surpassed $150 million. Chatterjee said the bookings figure includes the total value of multiyear contracts, including two- and three-year deals, rather than representing annual recurring revenue. He, however, declined to disclose the startup’s current annualized revenue run rate.

Chatterjee told TechCrunch that more than 90% of Ema’s customers have expanded beyond their initial use case, with some deploying the technology across dozens of workflows. The startup’s net dollar retention rate is around 180%, he said, meaning existing customers are spending substantially more with Ema over time.

Ema is also looking beyond the software itself. AI, Chatterjee said, can take over some of the implementation, integration, and consulting work that companies have traditionally paid IT services firms to perform around enterprise software.

“A lot of the services companies are working with us,” Chatterjee said. “They are also dramatically changing or disrupting their own business models because they understand the human-forward model may not be the best model going forward.”

Despite taking on work traditionally handled by software and services providers, Chatterjee said Ema has maintained gross margins of close to 80%. The startup, he noted, requires less human support as its AI systems learn from deployments, helping improve margins over time.

Ema also does not charge customers based on software seats or the number of AI tokens they consume. Instead, Chatterjee said, its pricing is tied to the completion of tasks and business outcomes.

Much of Ema’s new capital will go toward expanding its go-to-market operations, particularly sales and marketing, after spending its first years largely building the product, Chatterjee said. The Mountain View-headquartered startup has grown to nearly 200 employees and has its offices in Bengaluru, London, and Vancouver.

Ema has so far focused primarily on customers in the U.S. and Europe. However, it now plans to expand into new markets over the next year, particularly across Asia-Pacific, South America, and parts of the Middle East.

title: Eight Sleep Launches Pod 6 With Smaller Hub and Cheaper Entry Price
snippet: The sleep tech company launched the smallest Pod of its lineup yet and introduced new sizes.
fullText:
Eight Sleep, a sleep tech company, launched the Pod 6 bed-cooling system on Wednesday with meaningful hardware changes, including a hub that’s half the size of its predecessor, new solo-size configurations and a $1,999 starting price for the solo sizes — the lowest the company has offered. The entry price for standard sizes will be $2,699.

“We redesigned the hub, so it is 50% shorter than Pod 5, while increasing thermal power. That requires a more efficient approach to the system’s internal architecture, thermal management, fluid movement and overall packaging,” Matteo Franceschetti, CEO and co-founder of Eight Sleep, told CNET. The smaller hub can slide under most standard bed frames.

For the first time since the Pod launched in 2019, customers can choose solo-size options like twin XL and half sizes for queen, king and California king. Until now, the Pod has been built for couples with standard mattress sizes. 

“For six generations, the Pod’s dual-zone design has been extremely valuable for couples, because each person can independently control their temperature and receive their own sleep data. But there are many people who want that same experience for just one side of the bed, or in a bedroom with a twin XL or split-mattress configuration,” Franceschetti said.

The Pod 6 has nine times more sensors per side and AI-powered tracking for more accurate sleep insights. The redesigned hub delivers 40% to 50% more thermal power for faster temperature response. 

Eight Sleep

Franceschetti said that the main advantage of having more sensors is improved precision and consistent tracking across different sleep positions. “People move throughout the night, and a higher density of sensors gives the system more opportunities to maintain a reliable signal, whether someone is on their back, side or shifting position.”

With these updates, the Pod 6 aims to make advanced sleep technology more accessible and versatile for individual sleepers and couples alike.

title: Five ways that the new Siri AI is frustrating iPhone and Apple Watch users
snippet: The new version of Siri, Siri AI, launched to the masses this month as part of iOS 27. The new Siri is rolling out gradually to users via a waitlist, and is labelled as a ‘beta’ indicating that Apple still has some work to do in follow-up releases. The new Siri is much better at answering questions with access to rich knowledge, can search through your messages and notes for personal context queries, and can take action based on what is on your screen with onscreen awareness. However, the new Siri is not being welcomed with open arms by everyone … more…
fullText:
The new version of Siri, Siri AI, launched to the masses this month as part of iOS 27. The new Siri is rolling out gradually to users via a waitlist, and is labelled as a ‘beta’ indicating that Apple still has some work to do in follow-up releases.

The new Siri is much better at answering questions with access to rich knowledge, can search through your messages and notes for personal context queries, and can take action based on what is on your screen with onscreen awareness. However, the new Siri is not being welcomed with open arms by everyone …

Based on social media posts, there are a few reasons why the new Siri is disappointing users. Some expect it to be able to perform tasks that Apple simply never promised would be possible, while others note they are hitting performance and reliability bugs that make using the assistant on a regular basis a frustrating affair. 

Here’s the five main categories of complaints we’ve seen from people trying Siri AI so far:

Network connectivity issues 

Some users trying out new Siri repeatedly see a “Sorry, something went wrong” error when invoking it. This appears to be caused by some kind of network communication issue between the phone and the Siri cloud backend, potentially solved by disabling a VPN or changing Wi-Fi network settings. 

However, the Siri interface does not tell the user exactly what the problem is, so they are left stuck with a ‘useless’ voice assistant. We also suspect the Apple cloud infrastructure is experiencing some intermittent downtime, which can also cause requests to fail.

Indexing problems: new Siri cannot always find things that old Siri could 

While new Siri is meant to be much better at finding things on your device, some users are finding the opposite to be the case. When asking something like “Add eggs to my grocery list in Reminders”, Siri will say it cannot find the list. We have seen repeated cases of people trying to use new Siri to turn off all their alarms, only for it to answer to say the user has no alarms. Others report that their HomeKit accessories cannot be found consistently by name.

These issues are seemingly related to underlying search indexing bugs, but it’s unclear if there are steps user can follow to remedy the situation. Some Apple Watch users even hit extremely odd cases like ‘I can’t set a timer because the Clock app isn’t installed on this device’.

Requires iPhone to be unlocked to answer requests

New Siri seems to require the device be unlocked for many requests, even if the ‘allow Siri when locked’ toggle is turned on in Settings. This applies to all sorts of queries, which old Siri never required the device to be unlocked for. Naturally, many people often try to invoke Siri in situations where the phone is locked, like in a car or on the go with AirPods. 

It seems like whenever new Siri tries to access the semantic index to garner personal context, it fails if the phone is locked. But this makes even simple commands like ‘Send message to [person name]’ more annoying, when old Siri did not have such a requirement.

Slow to respond to queries, especially on Apple Watch

Another common refrain is that new Siri is just slower to answer for them. Although on-device models play a role in how new Siri operates, much of its processing happens on the cloud with Private Cloud Compute, and a slow network connection therefore makes new Siri slow to respond, even for basic requests like sending messages or checking notifications. 

The speed complaints are especially true when using Siri AI with watchOS 27 running on an Apple Watch Series 9 or later, where even saying something like ‘start a 5 minute timer’ can take many seconds to resolve, a disappointing regression as they used to be processed almost instantly. 

Missing features or unreliable commands compared to old Siri

Despite everything that new Siri can do, there are some features of old Siri that have not yet been exposed to the new Siri system. For instance, Apple documents that asking about your Health app data is not currently supported by Siri AI. People that used the ChatGPT integration can no longer prefix their command with “Use ChatGPT” to have their request directed accordingly. 

There are also some particular phrasings of commands that old Siri would understand but new Siri gets confused about. Naturally, this annoys users who have become accustomed to asking something specific on a regular basis. This is partly due to the fact that new Siri has the potential to do so much more, that some specificly-worded queries have become ambiguous compared to the much smaller scope of classic Siri.

Aside from these classes of bugs, we’ve also seen users complain about the way new Siri is presented in the user interface. This includes criticisms of the annoyingly prominent ‘Ask Siri’ buttons that have been added across the operating system, the lack of a visible transcript of what the phone heard the user said in the new Dynamic Island UI, the fact that the middle of the screen swipe-down gesture to reveal their notifications has been commandeered to show Siri & Spotlight instead, and other complaints.

As mentioned before, the new Siri is marked as a beta and this signals that more capabilities and fixes will follow in future updates. Apple has not yet disclosed a roadmap, though, apart from announcing a rollout to a handful of more languages, coming in October. 

	

In the meantime, if you are experiencing any of the sorts of issues described above, you may want to go back to classic Siri:

How to turn off Siri AI and go back to old Siri

The easiest way to disable Siri AI on your device and quickly switch back to classic Siri is to use controls in Screen Time. Open the Settings app and navigate to Screen Time -> Content & Privacy Restrictions -> Siri and change Allowed Siri version from “Siri AI (Beta)” to “Siri Classic”. 

You can then go back to this menu later and toggle it back if you want to try Siri AI again. 

If you don’t want to use Screen Time, you can also go into Siri settings directly and turn off Siri altogether. When you re-enable it, you should be able to choose between enabling Siri Classic or Siri AI.

title: Snorkel AI triples valuation to $3.5B as demand for AI training data booms
snippet: The seven-year-old startup has raised a $350 million Series E to fuel its data-as-a-service approach.
fullText:
Snorkel AI, a startup that helps AI labs and corporations build training datasets and simulated environments, has raised a $350 million Series E at a $3.5 billion valuation.

The new round, which was led by Insight Partners and S32, valued the seven-year-old startup at nearly triple the $1.3 billion valuation it garnered when it raised $100 million in a Series D 17 months ago. Existing investors, including Addition, Lightspeed, Greylock, GV, and Wells Fargo, also participated in the round.

While Snorkel originally provided software for data-labeling automation, it shifted last year to providing customers with completed datasets, an offering it calls data-as-a-service. Rather than operating purely as a human expert marketplace, Snorkel relies on a hybrid approach, using its software and models to generate data synthetically alongside subject matter experts.

Snorkel says its current annualized revenue run rate now stands at $375 million, an eighteenfold increase over the last 12 months. That growth is fueled by AI labs’ insatiable appetite for high-end training data.

Other data companies positioning themselves as AI data labs have seen a similar explosion in growth. Mercor’s gross annualized revenue has climbed to $2 billion, Handshake hit the $1 billion milestone earlier this year, and TechCrunch reported that Micro1 has scaled to $500 million. Since these companies pay out roughly 60% to 70% of their top-line income directly to the domain specialists doing the work, it’s important to note that their actual net annual revenue is substantially lower than those headline gross figures.

Given that Snorkel sells reinforcement learning (RL) environments and complete datasets rather than human labor, payments to its human experts are accounted for in its cost of goods sold rather than headline-generating annualized revenue numbers, according to the company.

Snorkel launched commercially in 2019 following four years of research by co-founder and CEO Alex Ratner and his team at a Stanford AI lab.

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Rabbit, the company behind the underwhelming R1 device, is rolling out a standalone AI agent that you don’t need its hardware to use, as reported earlier by Wired. The startup says its new OS3 “agentic operating system” runs in the cloud but operates locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices.

According to Rabbit, you can add up to five devices to one account, along with your preferred AI models. OS3 will automatically determine the devices, files, apps, and AI models it needs to complete a task. You can also access OS3 through its dedicated desktop site, a paired messaging app like Telegram or iMessage, as well as on Rabbit’s R1 device.

Though Rabbit founder Jesse Lyu tells Wired that the startup has stopped manufacturing R1 devices, it isn’t giving up on AI hardware entirely. It’s instead focusing on a new vibe-coding “cyberdeck” that will run OS3 when it launches within “months,” Wired reports.

Rabbit claims its OS3 system won’t store, copy, use, or sell your data. It notes that it will still keep your chats and memories stemming from them on its servers. Other AI providers linked to OS3 will also handle your data under their own privacy rules.

title: OpenAI upgrading ChatGPT and Codex with two more GPT-6 models
snippet: Earlier this month, OpenAI released the first GPT-6 model with Astra. Now GPT-6 is expanding with new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. more…
fullText:
Earlier this month, OpenAI released the first GPT-6 model with Astra. Now GPT-6 is expanding with new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are now available

Per the ChatGPT desktop app release notes, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna will use fewer tokens to run than GPT-5.6 versions of the same class model.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are rolling out to Codex and ChatGPT Work at lower token prices than their GPT-5.6 predecessors. Use Sol for complex coding and agentic workflows, and Luna for focused, high-volume tasks.

Both models are rolling out to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access Luna in the desktop app. Availability depends on rollout and workspace settings; Enterprise administrators must enable the new models. In ChatGPT, the models are available in Work and Codex, but not Chat.

Note the absence of a GPT-6 Terra model. It’s expected that OpenAI is dropping the medium model in favor of just three: Terra (small), Sol (large), and Astra (extra large).

GPT-6 Sol and Luna are out. Not only are they a very significant improvement across the board, but also in writing and general "you know when you try it" quality. 

We are also permanently reducing the API price by 50% making both of them viable for a ton of new usecases and… https://t.co/vbyUhVlKH3

While the most demanding and important projects still call for Astra’s full depth, work happens at different scales, rhythms, and budgets.

That’s why we’re expanding the GPT‑6 universe with GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna. GPT‑6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence—these models help distribute the benefits of that intelligence by advancing the frontier on cost efficiency. We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The company describes its two newest models as more capable than the GPT-5.6 versions as well as more affordable than Astra (and the GPT-5.6 versions they replace). For instance, the GPT-6 versions of Sol and Luna are 50% cheaper than the GPT-5.6 versions.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing. Together, these improvements make advanced AI practical for more everyday tasks and applications at scale.

In terms of coding, this is what OpenAI says about its new models:

This year, coding agents have begun tackling tasks with more complexity, scope, and duration than ever before. At OpenAI, our internal usage has grown exponentially. Valued at API prices, daily token usage has exceeded $600 for the median researcher and $7,000 for researchers at the 90th percentile (Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI⁠). As coding agents take on longer and more demanding tasks, the cost of sustained use matters more. GPT‑6 Sol and Luna combine strong coding performance with lower API prices, giving developers more room to iterate and teams the confidence to be more ambitious about what they ask Codex to take on.

ChatGPT also excels at Computer Use, and these new models continue that push:

While GPT‑6 Astra remains the world’s best model for computer use, GPT‑6 Sol and Luna offer more cost-efficient performance than their predecessors. On OSWorld 2.0 offline, GPT‑6 Sol at xhigh effort achieves a similar score to Claude Opus 5 at medium effort—60.5% versus 60.3%—at approximately 80% lower cost per task. GPT‑6 Luna (max) is able to exceed GPT‑5.6 Sol (medium) at one tenth of its cost.

In terms of availability, OpenAI says both new models will be rolling out throughout the day.

GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access GPT‑6 Luna in the desktop app. 

You can learn much more about the new models here.

Please welcome GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna to the GPT-6 universe.

title: Anthropic and OpenAI Drop New High-Efficiency Models
snippet: The new models prioritize faster speeds and lower prices.
fullText:
Both OpenAI and Anthropic dropped new models on Tuesday, each highlighting enhanced speed while being cheaper overall compared to predecessors. 

Anthropic said its new model, Opus 5.5, matches the capabilities of Fable 5.1 but cuts the cost by nearly 40% compared to Opus 5. OpenAI’s models, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, are follow-up models from the previous 5.6 versions that were released back in July of this year, but are hot on the heels of ChatGPT Astra, which was released in early September. 

Below, we’ll show you all the details for the new models.

GPT-6 Sol and Luna 

The latest models from OpenAI are designed to make the power of GPT-6 Astra more accessible at lower budgets while providing higher usage limits for business and developer workflows. Since GPT-6 Sol and Luna are trained with similar methods as Astra, you’ll still reap the benefits you’d get with the more powerful model, including enhancements in coding and computer use, though OpenAI still says that GPT-6 Astra is the “world’s best model” for computer use. 

OpenAI said the latest ChatGPT models also put a big focus on factuality, or the usefulness of the answers it provides you after your prompt. OpenAI says its latest models make less than half the mistakes of their predecessors. 

Efficiency in speed and cost is the game here, and while OpenAI shared some impressive benchmarks for the new models, it likely won’t translate too much for the everyday user.

Both GPT-6 Sol and Luna are rolling out to ChatGPT Work and Codex, but free users and lower-tiered subscribers will still get access to GPT-6 Luna.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Claude Opus 5.5

Anthropic is touting that its latest model, Claude Opus 5.5, is its strongest-performing model in terms of alignment to date. Alignment in AI is the idea of having the model match the intention, values and rules from a human perspective. AI agents made headlines this summer by going out of their way to complete tasks by any means necessary. Anthropic saying that its latest model is the strongest in alignment doesn’t mean it’s perfect, and we’ll have to wait and see how it performs with its agentic capabilities.  

Anthropic also says Opus 5.5 comes with the same safeguards it developed with its most capable models. That means it may revert to an older, less advanced model for certain cybersecurity or scientific tasks.

Anthropic’s latest model requires less compute than its predecessor, Opus 5. In its own testing at default settings, the newest model costs 40% less on typical workloads. On top of that, Anthropic is increasing 5-hour usage limits on Pro, Max and Team plans. 

The new models should be able to communicate more naturally than their predecessors as well. Anthropic said writing and instruction have been more easy to follow in tests — something taken directly from user feedback.

Meta has spent the last two weeks telling anyone who’ll listen how secure its new Muse personal AI agent is. The company boasted about its dedicated Secure VM, a monitoring system called Sentinel, and bug bounty rewards of up to $300,000. Mark Zuckerberg himself even publicly stated the agent is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”

Then Patrick Wardle, macOS security researcher and friend of Security Bite, found a 0-day vulnerability in the Muse app on Mac that made the last 24 hours particularly not-a-musing (what Wardle comically named the finding).

If you’re struggling to keep track of the AI news cycle too, Muse is Meta’s new personal AI agent, which launched on Mac earlier this month. It’s less of a chatbot and more meant to do things for you across your apps and accounts, like sending emails, filling out forms, handling payments, and making purchases on your behalf. BUT to do all of that, you have to hand it a lot of access (mistake #1).

Wardle found that any app or Terminal command running locally on a Mac can change a number of undocumented Muse settings, no special macOS permissions needed. One of those settings, endo_voyager_dictation_endpoint, controls where your dictated prompts get sent.

An attacker can point that setting away from Meta’s servers, and toward one in their control. So the next time a user dictates a prompt, it goes to the attacker instead. From there, they can grab the token that authenticates your Muse account and use it to control the agent.

Screenshot via Patrick Wardle

Wardle showed this off with a few proof-of-concept attacks, including writing malicious files to the Mac and even taking photos with the camera. He also used a hijacked Muse account to pull the location of a linked iPhone.

To be clear, this doesn’t give a remote attacker instant access to every Mac running Muse. It’s a local attack. They first need a way to run code on your machine. But all it takes is a ClickFix-style attack to trick a Mac user into pasting a command into Terminal. And voilà.

I recorded an entire Security Bite Podcast episode on why ClickFix is the #1 way to get malware on Macs today.

Wardle also pointed out that Apple already offers on-device dictation to developers. If Meta had used it, this bug wouldn’t exist. Instead, Muse sends your voice to its servers to be processed (mistake #2).

The good news is that Meta has reportedly pushed a fix. If you use Muse on Mac, update ASAP.

title: Qualcomm Wants You to Let AI Agents Spend Your Money
snippet: Someday, AI agents will buy you anything you want — or what they think you want. Here’s how the chipmaker for top Android phones thinks that may work.
fullText:
The keynote kicking off Snapdragon Summit 2026 in Maui had the latest forecast for how AI agents will organize our lives through the phones in our pockets. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon spent some time walking viewers through how the agents will buy things for them, preparing for the day when AI will have access to our bank accounts or credit cards — and why that’s a good idea.

For years, Qualcomm has pitched a future where AI agents on your devices know your habits and preferences well enough to make informed decisions on your behalf. Eventually, this will include the capability to spend your money on things such as necessities, gifts and travel. The question is how agents will decide whether or not to pull the trigger on a purchase — and how much input you’ll have on what decisions they make.

Nobody’s figured this out yet, and might not for some time. The fear is that an AI agent would run off with your bank account numbers, clear out your savings and run up your credit card. But at this year’s summit, Qualcomm suggested how this might actually work, wherein agents would repeatedly check in before they spend your money.

	

			

“When an agent is acting as a proxy of you, you need to trust the agent, and you need to trust the device, especially for something like shopping,” Amon said on the keynote stage. 

Naturally, the CEO was pitching a method with his company’s technology at the center, but it was at least sensitive to the uncertainties people likely have about an AI buying things for them. He said that the company is developing technologies to protect personal information and provide a secure device environment.

“The agent needs to authenticate and operate and keep you in control,” Amon said. 

Around 45 minutes into the keynote, Qualcomm presented a way this might go. A woman wearing smart glasses walks past a store when the AI agent suggests that, in the past, she’d bought sunscreen and lip balm from that location — did she want to buy more? She okays the purchase, and the AI agent says she can go pick up her goods. She then proceeds down the street and asks the agent about getting a laptop, and the AI agent guides her to a shop where she can view several on display. She decides on one, but the agent asks her to confirm the purchase first.

I didn’t love everything about the demo, as her purchase was followed by a reminder about her credit card rewards points in what felt like a nagging ad, but that’s probably a personal preference I could tell my AI agent to avoid. From a consumer standpoint, the most important part was waiting for confirmation before making a purchase — especially when plunking down several thousand dollars for a pricey computer. 

Qualcomm featured a prerecorded video from MasterCard’s CEO reassuring viewers that the financial institution could ensure trust in AI agent payments made on behalf of consumers.David Lumb/CNET

Qualcomm is treading carefully here, and shrewdly brought in execs from a trusted purchasing platform to reassure viewers that the financial institutions they already trust will be part of the process. MasterCard CEO Michael Miebach, speaking in a prerecorded video, reaffirmed that people will only use processes they trust to keep their payments and data secure; on stage, Amon was joined by MasterCard senior fellow Raja Rajamannar, who spoke plainly about the implicit trust that an AI agent would work on their behalf — which will come from a brand they already trust, such as Mastercard. 

This is all self-promotional, but they’re speaking to relatable uncertainty. Over the past decades, people have become a lot more comfortable with online shopping, with the initial skepticism thawing as the process became trustworthy. AI agents further separate people from the act of handing over their hard-earned cash, so another bridge of trust must be built. Envisioning the next process with clear moments when an AI agent will stop to ask people before making purchases on their behalf is reassuring amid uncertainty about a new way to spend money.

A screenshot from the Snapdragon Summit 2026 keynote showing an AI agent reminding a person that they could get 5% off a purchase today.David Lumb/CNET

The long road to letting AI agents pay for you

The technology at the center of the process is the AI agent itself, which runs on your smartphone. In a media roundtable discussion after the keynote, Chris Patrick, Qualcomm SVP and general manager of handsets, emphasized that building consumer trust in the process would take time.

Dino Bekis, Qualcomm SVP of premium mobile and AI business unit, reasoned that the answer will include a lot of reassurance by making financial institutions a central part of the process. Just as institutions now take care of fraudulent charges or other mistaken purchases when your credit card is stolen, there will need to be reassurances if AI agents wrongly buy something that consumers didn’t approve.

“Financials [will need to] do some level of backstop to say, hey, you as a consumer, if this happens, there’s going to be some level of consumer protection for you, right?” Bekis said.

Later on, I wandered into a demo room where Qualcomm showed off concepts revealed on stage, one of which simulated how an AI agent would buy something for you. The demonstration followed three clear steps: identifying something to buy, the AI agent finding a relevant suggestion to ask about buying it and the actual purchase process. 

Francisco Cheng, Qualcomm senior director of product marketing, had a demo walking through how an AI agent would make purchases.David Lumb/CNET

Qualcomm’s Francisco Cheng, senior director of product marketing, wearing off-the-shelf TCL Rayneo smart glasses, looked at a poster for an experience (aptly, a Hawaiian volcano). The AI agent recommended a particular tour of a nearby volcano, and when Cheng confirmed that he’d like to buy it, the agent — running on a connected smartphone — handed the transaction over to Mastercard to make the purchase. Any disputes could, in theory, be resolved by the credit card company.

“I think if there’s a level of mistrust by letting an agent handle things through and through, at least Mastercard can step in as a trusted payment provider to handle that piece of it,” Cheng said.  

People will still surely be gunshy about the whole process, Cheng admitted, but at least there are trusted brands handling every step of the process. And that’s exactly how it went with online shopping. 

“I’m old enough to remember when I was skeptical about making online payments, about doing banking transactions online. I was comfortable writing a check to somebody,” Cheng said. “But today, I wouldn’t even think twice about paying bills online. It’s a learning process.”

title: As Android XR nears, smart glasses are only getting more popular despite Meta backlash
snippet: There’s been a near-constant stream of backlash against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in recent months, but that hasn’t stopped people from buying them, as a new report reveals that shipments have grown by over 250%. more…
fullText:
There’s been a near-constant stream of backlash against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in recent months, but that hasn’t stopped people from buying them, as a new report reveals that shipments have grown by over 250%.

Counterpoint Research reports that, in the first half of 2026, shipments of AI smart glasses have risen by 263% year-over-year. Meta holds 94% of the market with its Ray-Ban and self-branded glasses models, with Xiaomi and Alibaba each holding 1% in second and third place, respectively. 

Display-less glasses make up 96% of all shipments, with brands such as Rokid, Meta, Even Realities, and others splitting the remaining 4% of shipments for glasses that have a built-in display, but that segment is up nearly 450% year-over-year. Notably, no figures have been shared on just how many glasses units are being shipped/sold.

North America is the biggest market for display-less smart glasses, taking up 50% of the global market share, while China is a slightly bigger market for glasses with a display. 

	

Meanwhile, competition is brewing as Samsung & Google prepare to launch the first Android XR-powered smart glasses. The initial release will be display-less, focusing on integrations with Android and Gemini for interactions through your smartphone, Wear OS watch, and audio to accomplish tasks and interact with the glasses.

title: Meta’s new Muse AI agent app overtakes ChatGPT as top iPhone app
snippet: Meta’s new Muse AI agent app has taken the top spot on the free iPhone charts for the U.S. App Store, displacing OpenAI’s ChatGPT from the first place. more…
fullText:
Meta’s new Muse AI agent app has taken the top spot on the free iPhone charts for the U.S. App Store, displacing OpenAI’s ChatGPT from the first place.

Muse by Meta only launched this month, although the app has been around for a couple of weeks. This means new installs are picking up and boosting the app on the App Store’s top charts beyond the day-one launch.

Just yesterday, Meta expanded Muse app availability to include the Mac. The desktop version of the app doesn’t contribute to the App Store ranking, however, as it’s downloadable from the web.

While OpenAI and Anthropic have pushed agentic tools through their existing apps, Meta and SpaceXAI have taken a different route recently.

Muse by Meta and SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot both treat agentic workflows like casual messaging interfaces, giving agents more personified character roles and appearances.

Meanwhile, Apple has just publicly launched Siri AI, which includes integration with iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch with Apple’s new OS 27 software releases. The new Siri includes a dedicated chat app as well, and it’s capable of taking system actions like editing photos and using on-screen content for context.

title: AI coding platform Bitrig adds iPhone Duo support with interactive 3D simulator
snippet: Following the release of Xcode 27.1 beta 1 last week, Bitrig has added support for building and testing iPhone Duo apps, complete with an interactive 3D simulator that lets developers fold, tilt, rotate, and position the device however they want. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following the release of Xcode 27.1 beta 1 last week, Bitrig has added support for building and testing iPhone Duo apps, complete with an interactive 3D simulator that lets developers fold, tilt, rotate, and position the device however they want. Here are the details.

Bitrig now lets users play around with a 3D iPhone Duo

Bitrig first launched as a simple vibe-coding app that allowed users to turn text or voice prompts into native SwiftUI apps that ran directly inside the main Bitrig app on their iPhone.

Since then, the platform has expanded considerably, adding a Mac app that gives users access to the full Xcode toolchain, an integrated iPhone simulator, on-device testing, and the ability to export projects to Xcode or distribute apps through TestFlight and the App Store.

Last Friday, following Apple’s release of Xcode 27.1 beta 1 with support for building and testing apps for the iPhone Duo, Bitrig rolled out its own iPhone Duo support with a more interactive take on the simulator.

Here’s Kyle Macomber, Co-founder and CEO of Bitrig, on what the update enables:

Try every pose. iPhone Duo can sit on a table like a laptop or stand by your bedside like a tent. Open, closed, or partially folded, in portrait or landscape, your app needs to adapt. Bitrig’s 3D simulator lets you grab it, fold it, turn it, and watch your app respond.

Respond to the hinge. Drive interactions and effects as the phone folds using onHingeChange, like Apple’s unfold effect that makes the outer display feel like a window into the inner one. Read the hinge data live as you open and close it in the built-in simulator.

Build hands-free experiences. Use ArrangementView to lay out media on the upper half and controls on the lower half when iPhone Duo is sitting on table. Support landscape orientation so people can use your app on the outer display when it’s standing on its edges.

Use both displays at once. Add a CameraCaptureAccessory to the outer display and give the person facing the camera something useful to see.

MAcomber also notes that “Bitrig helps you manage multiple versions of Xcode, so you can start preparing your app for iPhone Duo with the beta and switch back to Xcode 27 to build and release updates.”

title: Apple has reportedly ‘postponed’ AI pendant product
snippet: Apple launched arguably its first AI wearables last week with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, which are gaining new ‘Audio Intelligence’ features alongside Siri AI. But today a Bloomberg report says a different AI product—the rumored wearable pendant—has been put on hold. more…
fullText:
Apple launched arguably its first AI wearables last week with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, which are gaining new ‘Audio Intelligence’ features alongside Siri AI. But today a Bloomberg report says a different AI product—the rumored wearable pendant—has been put on hold.

Apple’s AI wearable plans no longer include a pendant, at least for now

The AI era has sparked a lot of software innovations, but so far that hasn’t really translated into brand new categories of products.

There have been attempts, to be sure, such as the failed Humane Ai Pin. And Meta has had some success with its AI smart glasses, but that market is still fairly niche.

Rumors indicate Apple has several AI-centric wearables in the works. And last week it arguably shipped the first ones: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

But according to a report by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the company has also been working on a wearable pendant equipped with a camera. For now though, it sounds like progress on that product has stalled.

Apple has also been working on an AI pendant with a camera, though that project has been postponed. The device was conceived as something users could wear as a necklace, attach to clothing or place elsewhere on the body, gathering visual data for processing by the new Siri AI assistant.

Gurman reported earlier this year that the pendant would “serve as an always-on camera for the [iPhone] that also includes a microphone for Siri input.”

Now it seems Apple has decided to put the project on hold. Instead, it is focused on infusing the Apple Watch with AI, alongside new AirPods with cameras and smart glasses coming in 2027.

It’s unknown how AI will factor in, but Gurman also says Apple is exploring a new health-focused wearable without a screen that could better compete with WHOOP.

title: Discord’s age-verification era is upon us, despite community backlash
snippet: According to Discord, 90% of users will not have to verify their age.
fullText:
Starting Wednesday, Discord, the community messaging platform, will roll out age-verification measures to all users.

The rollout comes after the company initially delayed its age-verification plans in February due to backlash from users concerned that biometric scans and ID checks could jeopardize their privacy. Those concerns weren’t unfounded; last year, a third-party vendor that works with Discord was breached, potentially exposing the data of 70,000 users’ data, including government ID photos and selfies used for identity verification.

“Age assurance draws strong opinions and skepticism, especially when it involves sharing biometric information or a form of ID,” Discord CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy wrote in a blog post, published Tuesday. “At the same time, age assurance laws are expanding, and since my last post we’ve had to launch age assurance in other regions, including in Brazil and in Texas.”

However, Vishnevskiy says more than 90% of Discord users won’t have to verify their age. He explains that Discord will instead use existing account data to detect “signals,” like account tenure (how long an account has existed), device and activity data, and other usage patterns, to determine whether a user belongs in the adult, teen, or unconfirmed age group.

Discord says that it doesn’t estimate users’ ages based on message content, profile data, or demographic attributes.

“The way a typical 15-year-old uses Discord (including how many communities they’re a part of and how they interact with others) looks different in aggregate from how a typical 30-year-old uses Discord,” the company wrote in a separate, technical blog post, also published Tuesday. “Our [machine learning] model has learned these patterns to predict whether a given account likely belongs to an adult or a teen.”

This doesn’t mean that Discord is collecting new user data. It’s standard for social media companies to retain this kind of data on their customers, even though it might feel unsettling to see it spelled out so overtly.

Because local laws have required Discord to use age-assurance technology in certain regions due to local law, the company was able to train its model on reliably confirmed data linking user behavior to age.

If Discord is not confident that a user is an adult, that user can still prove their age without a biometric or ID scan. They can appeal by sharing a credit card or age group data from their Apple App Store or Google Play Store account.

For confirmed adults, nothing about the platform will change. Teens accounts, however, will automatically be blocked from accessing age-restricted servers or channels. Message requests from people who aren’t their friends will go to a separate message requests inbox, and teens will get alerts when accepting friend requests from someone they don’t share mutual friends with.

As governments around the world continue passing age-verification requirements in an attempt to protect children online, experts warn that these age checks can create a host of new privacy and security issues. That leaves platforms like Discord with a difficult choice: comply or risk sanctions.

title: Google ‘AI contribution pilot’ tests paying websites when they’re used in AI results
snippet: Through a new “AI contribution pilot,” Google is testing directly paying websites and publishers when their content is used to flesh out AI Overviews and other AI results. more…
fullText:
Through a new “AI contribution pilot,” Google is testing directly paying websites and publishers when their content is used to flesh out AI Overviews and other AI results.

As AI has taken over the Google Search experience, the impact on the web hasn’t been quiet. Google insists that AI isn’t to blame, but repeated reports clearly show otherwise. Google’s AI, along with the myriad of other AI services being used, just aren’t distributing traffic to the web in the way traditional search used to, and everyone is suffering as a result.

The solution isn’t an easy one, but one idea that pops up pretty frequently is pushing AI providers, including Google, to directly pay websites and publishers when their content is used as the source of an AI result, replacing the revenue lost by direct traffic.

Google is now testing exactly that.

	

Digiday detailed this week a new “AI contribution pilot” Google is running with “at least dozens of publishers.” The program is apparently mainly being tested with “small and mid-sized” publishers and is covering a scope “far beyond news publishers.” A panel in Google Search Console includes a payout figure, with Google’s page explaining:

Accumulate earnings when your content contributes significantly to AI-generated responses in participating products.

Digiday spoke with publishers in the pilot who said that information provided is “basic,” with one explaining that they’re “hopeful that the fact that [Google is] setting a precedent for exploring paying publishers directly for content through this is meaningful.”

A support page hidden from the general public includes more details on the pilot program:

Google had teased these efforts publicly in June 2026, explaining that the company was “piloting a new way to partner with websites whose content meaningfully contributes to the freshness and factuality of generative AI responses.” In late 2025, Google announced a “commercial partnership program” with several major news publishers, but this latest effort is far wider in scope.
