title: LinkedIn adds new tools to fight fake profiles and bogus work histories
snippet: LinkedIn is rolling out new verification tools that let members vouch for colleagues’ work experience and give companies more control over accounts that falsely claim to employ them.
fullText:
AI has made it significantly easier for people to create fake accounts and identities to engage in online manipulation and scams. On Wednesday, LinkedIn announced a new set of tools to combat the problem while helping people and companies better control their presence on the platform. 

The company says it will now let members vouch for each other’s experience and give businesses new controls to manage who associates with their brand, among other changes.

The new features arrive at a time when impersonation has become an internet-wide problem, not one limited to LinkedIn. However, on a network where your professional persona includes your work experience, past job titles, certifications, university degrees, and more, being able to verify you are who you say you are is even more critical. 

Such claims can lead to career opportunities and advancement, prospects that those fudging or lying on their resumes haven’t earned.

“The backdrop for all this is that faking credibility has never been cheaper or easier than it is today; and conversely, showcasing credibility has never mattered more,” LinkedIn VP of Product, Oscar Rodriguez, told TechCrunch in an interview. 

To date, LinkedIn’s existing verification tools have been used to verify 115 million users and over 700,000 companies on the platform, he noted. 

“We’ve been invested in [verification] because we believe that authenticity will be the single most valuable currency on the internet,” Rodriguez added. 

Image Credits:LinkedIn

For starters, LinkedIn will now allow members to vouch for their colleagues and classmates, past or present. This feature is not the same as an endorsement, where you can recommend the member to others, but is more of a way to vouch that someone has the experience they claim on their profile. 

In short, it’s a way of saying, “Yes, I worked with this person during this time,” not whether you enjoyed it. 

The addition includes a number of built-in protections against abuse. For instance, the person doing the vouching must already have a verified profile, and they must have been connected to the person for at least a year. They also have to have a secure account that uses two-factor authentication to decrease the risk of hackers gaining access to their account to perform these vouches. 

Image Credits:LinkedIn

Another feature, which had previously been piloted with recruiters and execs, will allow companies to remove accounts that falsely claim employment from appearing on their page and in the search results associated with their page. 

To use this feature, page admins will be able to visit the account that belongs to the person falsely claiming employment at the company, then manually remove them. LinkedIn is also testing a setting that will allow page admins to require that any member account going forward that tries to associate with the page complete some sort of workplace verification, like a verification done through their work email address. 

When pages remove the member profile from their page, it won’t change the member’s LinkedIn profile — that’s something members themselves will retain control over. However, there will no longer be a clickable link to that company’s page from their profile, and their work experience won’t display as verified. 

Image Credits:LinkedIn

“We hope that this provides signals and context to members to make decisions,” Rodriguez said. He also clarified this feature focuses on full-time employees, not contractors or field workers, though they will have other means of claiming their rightful association with the company that employs them.  

Plus, LinkedIn will expand its partnerships with more companies to allow members to showcase their verified identities beyond LinkedIn. On this front, Truecaller and PeerSpot will join existing partners like Adobe and UserTesting in this effort. For instance, Truecaller members can add their LinkedIn verified identity so it displays to the recipient when they place a call. 

Overall, the new features expand LinkedIn’s push to invest in verification, something that it believes benefits members directly. “We have seen how, for members that are verified, they derive a lot of benefits from all of this,” said Rodriguez. “They receive, on average, 50% more post views than non-verified profiles, and they get 90% more impressions as well,” he noted.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max still uses a Qualcomm modem in the US, teardown confirms
snippet: TechInsights has published one of the first in-depth iPhone 18 Pro Max teardowns. Most notably, the teardown confirms that the iPhone 18 Pro Max sold in the United States still uses a Qualcomm modem. more…
fullText:
TechInsights has published one of the first in-depth iPhone 18 Pro Max teardowns. Most notably, the teardown confirms that the iPhone 18 Pro Max sold in the United States still uses a Qualcomm modem.

On its tech specs website, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro uses the Apple C2 cellular modem. In every country other than the United States, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max also uses its C2 cellular modem.

The company, however, doesn’t specify which modem the U.S. variant of the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses. Speculation suggested the iPhone 18 Pro Max used a Qualcomm modem, and this teardown confirms it.

According to the TechInsights teardown, the iPhone 18 Pro Max variant sold in the United States uses the Qualcomm Snapdragon X80 modem. This is the same modem used worldwide in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.

So, to recap, here’s how Apple’s transition to its own in-house modem technology has played out in the United States specifically:

iPhone 16 / 16 Plus / 16 Pro / 16 Pro Max: Qualcomm Snapdragon X71

iPhone 16e: Apple C1

iPhone 17 / 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max: Qualcomm X80

iPhone Air: Apple C1X

iPhone 17e: Apple C1X

iPhone 18 Pro: Apple C2

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Qualcomm X80

iPhone Duo: Apple C2

Apple touts that the C2 brings “AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability.” In comparison to the C1X, Apple says the C2 delivers “meaningfully faster uploads when compared to C1X while consuming 15 percent less energy.” The C2 modem also supports mmWave 5G, unlike the C1 and C1X.

It seems clear to me that Apple has caught up to Qualcomm, now that the C2 supports mmWave 5G connectivity. Apple’s C-series modems have always been more power-efficient than Qualcomm’s (which, I’d wager, is something most people care more about than raw download and upload speeds).

Apple hasn’t said why the iPhone 18 Pro Max still uses a Qualcomm modem. The likely explanation, though, is that the decision is purely contractual, and Apple will ditch Qualcomm once and for all as soon as it can.

title: Stolen passwords are exposing America’s water providers to hackers
snippet: Researchers say another looming threat hangs over some of America's most important critical infrastructure.
fullText:
New security research has found that well over a thousand U.S. water and wastewater providers are exposed to hacks due to malware that’s capable of stealing their employees’ passwords and active logged-in sessions.

The findings by cybersecurity defense firm SpyCloud underscore how water providers and other critical infrastructure can be compromised with relative ease amidst a wave of hacks targeting the water supplies of dozens of communities across the United States.

While password-stealing malware is not new, the research highlights how stolen passwords offer hackers an easy route to break into an organization’s network without using AI tools.

SpyCloud said it built a database of more than 66,000 public-facing systems that are registered with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, amounting to 10,000 organizations. The company found password-stealing malware had swiped passwords and credentials from 1,787 organizations, or nearly two in 10 providers they checked. The firm noted at least 250 organizations had credentials exposed that appeared to allow access to their operational networks and remote-access systems, which control the physical pumps and water flows.

The analysis covered an unnamed metering tech provider, which had a device on its network that was infected with password-stealing malware. The malware stole reams of credentials, including passwords for 167 U.S. utility companies that rely on the metering tech provider.

SpyCloud Chief Investigations Officer Jason Lancaster said in the post that this single breach handed criminals the keys to access “a hundred otherwise unrelated organizations.”

Password-stealing malware, also known as infostealers, allows hackers to steal a person’s stored passwords as well as the session tokens that are used to keep them logged in. These session tokens can allow a hacker to log in as if they were the legitimate user, and can often bypass multi-factor authentication systems. Hackers regularly trade stolen credentials in order to obtain passwords or session tokens for accessing specific organizations.

This research comes weeks after a spate of hacks targeting water providers around the United States, which the U.S. government has privately tied to Iran-backed hackers. SpyCloud said it found no evidence that those Iran-linked hacks relied on stolen passwords. In those cases, the signs point to security weaknesses, such as manufacturer-set default passwords, in the mechanical switches and physical controllers used by critical infrastructure, SpyCloud said, echoing earlier findings from U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA. 

Rather, the researchers note that stolen passwords are a major source of access to “whoever wants to buy or find it,” in parallel to the known security risks with critical infrastructure tech. Lancaster said that the water-sector “has to hold both stories at once.”

Apple’s new texture and grain controls for stylizing photos will be more limited on older phones than initially expected.

A confusingly worded press release from Apple indicated that the new features, announced alongside the iPhone 18 and 18 Pro earlier this month, would be “available” on older devices like the iPhone 16 and iPhone Air that “support the latest generation of Photographic Styles.”

But it turns out that “available” didn’t mean that older iPhone models would have full access to those new features.

Making texture adjustments to enhance or smooth a subject’s skin and adding film grain will only be an option when those phones are being used to edit shots taken with the latest iPhone models. Apple has since updated recent press releases to state that those controls will only be available for “photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and the Ultra Wide, Main, and Center Stage cameras on iPhone Duo.”

The original version of a September 11th release, which was issued the day before the latest versions of the iPhone and Apple Watches became available for preorder, is still available in its original form on other websites with a footnote specifying that the new “texture and grain controls in Photographic Styles will be available on iOS 27 on iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.”

This limited compatibility was corroborated by a Reddit user who was able to make adjustments to texture and grain on their iPhone 16 Pro Max, but only while editing sample photos taken on an iPhone 18 Pro by photographer Austin Mann who made them available for download on his website. I also had access to those new Photographic Styles controls when editing Mann’s samples on my own iPhone 16 Pro running iOS 27, but they were not available on photos I captured myself.

The Verge has reached out to Apple for clarification on how the feature is supposed to work on older phones but did not immediately get a response.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Eight Sleep announced the next version of its “intelligent sleep system” designed to regulate the temperature of your bed in response to tracked health and sleep metrics like breathing and heart rate. The company calls its new Pod 6 system its “most significant hardware launch to date,” and it’s centered around a redesigned cooling hub that’s now small enough to hide beneath most beds. The new system is cheaper than Eight Sleep’s Pod 5 that launched in 2025, but is still by no means cheap.

The Pod 6 is now available through Eight Sleep’s online store. The Standard version ranges in price from $2,699 for a full-size mattress to $2,999 for king and California king sizes. But for the first time Eight Sleep will offer a smaller Solo option for single sleepers with a cover that fits half of any size mattress for $1,999. The Pod 6 system is still compatible with Eight Sleep’s optional accessories, like its $999 cooling pillow cover, and there’s a mandatory subscription that ranges in price from $199 to $399 per year for two sleepers.

Eight Sleep claims the Pod 6’s control hub was “rebuilt from scratch, with the electrical, mechanical, and software systems re-engineered together,” resulting in it being half the size of previous versions while delivering more performance. The hub, which circulates temperature-controlled water through the mattress cover to help deliver a better night’s sleep, is now 20 percent faster at making temperature adjustments.

The Pod 6’s health and sleep tracking capabilities have also been upgraded with additional sensors. While last year’s Pod 5 featured two biometric sensors integrated into the mattress cover, the Pod 6 increases that to 18 sensors. It can track health metrics like heart rate, heart rate variability, breathing rate, sleep stages, and detect snoring for two individuals whether they’re sleeping next to each other or on opposite sides of the bed. The system is also smart enough to distinguish between adults, children, and pets. All of that collected data is used by Eight Sleep’s AI-powered Autopilot feature (which is what the subscription covers) to make automatic temperature adjustments throughout the night to maintain comfort without any manual input.

title: Motorola Signature 27 is a proper flagship with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Alongside Qualcomm’s latest announcements, Motorola has officially shown off the Motorola Signature 27, a true flagship offering that’s set to launch before the end of this year. more…
fullText:
Alongside Qualcomm’s latest announcements, Motorola has officially shown off the Motorola Signature 27, a true flagship offering that’s set to launch before the end of this year.

Building on the Motorola Signature, a pseudo-flagship that launched earlier this year, the Signature 27 adopts a new naming scheme (based on the coming year), a wild-looking design, and a proper flagship spec sheet.

While its predecessor was based on Qualcomm’s step-down Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, the Motorola Signature 27 uses the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, a new chip that’s just as powerful as its mouthful of a name. It’s a big deal on Motorola’s part, as the brand hasn’t used any flagship chipsets in quite a while. The Motorola Razr Ultra (2025) used the Snapdragon 8 Elite, but its successor didn’t upgrade, and other devices in the company’s lineup, including the $1,900 Razr Fold, haven’t gone beyond the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5.

Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

Motorola says to expect stronger on-device AI features with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, as well as “responsive” gaming, faster download speeds over various networks, and improvements to the camera, too. There’s an “ArcticMesh” cooling system that combines a 40% larger vapor chamber with liquid metal, copper mesh, and “diamond-infused thermal gel.”

	

Motorola Signature 27 is promised 7 years of Android OS and security updates and has quite the look with its quad-camera setup on the back. That includes a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 main sensor and 200MP periscope telephoto lens. The other two haven’t been confirmed just yet. The design itself brings back some Droid Razr vibes from over a decade ago. 

Signature 27 will come in “Coal Smoke” with a “Tactical Weave” finish, or “Capulet Green” with a “brushed textile-inspired finish.”

A firm release date hasn’t been announced, nor has Motorola spilled the beans on exact launch markets. The company says it will debut “worldwide” in 2026, and also confirmed a launch in North America in the “coming months.”

Right before all of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo craziness, I was lucky enough to attend my first IFA in Berlin. For those unaware, IFA is the CES of Europe. There are thousands of brands and companies, ranging from tiny start-ups to giant juggernauts. They all have one goal: to show off what they have been creating to the 100,000s of visitors that attend. 

I saw everything from flying cars to mini robots to 200-inch transparent displays, and while all of those products are awesome for a quick demo and to show off, I was not there for them. I wanted to see the tech that is actually about to come out, not the tech that maybe one day will see the light of day. So here are my favorite products from IFA, with a bit of an Apple twist, of course!

Lexar Muse

I have been, and still am, a huge Lexar SSD user. They make reliable, fast, and compact SSDs that I use in my workflow daily. I currently use their SL500 and their magnetic SSD with my iPhone 18 Pro Max. They are versatile and work in my Apple ecosystem because they have the speed to support that ProRes Raw footage. But their newest announcement, the Lexar Muse, blew me away. I am a huge fan of thin tech, so when I saw that this SSD is just 3.8mm at its thickest point, I was all over this. 

Just 3.8mm at its thickest point, tapering to 1mm at the edges

Up to 1,050 MB/s read and 1,000 MB/s write

512GB and 1TB

Proprietary PogoPin connection with a SnapLink Magnetic Cable

Supports direct external Apple ProRes 4K recording at up to 120 fps on compatible iPhones

The main thing I was curious about was how you can fit a USB-C port on such a small device. The answer is: you can’t. So what they created was a pogo pin connection. You just slap the SSD to the rear of your iPhone with the Magsafe accessory, and it comes with a USB-C to pogo pin cable. It’s sized perfectly to be long enough to not be in the way and reach the back of the Lexar Muse. I thought this was a genius use case. 

As of now, given how thin it is and the current storage crisis, Lexar will be offering these in 512 MB and 1 TB sizes, with higher capacities in the future. It is set to release in October of 2026!

Belkin LilyPad

Now this one is more of a guilty pleasure than anything else. I recently took my 5-year-old to her first movie theater experience, and we went to see the new Toy Story 5. If you have yet to see it, the main villain in the movie is an iPad-like tablet called LilyPad that eventually turns good and becomes an ally of all the main characters. So when I saw the actual LilyPad character at the Belkin booth, I had to stop by. Turns out that this is part of a much bigger collaboration that brings all the characters to a bunch of Apple-friendly accessories. But the show stopper here is the LilyPad case because it turns your iPad into that character. 

Officially licensed Disney Pixar Toy Story 5 Lilypad character design

Compatbile with iPad 10th generation (10.9-inch) and iPad 11th generation (11-inch A16)

Shock-absorbing EVA foam construction with rounded edges and 4-foot drop protection

Integrated handle with an easy-grip texture designed for smaller hands

Built-in kickstand

Exclusive and licensed Lilypad wallpapers included

But as I mentioned, this is an entire collection. Belkin has also made a Toy Story iPhone case, a MagSafe power bank, and a larger power bank that resembles one of the toys from the movie. I think these were tastefully done, as they still provide plenty of functionality and look fun for any Toy Story fan. All of these products are available today and range from $35 to $55, with the LilyPad being $49. 

Wokyis i5 Docking Station

I am a huge fan of Wokyis products. They have found a way to bring a nostalgic look and feel to products that bring modern functionality. I recently reviewed their G5 and G7 docks for the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. But those are built to physically be attached to the Mac. So what Wokyis did was bring all that function and nostalgia to a standalone dock that works with any computer. You get all the pro-level ports you needed and a display as well!

Built-in 5-inch HD IPS display with a 1280 × 720 resolution

Four dedicated shortcut keys and a rotary control knob for frequently used functions

Built-in M.2 NVMe SSD enclosure for additional storage

Four USB-A ports, one USB-C data port, SD and microSD 4.0 card readers, HDMI input, and a 3.5mm headphone jack with up to 10Gbps speeds

Supports up to 65W pass-through charging for compatible laptops

As I mentioned, I love products with a bit of character. I want my accessories to be conversation starters, making people wonder and say, “What is that?” That is exactly what Wokyis products do, and the i5 Docking Station is no different. It brings some awesome personality at a time when most docks are completely sterile. 

The i5 Docking Station is available on Amazon today for $153. If you need a new docking station that adds a bit of fun and tactility without sacrificing function, this is a good one to grab.

iPhone cases 

You can just imagine the thousands, if not millions, of different iPhone case brands that were at IFA. From every shape, material, size, and function, there is a case for any type of person. The thing about cases is that they are completely subjective. There is no real good or bad, or right or wrong. You either like it or you don’t. But there are two cases I wanted to highlight because they are different from some of the others I have seen. 

First is the Xtrem Inno cases. I reviewed their first gen last year and loved it because I had never seen another case do this. The Xtrem Inno case has a Color E ink display that allows you to change what it shows on the rear of the case to anything you want. 

Circular, customizable rear display with four-color reproduction and a resolution of 212 PPI

The display requires no separate charging and retains its image without continuously consuming power

Supports MagSafe wireless charging and magnetic accessories

On the surface, it looks like a nicely designed case, but when you pair it with their app, you can send an image via NFC to the case. It’s so cool how it all works. The amazing thing is that since it uses NFC and E-ink, that means no batteries, Bluetooth, or wired connections are needed. The phone uses a tiny bit of power to send the image via NFC, and since it’s E-ink, once it’s on, it stays on without persistent power.

The case is available today on Amazon for $75 and comes in a ton of new colors. If you need a fun new case, this is the way to go. 

Moft Movas Coffee Edition

Last year, Moft introduced a new ultra-thin case for the iPhone 17 lineup. The base itself was great for anyone who wanted a super-slim, minimal case. They ended up bringing it back for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, but the interesting part is the material they went with, more than anything else. At a time when sustainability is high on the agenda, Moft decided to use a new coffee-based bio-leather for this case, and it’s awesome. The best part is that it gives off a bit of a coffee aroma. So this is the case for all my coffee lovers out there! Outside of that, you get all the trimmings you want out of a rthin case.

Built-in magnets for MagSafe

Weighs just 28g and is ultra-thin

Reinforced TPU corners provide basic drop protection, while the open-sided frame design preserves the natural feel of the iPhone

Available in a Coffee Brown and Sapphire Blue color combination

Again, the innovation here is the choice of material. I had never heard of or seen this choice of using coffee grounds to create a sort of bio-leather. They are also using this material for their famous moft wallet stand. They are all available on Amazon today for $49. 

Final thoughts

Again, there was a ton, and I mean a ton of things that came from IFA that I am excited about. I was able to see things like ultra-fast supercars, the Xiaomi iPhone Duo clone before it was announced, and so much more. But these were just a few of the things that caught my eye and made sense to me in our Apple-focused world.

title: Review: Beats 360 are the closest Apple headphones to AirPods Max, with one caveat
snippet: The highly anticipated Beats 360 are now available for purchase. After being teased prior to the World Cup, Apple’s latest pair of Beats headphones are now on the market. I got an early hands-on with them, and they’re quite an interesting product offering that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using – though they have one key flaw: no wired connectivity, which will bother some more than others. more…
fullText:
The highly anticipated Beats 360 are now available for purchase. After being teased prior to the World Cup, Apple’s latest pair of Beats headphones are now on the market. I got an early hands-on with them, and they’re quite an interesting product offering that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using – though they have one key flaw: no wired connectivity, which will bother some more than others.

Product overview

First things first, the Beats 360 come in at $349.99. At that price, they’re leaning towards the high end of the market, though they still fall well below the AirPods Max at $549. Alongside this launch, the existing Beats Studio Pro are being permanently reduced to a new price of $299.99. Of course, you can find them much cheaper at retailers: they currently run $169.95 on Amazon.

If you’ve been following Beats launches, you’ll know that they sometimes use Apple H1 or H2 chips, and sometimes they use custom Beats silicon. The Beats 360 do use Beats silicon, however there’s one key upgrade here: they now finally support automatic device switching with your Apple Account, Hey Siri support, as well as proper Find My integration. If you’re an Apple fan who’s been eyeing Beats as a more affordable version of AirPods Max, the Beats 360 are closer than ever to providing a true Apple experience. I was certainly pleased when I learned this.

There is one loss compared to most high-end headphones: there’s no automatic pausing when you take them off your head. You learn to live with it, though it takes some time to get used to.

Compared to Beats Studio Pro, the Beats 360 get 12dB louder, and offer 1.75x more active noise cancellation. They also support Adaptive EQ in iOS 27, and are the first Beats headphones to be IPX4 sweat and water resistant. Both offer spatial audio with dynamic head tracking, and the Beats 360 last around 8 hours longer than Beats Studio Pro with ANC turned on.

Beats 360 come in four colors: Cloud, Sky, Black, and Pink. I’ve personally been trying out the Sky’s, but they’re all pretty elegant colors.

Customization

The headlining feature of Beats 360 is their customizable design. You can easily swap out the ear cushions and head cushion for different color options. The ear cushions also have two variants, UltraPlush and Performance Knit. The former will be more comfortable for everyday wear, whereas the latter is better for working out.

Each set of cushions is available for $49.99, though there’s a launch promo while supplies last where you can pick them up for just $9.99. This is an incredible promo for those who want to customize their headphones based on their outfit, or to match their mood. I’d personally take advantage of it.

Customization is really the name of the game with Beats 360. With the four base color options, as well as eight additional cushion options, there are 32 total ways you can mix up your Beats 360. If you mix headband cushions from the earcups, there are up to 256 different options.

You can truly make these headphones yours – which is quite fun. Another advantage to this is the fact that when your ear cushions wear down, you can easily swap them out instead of calling the headphones a loss.

Plethora of Beats 360 color combos
My personal Beats 360 color combo

9to5Mac’s Take

The Beats 360 are good headphones for most Apple enthusiasts. If you’re looking to switch away from your AirPods Max to something lighter and more comfortable, I’d say these fit those criteria pretty well, though you’re taking a hit on sound quality. I’d also highly recommend picking up an UltraPlush cushion kit, as I personally find the fabric ones a bit uncomfortable for casual use. With the launch promo for cushion kits, there isn’t much reason not to.

As someone who primarily used AirPods Pro 3 prior to testing out the Beats 360, I’ve actually found myself to much prefer the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is solid, transparency didn’t disappoint, and the fact that they fold down flat didn’t make them too much of a hurdle to fit in my everyday backpack. Of course, earbuds will simply be more convenient for many scenarios, but I found myself missing these headphones when I was away from home (as I couldn’t wear them outdoors during review), which I’ve never really thought for any pair of over-ears in the past.

Frankly, the only major complaint I have with the Beats 360 is that they don’t support wired connectivity. There’s no headphone jack, and USB-C seemingly doesn’t support it either. This is a little bit of an inconvenience if you’re looking to use them in an environment that doesn’t play super nicely with Bluetooth, such as an airplane or with a game console.

Regardless of that, I truly adore what Beats has done with the customizable design. These have been some of my favorite headphones I’ve tested out, even compared to AirPods Max, which I could never get comfortable with because of their weight. Beats 360 have no comfort issues whatsoever, so long as I use the UltraPlush cushions.

Pricing & availability

Beats 360 are launching at $349.99, with deliveries and in-store availability beginning September 24th. You can order them on Amazon and at Apple.com.

The limited-time $9.99 cushion kit promo is available in the US, Canada, the UK, France, China, Australia, and South Korea. It’s valid through October 31st, while supplies last.

title: iPhone users running iOS 27 can no longer downgrade to iOS 26
snippet: Apple today stopped signing iOS 26.6.2, which means iPhone users can no longer downgrade to non-iOS 27 system versions. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Apple today stopped signing iOS 26.6.2, which means iPhone users can no longer downgrade to non-iOS 27 system versions. Here’s why.

Apple no longer signing iOS 26.6.2 installs

When a user tries to install a version of iOS on their iPhone, part of the process involves checking with Apple’s servers to make sure that version is still authorized for installation. This is what’s referred to as signing, and it works for both upgrading or downgrading to any iOS version.

Because iOS updates often patch known security vulnerabilities, Apple keeps a rather short list of signed iOS versions. This prevents users from installing or downgrading to older versions that may contain flaws that could be exploited by attackers.

Today, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple stopped signing iOS 26.6.2. This means that users running iOS 27 can no longer downgrade to iOS 26.6.2, essentially closing the window on official downgrades to iOS 26.

Apple is no longer signing iOS 26.6.2, this means you can't downgrade to iOS 26 anymore from iOS 27

— Aaron (@aaronp613) September 21, 2026

It is worth noting that although Apple released iOS 26.7 last week, the company currently doesn’t officially offer a restore image for it, unlike iPadOS 26.7.

In practice, this means that iPhone users who are still running an earlier version of iOS 26 can install iOS 26.7 as an over-the-air update, but those already on iOS 27 cannot officially use it to downgrade.

fullText:
Following WhatsApp’s initial limited rollout of emoji reactions on the Apple Watch, the app is now rolling out support for the full set of emojis available on watchOS. Here are the details.

WhatsApp expands watchOS emoji reactions

Late last year, WhatsApp launched a full-featured Apple Watch app, with support for call notifications, voice messages, chat history, and emoji reactions.

The launch was largely good news for Apple Watch users, especially since WhatsApp’s presence on watchOS had previously been very limited, relying almost entirely on system notifications to read and reply to messages.

Still, emoji reactions came with one notable limitation: users could only choose from six preset emojis. Reacting with anything else required reaching for an iPhone.

Now, as reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is rolling out support for the full set of emojis available on watchOS. The site notes that tapping and holding a message still reveals the six default reactions, but users can now open a larger picker with recently used options and the full system emoji library split into categories.

Image: WABetaInfo

From WABetaInfo:

WhatsApp organizes emojis into 8 categories: Smileys, Nature, Food, Activity, Travel, Objects, Symbols, and Flags. Users can scroll through these to find the emoji they want to use as a reaction. They can tap any emoji category to expand the list. It is also possible to choose a recent emoji from the top of the list.

The site notes that although the feature is now officially rolling out, it may still take a few weeks to reach everyone, as WhatsApp is known for its gradual rollouts.

title: What do you actually use a laptop for, and would Googlebook be able to do it? [Poll]
snippet: Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced. more…
fullText:
Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced.

Our initial coverage of Googlebook is live, with Abner, Jordan, and Damien all walking away with a good first impression of Google’s efforts.

Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]

Yet, I’m unconvinced thus far. I’ve yet to get my hands on a Googlebook and, as someone sitting mostly in the same boat as you, our readers, I’m yet to be sold on this new platform. I simply don’t understand why it exists, even more so why Google seems to think it will succeed.

Google’s entire pitch around why you should buy a Googlebook more or less boils down to smartphone integration – specifically Android integration. Googlebook takes existing tools from ChromeOS and supercharges them, giving you the ability to mirror apps, sync files, and do a whole lot more between your Android phone and your laptop. And it does sound pretty good! As someone who currently juggles a MacBook with various Android phones, there are integrations I wish existed; instant hotspot and proper Quick Share support (AirDrop works, but tends to be wildly slow) are at the top of that list. 

	

Googlebook is delivering the MacBook + iPhone experience, just for Android users. That’s the pitch.

Where it falls flat for me is in the apparent functionality. At its core, Googlebook is Android, just with a desktop experience built on top. The core stuff is there – desktop-class Chrome browser, customizable desktop, keyboard shorts, the lot. But the app ecosystem is built around Android apps, web apps, and Linux apps. The same core as ChromeOS, just with a different priority and with better performance on the Android app side, as Abner and Damien both noticed.

That’s where I’m struggling to get on board.

There’s plenty you can do on a Googlebook, sure, just like there was plenty you could do on a Chromebook. But you’re still making a trade-off. Google pointed out that around 70% of things people do on a laptop are done through their browser (Chrome, of course). And, yeah, I’d say that’s about how much I do in the browser on my Windows desktop or my MacBook. That other 30%, though, is the “make or break” that eventually broke me on ChromeOS. For me, it largely came down to Adobe’s apps which, as it stands, still aren’t replicated on Googlebook. On Google’s own website, the company touts a Googlebook’s ability to use Photoshop and Lightroom, but that’s just with the mobile apps – not the full-featured apps you can use on you know, most other laptops. 

Google knows people use these apps; otherwise, it wouldn’t take up a place on this site in the first place – the same goes for games, where Google advertises tons of popular titles like Forza Horizon, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, and more, with only two of the games shown running natively and the rest delivered via GeForce Now.

The market has pretty clearly spoken in this regard. Chromebooks are out. There are remarkably few consumer-focused Chromebooks on the market today and, especially on the high end, it seems like hardly anyone is buying them – Google itself gave up on first-party Chromebooks over five years ago. 

To me at least, the reasoning seems obvious. When Chromebooks hit their stride, the market was full of compromises everywhere. There was no one perfect answer. But that’s changed in recent years. Apple’s M-series chips ushered in a new era for the MacBook which, in turn, influenced some major improvements across Windows laptops. Fast forward to today and there’s no lack of powerful, battery-efficient, thin & light laptop options and, despite “RAMageddon” ruining the price side of things, there’s been a huge push for more affordable machines in the wave of MacBook Neo and its clones – and those are very popular too. Giving up access to a full collection of full-featured apps for a lightweight operating system that gets roughly the same battery life for roughly the same price is a no-brainer, which means that Chromebooks are relegated to a niche. In enterprise/schools, for more affordable machines, for low-end hardware, ChromeOS still makes a lot of sense, but it’s a tough sell basically anywhere else, so you might be able to see why I’m so confused by Googlebook.

Googlebook’s pitch, again, isn’t bad, but does it make sense in today’s market? Who’s buying a laptop that’s inherently (and inarguably) restricted in what it can do, especially at a time when laptops are wildly inflated in price in the first place due to component shortages? 

This is the part where I turn the floor over to you.

Do you think Googlebook has stuck the landing? Has Google’s pitch resonated with you? 

	

Even more so, what are you using a laptop for in the first place? That’s perhaps the most important question around this. As mentioned, I’m personally using my laptop mostly in Chrome, with non-Chrome apps including the likes of Photoshop/Lightroom/Premiere, Spotify, Slack, and a handful of assorted other tools. There are a few of those I can replace – Spotify’s tablet interface should be a treat on a laptop, though I think Slack will be awful given how the Android app lacks any semblance of big-screen optimizations (on Android, as they’re immediately giving Apple something better), so maybe the Linux app will be better.

That’s just me. There are infinite ways people use their laptop. So, looking at what you do today, do you think a Googlebook can do it all? Vote in the poll below, then leave a comment.

title: Android Auto rolls out game support, no longer in beta
snippet: Google is graduating game support on Android Auto from a limited beta to broad availability, allowing developers to bring games to your car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is graduating game support on Android Auto from a limited beta to broad availability, allowing developers to bring games to your car’s display.

First available last year, games in Android Auto and Android Automotive bring a bit of interactive fun to the car’s display. While there’s no direct integration with things like the car’s steering wheel, it’s a nice way to add something fun to the biggest screen in your vehicle for times you might be stuck on the side of the road, waiting on an EV to charge, or other times where the vehicle is not moving.

Around 30 games are available on Android Auto today, but that list is likely to start expanding soon.

Google announced this week that game support on Android Auto is no longer in beta, meaning that game support is open to all developers rather than requiring specific approval from Google. 

	

Google says:

Bringing your game to cars lets you reach users in their vehicles during natural downtime, such as while waiting at a charging station or for a curbside order pickup. Today’s milestone means that we’re opening up access so developers can now publish games to the open testing and production tracks on Google Play. In this post, we’ll cover how to adapt your existing Android game for the car screen, focusing on key technical requirements and publishing criteria.

Android games must declare support for Android Auto and Android Automotive OS – they’re separate declarations behind the scenes, and there are many more games that support Android Automotive without Android Auto support as it stands today.

Games on Android Auto should be able to adapt to different display sizes and need to recognize when a vehicle is parked or not – games can only be played if the vehicle is parked. Games can also support controllers on Android Auto and Android Automotive. 

Google’s full documentation on what developers need to do can be found here.

title: Nothing Phone (4a) and (3a) Pro can now join Android 17 open beta
snippet: Right on schedule, Nothing is releasing Nothing OS 5.0 open beta for the Phone (4a), Phone (3a Pro, and Phone (3a) before the company’s official Android 17 release next month. more…
fullText:
Right on schedule, Nothing is releasing Nothing OS 5.0 open beta for the Phone (4a), Phone (3a Pro, and Phone (3a) before the company’s official Android 17 release next month.

The Android 17 package contains a few changes for Nothing phones. It was first released as a beta update for the Nothing Phone (3) with visual changes to the system UI and animations across the board. The update also includes new widgets, updates to the camera app, and a dedicated Glyph app for light controls and features.

You can check out the full changelog in our previous coverage. At its core, it brings Nothing’s devices up to date with the latest version of Android. Of course, this company is known for creating its own spin on both hardware and software.

Right now, though, Nothing is actively rolling out Android 17 beta access to the Nothing Phone (4a), Phone (3a) Pro, and Phone (3a). The update leaves out the Phone (3a) Lite, which is expected to get access later in the year. Users with either of those devices should now be able to access the Nothing OS 5.0 open beta, which puts it on par with the Phone (3).

	

In terms of scheduling, Nothing is right on time. The company posted its release schedule when the first open beta rolled out, and it remains unchanged. The three devices announced today will be followed by the Phone (2a) and Phone (2a) Plus in October.

The same post also notes the Phone (4a) and Phone (3a) series will be pushed to the official Android 17 build in early November. The rollout is expected to end sometime in January 2027.

For the time being, Phone (4a) and (3a) series users should now be able to access Nothing OS 5.0 in its early stages.

snippet: Samsung appears to be delaying the rollout of its Android 17 update, at least slightly, with pushback in some regions. more…
fullText:
Samsung appears to be delaying the rollout of its Android 17 update, at least slightly, with pushback in some regions.

The launch of a stable One UI 9 rollout for Galaxy S26 was first announced last week, with the Android 17-based update landing first on Samsung’s current flagship before expanding to more devices. Samsung explicitly said the rollout was supposed to start on September 16, but it doesn’t appear to have shown up for anyone just yet. 

While the reason is unclear, SammyGuru spotted a sort of confirmation that Samsung has delayed its Android 17 in some capacity.

A press release around the One UI 9 rollout on Samsung’s Newsroom in Thailand noted a rollout date of September 21 originally, but was updated to say September 28, and now appears to have been updated again to remove a specific date altogether, only saying “September 2026” at this point.

	

This isn’t unprecedented; Samsung has had numerous major updates be delayed quietly at the last moment, but it’s certainly not the best start for One UI 9’s rollout. Hopefully, whatever issues are pushing Samsung’s schedule back can be fixed as soon as possible.

title: Adobe Premiere for Android launches for free with layered video editing, YouTube templates
snippet: Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere’s mobile version is now available on Android devices with layered video editing, templates, foldable optimization, and more. more…
fullText:
Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere’s mobile version is now available on Android devices with layered video editing, templates, foldable optimization, and more.

Adobe Premiere Pro is widely recognized as a powerful video editing suite on desktop machines, but Adobe’s last version for mobile devices vanished a while back. Now, Adobe Premiere is once again available on Android, delivering what appears to be a very capable video editor that promises to be a solution across all Android devices.

This is the same app that debuted on iPhone in late 2025, and it brings quite a few features with it.

Some of the key features include:

	

Enhance Audio: Reduce background noise, clean up voiceovers, etc

Multi-track timeline: Manage multiple videos, sound effects, music, etc

Templates: Custom-made templates to speed up editing

Effects: Transitions, creative assets, Adobe Stock integration

Export: Up to 4K editing + export

The app already has wide support of different Android devices and form factors, including optimization for foldable smartphones. There’s also a built-in voice recorder.

Adobe says that more features are coming, including support for Adobe Fonts in creating text overlays, the ability to transfer projects to Premiere Pro on desktop, “beat detection,” cropping, and more. 

The big deal here, though, is that Adobe Premiere for Android is free. You don’t need a Creative Cloud subscription, you don’t need to sit through ads, and there are no watermarks either. Adobe says you can purchase upgrades for “additional generative credits and storage,” but that’s optional.

Requirements for Adobe Premiere on Android include 5GB of RAM or more and Android 13 or newer.

title: Noble Carbon will show how it’s making EV charger installs painless at TechCrunch Disrupt
snippet: Noble Carbon has developed a smart circuit breaker that allows households to electrify without the pain of a main panel upgrade.
fullText:
Plenty of people want to buy electric vehicles, but not everyone is prepared to shell out for an upgrade to their home’s electrical service just to add an EV charger. The worry is reasonable. One study found that upgrading things like electrical panels (that box in the garage or basement that delivers power throughout a home) can more than double charger installation costs.

Rather than rip out the old panel, Noble Carbon has developed circuit breakers that can take the headache out of installing an EV charger, or a heat pump or an induction stove for that matter.

The Pittsfield, Massachusetts, startup is one of 200 startups in this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield, a pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in October in which 20 finalists will present on the main stage.

Noble Carbon’s breakers can adjust how much electricity they deliver to an EV charger in real time, allowing the chargers to squeeze into otherwise at-capacity panels.

Electrical panels in people’s homes are typically designed to handle absolute peak usage, something that might happen only “a handful of hours per year,” Spencer Fields, Noble Carbon’s head of marketing, told TechCrunch. 

For example, if someone is hosting family for a holiday, they might find themselves simultaneously using the water heater, air conditioning, oven, and several TVs, all while every light is on in the house. The rest of the time, the electrical panel has room to spare.

Jared Lebos explains how Noble Carbon’s breakers work to Massachusetts Gov. Maura HealeyImage Credits:Josh Qualls, Director of Photography, Office of Governor Healey

In that scenario, Noble Carbon’s smart breakers would turn down the power flowing to the devices they control, essentially guaranteeing that the entire house doesn’t draw more power than the panel can provide. 

“In order to avoid a main panel upgrade, you really only need control on your three to six largest loads [the biggest power-drawing appliances],” Fields said.

Co-founder and CEO Jared Lebos was inspired to create the product after experiencing rolling blackouts in his home country of South Africa. He worked with Andrew Crane, the company’s co-founder and CTO, to turn it into reality.

The result is a breaker that fits into existing slots in a home’s electrical panel and, according to the company, takes less than five minutes to install. Some of the startup’s employees have been testing the breakers in their homes for more than a year, and the product is now undergoing evaluation for UL certification, a widely recognized electrical safety standard.

Noble Carbon currently is partnering with the utility Eversource to install its breakers in up to 200 multifamily units in Massachusetts.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. 

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. fullText:

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

OpenAI has hired three former Patreon execs to anchor its product strategy for creators. After starting the creator subscription platform 13 years ago, co-founder and technology chief Sam Yam announced on X that he’s joining OpenAI to lead Creator Product. He’s also bringing Patreon’s former product head Drew Rowny and engineering head Shannon Ma with him on the new venture, both of whom stepped down in the past few weeks.

“We’re going to build together with Creators at OpenAI and share early access to a new set of tools that I think will be critically valuable to Creators and their communities,” Yam said in his announcement. “Pay attention to OpenAI DevDay next week! I’m becoming active today (and experimenting with some innovative early tools here!)”

Dev Day is set for Tuesday, September 29th, though Yam also links to a post from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that teases another big announcement will be coming this week.

Bringing key Patreon execs on board suggests that OpenAI is exploring ways to enter the creator monetization business, given Patreon effectively set the blueprint for the creator-subscription economy as we know it. Losing Yam is another blow for Patreon, which recently announced an extensive update roadmap to overhaul its user features after laying off 20 percent of its staff in January.

title: Tim Cook meets EU chief Ursula von der Leyen as bloc pushes new child safety rules
snippet: Keeping with Apple’s pledge that Tim Cook would remain involved in Apple’s government relations around the world after stepping down as CEO, he met this week with Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Keeping with Apple’s pledge that Tim Cook would remain involved in Apple’s government relations around the world after stepping down as CEO, he met this week with Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission. Here are the details.

Tim Cook discusses EU Kids Act with EC President

When Apple announced that Tim Cook would step down as CEO on September 1, the company said:

As executive chairman, Cook will assist with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world.

Since taking up the job of executive chairman, Cook has kept with this promise.

Just days ago, Bloomberg reported that Cook would attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping, which is scheduled for Thursday evening, September 24.

The report came just a few days before Cook posted on X that he had welcomed Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at Apple Park.

It was great to welcome @AlboMP to Apple Park this morning to talk about the incredible work of our teams and our longstanding commitment to Australia. I was grateful to share some of our newest innovations, including strong and intuitive controls to help keep kids safe online. pic.twitter.com/EQKmIkP3uC

— Tim Cook (@tim_cook) September 19, 2026

After the meeting, Albanese reportedly shared that Cook described Australia’s social media restrictions for children as “world-leading.”

Yesterday, Cook continued his string of encounters with world leaders, sitting down with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

In a post on X, von der Leyen said the two discussed the EU Kids Act and “agreed on the importance of privacy, safety and security for children.”

Good discussion with @tim_cook in the margins of UNGA.

 We discussed the EU Kids Act, and agreed on the importance of privacy, safety and security for children.

Tech companies innovate and bring huge benefits to our society.

They must do so in a way that empowers parents and… pic.twitter.com/Ygv2x8893X

— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) September 21, 2026

This proposed legislation is set to restrict social media access for minors across the EU and require platforms to provide stronger protections for young users.

The meeting happened in Manhattan, where world leaders are currently gathering for the United Nations General Assembly.

It is currently unclear whether Cook will meet or has already met with other world leaders, but if he has, there is a good chance we’ll hear about it from the officials themselves sooner rather than later.

title: iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster in these 30+ ways
snippet: iOS 27 is now available to everyone, and one of the big changes is that it makes your iPhone a lot faster. In fact, Apple has outlined more than 30 ways in which your iPhone will be faster after you update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is now available to everyone, and one of the big changes is that it makes your iPhone a lot faster. In fact, Apple has outlined more than 30 ways in which your iPhone will be faster after you update.

How iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster

When Apple announced iOS 27 in June, the company emphasized that it combed through its software to make it faster and more reliable. “Improvements across platforms push key system capabilities forward so everyday tasks feel faster, smoother, and more enjoyable,” Apple said.

Here are more than 30 ways iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster:

Faster loading of new captures in Photos (up to 70% faster)

Faster to open full-screen view from Photos widget

Faster rendering of Collections tab in Photos

Faster to start uploading to iCloud Photos

Faster Camera launch in Low Power Mode

Faster to add recent camera captures in Messages

Faster start page content loading in Safari

Faster web application performance in Safari

Faster handling of JavaScript in Safari

Faster message loading in Mail

Faster HomeKit accessory pairing

Faster smart home accessory updates

Faster Now Playing view loading in Music

Faster Apple Music playback start

Faster board previews in Freeform

Faster data updates in the Health app

Faster workout start in the Workout app

Faster Lock Screen switching

Faster app launches (up to 30% faster)

Faster AirPlay connections to Apple TV and HomePod

Faster network file browsing

Faster and more reliable NFC reading

Faster Voice Control response in iOS

Faster entry and exit from Assistive Access and Guided Access modes

Faster PDF saving

Faster Text Recognition in photos and documents

Faster Rapid Return to Service

Faster loading of emoji and sticker keyboards

Faster shortcuts and actions indexing in Spotlight

Faster multilingual text processing for handwriting in multiple languages

Faster AirDrop transfers (up to 80% faster)

Faster AirDrop recipient discovery

Faster access to shared content on iCloud.com

9to5Mac’s Take

iOS 27 is compatible with iPhone models dating back to the iPhone 11. In fact, Apple even says that some of its performance metrics are based on testing it conducted with the iPhone 11 lineup.

For example, Apple says that apps launch up to 30% faster with iOS 27. This statistic is based on testing Apple performed on the iPhone 11 Pro Max, comparing app launch speeds between one model running iOS 26.4.2 and another running iOS 27.

All of this is very impressive — especially for people using “older” iPhone models. Apple has fixed enough bugs and made such a jump in performance that I think most iPhone users will notice a big improvement when they install iOS 27 later this year. It’s particularly impressive when you consider Apple made all these improvements to performance while simultaneously implementing a ground-up revamp of Siri.

title: Brazil court tells Apple to add age checks for casino app purchases
snippet: A Brazilian court has ordered Apple to tighten age controls around a casino-style app on the App Store, including requiring age verification before making in-app purchases. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A Brazilian court has ordered Apple to tighten age controls around a casino-style app on the App Store, including requiring age verification before making in-app purchases. Here are the details.

Apple ordered to strengthen App Store age checks in Brazil

As reported by Tilt, São Paulo’s Court of Justice has granted an emergency injunction requiring Apple to restrict minors’ access to the “Casino Roulette: Roulettist” app.

The decision came after four child and adolescent rights groups filed a civil lawsuit in July, alleging that minors were able to download casino-style games from the App Store and purchase virtual chips with real money, despite Casino Roulette: Roulettist carrying an 18+ age rating.

In the decision, the court gave Apple five days to block new downloads of Casino Roulette: Roulettist by users registered as minors, and require “age verification for purchases of virtual chips with real money to continue playing or expand the in-app experience,” says Tilt.

Beyond the specific app, the decision also bars Apple from allowing new apps with equivalent casino-style mechanics onto the App Store without effective age controls.

Tilt says the court also told Apple to preserve all records related to the app and present a technical report detailing the measures it has taken. The court also established a daily fine of R$100,000 (roughly $19,500) for noncompliance.

Tilt reached out to Apple for comment, but the company had not responded at the time of publication.

title: Apple challenges OpenAI’s forensic analysis in trade secrets case, seeks access to hardware R&D
snippet: Apple has asked the court overseeing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to let its own experts review forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to parts of OpenAI’s hardware R&D. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has asked the court overseeing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to let its own experts review forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to parts of OpenAI’s hardware R&D. Here are the details.

A bit of background

In early July, Apple sued former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, accusing them of trade secret misappropriation.

The lawsuit involves former Apple employees who allegedly took confidential information with them when they left the company. Apple also alleges that former employee Chang Liu coached another Apple employee on materials to review ahead of an OpenAI interview, while Tang Tan directed Apple job candidates to bring hardware components and other materials to interviews.

More recently, Apple said an initial forensic inspection of a MacBook used by Liu after leaving the company showed that he had used a confidential Apple circuit schematic to run a simulation while working at OpenAI. Apple also said the MacBook pointed to Liu’s use of a Mac mini, which the company has since sought access to as part of the case.

OpenAI has since refuted Apple’s allegations, arguing that this situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making,” since the company’s allegedly lax offboarding and security practices made it easier for employees to unintentionally retain access to confidential information after leaving.

One of the many points of contention in the case is Apple’s request for expedited discovery, which OpenAI has opposed. Another is Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction that would restrict OpenAI’s use of Apple’s alleged trade secrets while the lawsuit proceeds, potentially affecting its ongoing hardware development.

Apple argues that it needs expedited access to certain evidence precisely because OpenAI is still developing its hardware product, meaning that any alleged use of Apple’s trade secrets could become further intertwined with that work and increasingly difficult to undo.

OpenAI, in turn, argues that Apple has not shown why a separate expedited discovery process is warranted, and says that Apple’s requests are too broad.

Due to this impasse, the court asked both sides to submit a joint filing laying out their respective positions on expedited discovery. That document, filed last Friday, has now been made public.

Apple wants access to forensic images, R&D material

In the joint filing, Apple asks the court to allow its own forensic experts to review the underlying forensic images that the defendants’ experts relied on to analyze Liu’s devices and determine whether he accessed or used Apple’s confidential information after leaving the company.

Apple says one of its forensic experts has already identified what it describes as “critical flaws” in that analysis, and argues that its experts need direct access to determine whether there were other problems with the defendants’ forensic analysis.

Here’s Apple:

Apple’s forensic expert has already uncovered several critical flaws in the analysis conducted by Defendants’ experts, including (1) failures to locate files on Mr. Liu’s Mac Mini that were demonstrably used and stored on that device and (2) incorrect conclusions that the presence of files with zero bytes or an empty kMDItemLastUsedDate field on the Mac Mini means those files were not accessed. […] Giving Apple’s experts direct access to these forensic images is critical to understanding what other errors Defendants’ experts may have committed.

OpenAI argues that Apple’s experts should not be given unrestricted access to the forensic images, proposing instead that a neutral forensic expert handle them under a jointly agreed protocol.

Apple argues that this would put it at a disadvantage, since the defendants’ own forensic experts have already had direct access to the same material.

In addition to the forensic material, Apple is seeking expedited access to documents related to OpenAI’s hardware development, including work on metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI previously argued that its metal finishes were developed independently, without using Apple confidential information, and that a simulation Liu ran using an Apple confidential file had nothing to do with its upcoming product.

Apple is now asking for the underlying development records so it can test those claims, which OpenAI says is just an attempt to “snoop on a competitor.”

Here’s Apple:

As Defendants have now put their development at issue, they must prove their assertions that they “developed their own standard metal finishes and colors” by producing supporting documents. Apple is not requesting “a complete technical record of OpenAI’s development of any technology,” as OpenAI asserts, but rather technology related to “metal finishes, power management, or battery functionality,” the technology that Defendants have put at issue in defending against Apple’s claims.

And here’s OpenAI:

This demand for a complete technical record of OpenAI’s development of any technology within Apple’s broad categories is overbroad and premature, and an apparent attempt to snoop on a competitor. Apple’s request is not even limited to OpenAI’s first product under development, which Apple expressed ostensible concern about […]—it encompasses any research and development. And it requires OpenAI to reveal its trade secrets before Apple has revealed its own (which are the subject of this lawsuit)—placing this request far beyond the scope of merits-based discovery, let alone “expedited” discovery.

The joint filing also touches on several other points of contention, including:

Apple’s broader request for forensic images from devices used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting “Alyssa” Peng, and another OpenAI employee that contain or previously contained what Apple defines as “Apple Originated Information;

Records related to Liu’s use of AI tools, after the defendants said a forensic investigation found no evidence that he used an Apple confidential file with platforms including ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;

Interview-related documents from OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group, including materials showing what the group actually uses during interviews and communications with departing Apple employees;

Interrogatories that OpenAI says could reach more than 400 former Apple employees now working at the company.

Apple is also seeking the full LINE conversations between Liu and Peng, which include exchanges in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about Apple work after he had left the company.

The defendants had already submitted excerpts from those conversations in opposing Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction, but Apple argues that it should be allowed to review the full exchanges rather than only the messages the defendants chose to submit.

title: iOS 27 adds convenient new iPhone feature you’ll use all the time
snippet: iOS 27 has arrived, with Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features as big highlights. But one of my favorite features is a convenient addition for quickly pasting items from your iPhone’s clipboard. Here’s how it works. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has arrived, with Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features as big highlights. But one of my favorite features is a convenient addition for quickly pasting items from your iPhone’s clipboard. Here’s how it works.

iOS 27 adds paste shortcut above keyboard for one-tap access to your clipboard

Every year Apple adds a bunch of new features to iOS, and this year that includes upgrades to Apple Wallet, Messages, CarPlay, and more.

Many new features might go easily overlooked by the average iPhone user.

But there’s one iOS 27 addition in particular that I suspect readers will find themselves using a lot.

After you copy text to your iPhone’s clipboard, or a link or photo, iOS 27 adds a paste shortcut above the keyboard when you open a new text field.

The idea is simple: if you copy something, then immediately switch to another app, or open some other text field, Apple knows there’s a very good chance you want to paste there.

So rather than requiring you to open the copy/paste menu and hit paste from there, the paste suggestion appears automatically above the keyboard—offering one-tap convenience.

You’ll even see a preview of what’s on the clipboard, right there in the top keyboard row. So if it’s text, you’ll know what that text is, and if it’s an image you’ll see a small thumbnail preview.

It’s the kind of feature that I never would have thought to ask for, but in using the iOS 27 beta over the summer it quickly proved very convenient in everyday use.

title: Spotify’s is giving you the keys to its recommendation algorithm with US launch of ‘Taste Profile’
snippet: Spotify is rolling out Taste Profile to Premium users in the U.S., letting listeners see how the streamer understands their tastes and use natural language to reshape their recommendations
fullText:
Spotify is giving listeners a new tool to shape the recommendations it delivers to their app’s Home feed. 

The music streaming giant on Wednesday began rolling out a feature called “Taste Profile” to its Premium subscribers in the U.S. that allows users to see, for the first time, how Spotify understands their taste across music and other audio. Users can request changes using natural language commands to fine-tune their recommendations, or make broader changes.

Powered by Spotify’s AI, Taste Profile was first unveiled in March at the SXSW conference in Austin by Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström. However, the feature was initially available in beta only to listeners based in New Zealand.

Now, the feature is arriving in Spotify’s largest market in terms of traffic and revenue, where it will be put to a larger test among listeners ages 18 and up.

In some ways, Taste Profile essentially gives you the keys to Spotify’s algorithm. It is how the streaming platform chooses what music and podcasts to suggest, including in its flagship Discover Weekly playlist, its Made for You recommendations, and the highly anticipated annual review known as Spotify Wrapped.

Image Credits:Spotify

Though Spotify’s algorithmic understanding of a listener’s habits is largely credited as the secret to its success, those recommendations don’t always reflect users’ evolving tastes. The platform often ends up recommending too-similar music when a user would rather branch out. 

Now, by editing their Taste Profile directly, Spotify users can request more variety or ask for more or less of a certain genre, artist, or overall vibe.

The feature could be used to remove recommendations based on music that users may regularly stream, but not necessarily care to see more of — for instance, sleep sounds played at night, or whatever music a teenager plays while in the car on their parent’s account.

Until now, Spotify has offered some options to remove music from your Taste Profile, but they only let you exclude certain tracks or playlists. More recently, the company added a much-requested toggle switch that would prevent kids’ music from impacting their parents’ recommendations.

Image Credits:Spotify

To access Taste Profiles on the mobile app, first tap on your profile pic, then scroll down and select Taste Profile. From here, you’ll be able to explore how Spotify currently understands your taste across music, podcasts, and audiobooks. Under “Tell us more,” you’ll then enter what you’d like to adjust and send the message.

After a few hours, your app’s Home Page will reflect a different set of suggestions. 

Spotify says the feature can be used when you want to explore a new genre or era, but aren’t sure where to start, or if you want to adjust the vibe of the music — like if you want more energizing tracks. You can also tell Spotify what sort of podcasts and audiobook you want to better shape those recommendations.

The feature is still in beta. The company didn’t offer a timeline as to when it would reach a wider audience.

title: RatHat Malware Can Hijack Your Android by Disguising Itself as a Legitimate App
snippet: The malware pretends to be a legitimate download for an app like Google Chrome.
fullText:
A new Android malware strain called RatHat is spreading through unofficial app sources and posing as legitimate downloads, including familiar apps like Google Chrome, to get installed on devices before most users realize what they’ve agreed to. Once it’s in, RatHat uses an AI component to automatically escalate to admin-level control, requiring no further action and giving attackers broad access to the device and everything on it. Here’s how the malware works and what Android users can do to avoid it.

RatHat was discovered by mobile security firm Zimperium, which notes that the program tricks people into downloading what appears to be a legitimate app, such as Google Chrome, via a fake web page that mimics the Google Play Store. Once opened, the app seemingly innocently asks for accessibility permissions, which it then uses to take over your entire device. 

RatHat uses the accessibility permissions users grant it to navigate your phone’s menu system and unlock Wireless Debugging, a legitimate developer tool commonly used in app testing, then grants itself ADB Shell permissions. This effectively grants the malware admin access to your device. Next, RatHat installs an AI-assisted agent that runs system commands to steal information and a proxy client that tunnels that stolen information back to the hacker. 

“That sort of infection chain isn’t necessarily more complex than, say, following a phishing email on Windows and saying yes when the program asks for administrator permissions,” Sav Wheeler, a research engineer for Malwarebytes, said in an email. “Escalation in the Android landscape often relies on granting apps additional permissions that the OS locks away by default to keep the devices secure.”

Per Zimperium, the malware can be traced to attackers in China and primarily targets apps like WeChat Pay and Alipay, which are as popular in China as Apple Pay and Venmo are in the US. Malwarebytes notes that other financial apps can also be targeted. So far, researchers have found 162 infected apps in the wild, which report back to a dozen servers run by attackers. 

What can this malware do?

The worrisome part is that the malware doesn’t do anything wonky the user would notice immediately, unlike with a ransomware attack. Instead, it bides its time, runs in the background, and captures information that appears on the screen, including usernames, passwords and two-factor authentication codes. 

It can also steal raw touch input from your touchscreen, allowing it to recreate PIN codes and pattern unlock codes. It can capture SMS messages, too, thereby intercepting security codes. There isn’t much that the app can’t steal if it wants to.

How can I find out if I have RatHat on my phone?

Most folks are likely to never run into RatHat. You have to sideload a malicious app to do this, and so sticking to the Play Store prevents this entire problem. 

A Google spokesperson confirmed to CNET in an email that Google Play Protect — which is enabled by default on Android devices with Google Play Services — already recognizes and protects against RatHat and that “no apps containing this malware are found on Google Play.”

The only other way to find it is to run an antivirus scan that detects the software. Malwarebytes on Google Play is a solid choice. It starts with a 14-day free trial of the pro version, which includes real-time protection. But even if you stick with the more limited free version after the 14-day trial, you can still run scans to catch malware. RatHat is publicly documented malware, so most other reputable Android antivirus apps should be able to find it as well.

The bad news is that RatHat is sneaky and difficult to quarantine. 

“Unfortunately, because of the behavior of the program itself — remasquerading as other apps, dynamically changing its behavior using the AI endpoint — static analysis and quarantining is not enough to remove the malware,” Wheeler said. 

In short, the only way to actually get rid of this malware is a complete factory reset of your device. This effectively removes the hidden secondary files the malware installs, which antivirus apps can’t deal with. Uninstalling the app doesn’t work because the malware retains its admin access through those hidden files, which then let it reinstall the app over and over again. 

How do I avoid RatHat?

This is also good news. RatHat’s infection method is complex and can be thwarted at multiple points during the process. First, you should never click a link from an SMS or email from a source you don’t know or trust. That stops almost all social engineering threats right out of the gate, including RatHat. Verify that you’re using the official Google Play app rather than a deceptive imitation website. Look at the top of the screen. If it has an address bar where you type URLs, it’s just a website disguised as an app. Real apps do not have address bars.

Also, note that preinstalled or existing versions of Chrome do not require reinstallation, so if you’re being asked to reinstall an app you know you have, think twice.

Denying accessibility permissions is the critical final line of defense against mobile malware. While downloading a malicious application is risky, the software remains largely powerless until you grant it advanced system privileges.

Wheeler says that SMS phishing is targeted to each specific user, so you won’t see the same phishing attempt as another person, and the tactics the app uses vary from region to region. Following standard antiphishing practices and not enabling accessibility permissions largely removes the threat of RatHat.
