A new Android malware strain called RatHat is spreading through unofficial app sources and posing as legitimate downloads, including familiar apps like Google Chrome, to get installed on devices before most users realize what they’ve agreed to. Once it’s in, RatHat uses an AI component to automatically escalate to admin-level control, requiring no further action and giving attackers broad access to the device and everything on it. Here’s how the malware works and what Android users can do to avoid it.

RatHat was discovered by mobile security firm Zimperium, which notes that the program tricks people into downloading what appears to be a legitimate app, such as Google Chrome, via a fake web page that mimics the Google Play Store. Once opened, the app seemingly innocently asks for accessibility permissions, which it then uses to take over your entire device.

title: Samsung’s battery upgrades for Galaxy S27 Ultra and Pro leak – is it enough?
snippet: A new leak reveals the battery sizes of Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro including some long overdue upgrades, but do you think it’s enough? more…
fullText:
A new leak reveals the battery sizes of Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro including some long overdue upgrades, but do you think it’s enough?

Following Samsung’s adoption of silicon-carbon battery tech on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series, it was inevitable that the Galaxy S27 series would jump on board. That’s not directly confirmed yet, but a regulatory leak (via GSMArena) offers a look at the rated capacities of Samsung’s new flagships.

These are rated capacities, with advertised capacity generally being a bit higher. As a comparison, the Galaxy S26 Ultra has an advertised battery capacity of 4,855 mAh, but an advertised capacity of 5,000 mAh. So, with that in mind:

Galaxy S27 Ultra: Rated 5,534 mAh | Advertised likely 5,700~ mAh 

Galaxy S27 Pro: Rated 5,087 mAh | Advertised likely 5,200~ mAh 

There’s no direct comparison for the Pro model, but the Galaxy S26 sits at 4,300 mAh at around the same physical size, so this is a huge jump. 

	

For Samsung’s full-size flagship, the Galaxy S27 Ultra is looking at a jump of around 700 mAh. It’s only 14%, but that’s a considerable step up after years of stagnation. Both devices are also listed with 60W wired charging.

But, in a world where silicon-carbon batteries are pushing Android flagships upwards of 6,000, 7,000, and even bigger batteries. The Oppo Find X10, for example, is rumored to pack in an 8,000 mAh battery when it debuts later this month. 

What do you think? Did Samsung do enough? Sound off in the comments below.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Homey’s new Device Updates feature shows what Matter was supposed to be all along
snippet: Firmware updates have been the weakest link for a decade with smart homes. Every sensor, light bulb, and smart lock in your house runs software that should be updated regularly. This is on top of even if they have software updates. Homey just announced a fix for a big piece of that, and the way it handles Matter devices is the part that Apple Home users should take note of. more…
fullText:
Firmware updates have been the weakest link for a decade with smart homes. Every sensor, light bulb, and smart lock in your house runs software that should be updated regularly. This is on top of even if they have software updates. Homey just announced a fix for a big piece of that, and the way it handles Matter devices is the part that Apple Home users should take note of.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Device updates from one place

Homey’s new Device Updates feature lets you update Matter, Z-Wave, and Zigbee devices directly from the Homey Mobile App or Web App. You can update a Matter light, install a security patch for a Z-Wave lock, or improve a Zigbee sensor’s reliability, all without ever opening a manufacturer’s app. You start the update, and Homey handles the rest, including delivery, progress tracking, and a notification when it’s done. Updates are available in More > Settings > Device Updates or in each device’s Maintenance settings.

For Z-Wave and Zigbee gear, updates are delivered via their respective Homey apps, so availability depends on the developer and manufacturer. The launch list of supported vendors is already pretty solid: IKEA, Aeotec, INNR, Niko, Inovelli, Zooz, frient, ThirdReality, EcoDim, HeatIt, Namron, amina, CTM Lyng, and Nous have added support, with more to come soon.

“Device firmware rarely gets updated because the process is cumbersome,” said Stefan Witkamp, CEO at Athom. “By handling device updates inside Homey, we make it practical for both users and developers. That makes the whole smart home more dependable.”

The Matter part is the real story

For Matter devices, Homey doesn’t rely on manufacturer apps at all, and manufacturers don’t need to update their Homey app for it to work. Homey checks the Connectivity Standards Alliance’s Distributed Compliance Ledger for available Matter firmware updates. The DCL provides the firmware version, download URL, file size, checksum, and applicability information. Homey then retrieves the firmware from the manufacturer-provided URL and delivers it to the device using Matter’s standardized OTA update mechanism.

The DCL is basically a trusted public registry for Matter products, run by the same organization that certifies them and is behind the Matter standard itself. Manufacturers publish firmware update metadata to the Matter Distributed Compliance Ledger, allowing Homey to discover and grab the available updates.

This means that the update path for Matter devices isn’t tied to any one company’s app or cloud service. It’s part of the actual Matter standard itself, verified by the certification body, and any Matter controller could implement it.

If you don’t see an update you expect, it’s usually because the device’s Homey app doesn’t offer it yet, or the manufacturer hasn’t published one. Device Updates is available on Homey Cloud, Homey Pro (2023 through 2026), Homey Pro mini, and Homey Self-Hosted Server, and requires v13.2.0 or later of the Homey Mobile App.

Eve devices now work with Homey, thanks to Matter

Speaking of Matter doing what it promised, there’s a second piece of Homey news worth covering. With Homey Pro and Homey Pro mini acting as Matter Controllers and Thread Border Routers, Matter-enabled Eve devices now work with Homey. That covers favorites I’ve written about plenty in this column: Eve Energy, Eve Door & Window, Eve Motion, Eve Thermo, Eve Weather, Eve MotionBlinds, and more.

Eve has always been one of the most trusted and privacy-focused brands in the smart home (with deep Apple Home integration), with no cloud service, no registration, and no tracking. If you’re running Eve gear in Apple Home today, nothing changes. What’s changed is that the same Thread and Matter foundation that made Eve great in Apple Home now makes it portable across other platforms, and that flexibility is exactly the point of the Matter standard. It’s a protocol vs a platform.

Wrap up

For years, the smart home industry has promised interoperability and delivered walled gardens with extra steps. Simply working with the big 3-4 major platforms isn’t enough. This Homey news is what the long-term benefits of Matter are proving to bring: firmware updates going through the standard body itself.

Matter has taken plenty of criticism for moving slowly, but features like this are why it matters.

Apple is opening a new live music venue in Battersea Power Station, London. The new location is called Apple Music Hall, and even has its own website where fans can sign up to get alerted when the first tickets are available.

title: AT&T seemingly has no plans to support Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature
snippet: Apple last week launched a new iPhone Handoff feature, which lets you use a single phone number across two iPhones. The number intelligently moves between each iPhone based on whichever one you pickup. iPhone Handoff requires support from cellular carriers, and it sounds like AT&T isn’t interested in adopting the feature. more…
fullText:
Apple last week launched a new iPhone Handoff feature, which lets you use a single phone number across two iPhones. The number intelligently moves between each iPhone based on whichever one you pickup.

iPhone Handoff requires support from cellular carriers, and it sounds like AT&T isn’t interested in adopting the feature.

Will AT&T support iPhone Handoff? 

As reported by CNET, AT&T seemingly has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. According to the report:

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

This will be upsetting news AT&T subscribers. The carrier’s emphasis on “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” seemingly indicates it doesn’t have a complete grasp on how iPhone Handoff works, and why it’s significantly more seamless than manually moving an eSIM back and forth between two iPhone models.

I’ve been using iPhone Handoff for the last week as I’ve been testing the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, and it really does feel like magic. As Apple promised, my number instantly switches to whichever iPhone I pick up.

It is a bummer that T-Mobile is charging $5 per month for iPhone Handoff, though it’s not necessarily surprising. It’s still significantly cheaper than having a second cellular plan altogether.

As of right now, T-Mobile is the only carrier in the United States to support iPhone Handoff. Apple says that Verizon will add support by the end of the year, “with more carriers to follow.” Outside the United States, Telekom Germany is a launch partner for the feature. Apple says EE will add support by the end of the year.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff yet? Is it a feature you’ll use on a regular basis? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Apple working on Whoop-style screenless fitness tracker, per report
snippet: Apple is developing a screenless health and fitness tracker to compete with Whoop, according to a new report from Bloomberg. The company is reportedly “developing prototypes,” but has yet to decide whether to ultimately release the product. more…
fullText:
Apple is developing a screenless health and fitness tracker to compete with Whoop, according to a new report from Bloomberg. The company is reportedly “developing prototypes,” but has yet to decide whether to ultimately release the product.

The prototypes being developed inside Apple reportedly have a “thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module.” The project is currently in the “technology investigation” phase, and Bloomberg says the product won’t be released before 2028 — if Apple decides to release it at all.

The project is said to have support from top Apple executives, including Eddy Cue and Tim Cook. Cue took charge of Apple’s health team last October, following the departure of Jeff Williams.

Cue has pushed Apple’s health team to adopt features from the newer rivals, whose products offer simpler interfaces focused squarely on fitness and health tracking. The Apple Watch serves a broader range of purposes.

Products like Whoop and Oura Ring are popular among people who want to track their health and fitness without wearing a smartwatch. As Reuters reports, Oura is prepping for an IPO and recently revealed that it sold 3.6 million Oura Rings in the 12 months ending June 30. Revenue grew 74% to $1.21 billion for the nine months ending June 30.

Apple is still the dominant player in the smartwatch market specifically, though. The Apple Watch also offers a far wider array of features than health and fitness-focused wearables like Oura and Whoop.

Bloomberg also reiterates that next year will be a big year for the Apple Watch:

The company is also working on a major update to its smartwatch lineup for release as early as late 2027. This redesign would follow years of more incremental changes. Apple made its main watch thinner with the Series 10 two years ago, but the larger Ultra model has retained the same look since its debut four years ago.

title: Apple Is Reportedly Developing a Screenless Fitness Tracker
snippet: Do you find the Apple Watch too bulky and distracting? A screen-free solution may be coming.
fullText:
The parade of screenless fitness trackers continues. This year alone, Google released the Fitbit Air, Garmin launched its Cirq Smart Band, and Amazfit came out with the Helio Strap Pro. Now, Apple is reportedly working on its own screenless fitness tracker, one similar to the Whoop wristband. Screenless fitness trackers collect health data via sensors and beam it straight to your smartphone app using Bluetooth.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Guman, Apple has been investigating screenless wearable technology for months and is currently working on prototypes featuring a thin fabric band and a computing module with sensors. The company’s Vision hardware team, those behind the Vision Pro headset, worked on this project, according to Gurman’s sources.

However, the company reportedly hasn’t decided whether to launch the product, despite interest from Executive Chair Tim Cook and Senior Vice President of Services and Health Eddy Cue.

A representative for Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Where Apple Health is headed

This news comes after Apple’s recent announcement of its redesigned Health app and its new features, which will be available to the public later this year. Two of those features, readiness score and Health Age, function much like Whoop’s recovery score and Healthspan. The readiness and recovery scores tell users how prepared their bodies are to take on the day ahead, while Health Age and Healthspan display one’s biological age, or how the user is aging on a cellular level, when compared to their actual chronological age.

The Oura Ring also offers a readiness score and Cardiovascular Age to estimate how your heart is aging. 

The Apple Watch, Whoop band and Oura ring all help track fitness and health information.Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

Screenless wearable benefits

A screenless wearable makes sense as a next step for Apple. Aside from giving people one less screen to stare at, these wearables don’t have screens draining their battery life. They’re often less bulky, making them more comfortable to wear while sleeping and more discreet, which is ideal for people who don’t want their wearable to be the first thing someone notices about them.

While the Apple Watch has a host of features beyond health and fitness, a screenless wearable dedicated to a user’s wellness would also tap into the market of people who want a wearable solely for tracking their workouts and vital signs.

But one thing is for sure: If Apple were to release a screenless fitness tracker, Siri AI, the AI assistant currently in beta, and Apple Intelligence, the company’s AI platform, will likely feature prominently. In the revamped Health app, for instance, Apple Intelligence analyzes health metrics and provides timely summaries and suggestions. This would work well for a screenless wearable, especially if users can talk to Siri to log their health information and ask questions, as with the Luna Band.

According to Gurman, if Apple were to move forward with a screenless fitness tracker, it wouldn’t be released before 2028. 

The Oura Ring is also screenless, but in a different format.

Anna Gragert/CNET

Put a ring on it

Personally, I’d like to see Apple focus more on an Apple Ring and less on a screenless wrist-based wearable. As someone who has tested both smart rings and wristbands, I prefer the former because they’re inconspicuous and more comfortable for sleep, which is important for capturing the sleep data that powers other features.

But I’m not a fan of how these devices tend to require recurring subscriptions, whereas the Apple Watch and the company’s Health app don’t require them. If there’s a world in which Apple’s future fitness tracker, whether a ring or wristband, is both screenless and subscription-less, that would be the best of all.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Anna Gragert
						

						

							Senior Editor, Health and Home						
					

											

								

											Anna Gragert (she/her/hers) was previously the lifestyle editor at HelloGiggles, the deputy editor at So Yummy and the senior lifestyle editor at Hunker. Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. At CNET, she's a senior editor on the Healthy Home team, and her coverage includes health, wellness tech, meal kits and home and kitchen tech with a focus on the technology that aims to help us live our healthiest, happiest lives.
															
						See full bio

title: Clicks Communicator lands in December with 12GB RAM, two months of free data
snippet: Clicks — the company bringing physical keyboards back to mobile — is getting ready to ship its first-ever Android smartphone, and it’s shaping up to be a pretty interesting device. Ahead of its launch later this year, the company is upgrading a handful of the Clicks Communicator’s specs and announcing new accessories, protection coverage options, and eSIM plans. more…
fullText:
Clicks — the company bringing physical keyboards back to mobile — is getting ready to ship its first-ever Android smartphone, and it’s shaping up to be a pretty interesting device. Ahead of its launch later this year, the company is upgrading a handful of the Clicks Communicator’s specs and announcing new accessories, protection coverage options, and eSIM plans.

When the company announced the Clicks Communicator back at CES this year, it was primarily pitched as a secondary device meant to pair with your main smartphone. It seems like the team has heard from its potential customers that some might be satisfied with this being their main smartphone, which has prompted a handful of changes to improve the overall experience.

By far, the biggest upgrade is a move from 8GB to 12GB of RAM, something I’ll be calling a “reverse Pixel 11 Pro” situation. While other smartphone makers are doing whatever they can to reduce RAM — while increasing prices along the way — Clicks is adding additional memory to the device to better futureproof the phone. Its upgrade policy isn’t quite on par with Google or Samsung, but three promised OS upgrades and five years of security updates will, at the very least, pull your Communicator through to around 2032. Clicks has also moved its launch platform to Android 17 out of the box and bumped its battery capacity up to 4,350mAh. 

On the accessory side, Clicks and Dbrand are bringing the latter’s new MNML cases to the device, along with its Prism screen protector that includes a self-aligning tray — is there any other way? Clicks will also continue to offer its bumper Ring case for those looking for a more minimal approach to protection. Dbrand’s case and screen protector will run you $39 and $35, respectively, while the Ring bumper case is $49. Additional Charging Covers, allowing you to switch up your phone’s design, will also be available for $50 or $80, depending on material.

	

Finally, Clicks is launching both a protection plan and eSIM options for its users. Clicks Care is a $129 protection plan that delivers replacements or repairs for accidental damage over a two-year term with a $49 deductible; it’ll be available in the US and Canada. Clicks Mobile, meanwhile, is a new MVNO offering that brings voice and data to the Communicator via eSIM in the US and UK. Subscribers will receive two months of free service when activating their device at launch.

Clicks Communicator is set to ship in December, with reservation holders getting invites today to configure their final orders. September 30th — about two weeks away — is the last day to pre-order the device at its $499 launch price; starting October 1st, it moves to its base MSRP of $650. Anyone who scores the device as its cheaper starting price won’t be asked to pay more for its battery or RAM upgrades.

fullText:
After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward.

On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community.

The nine-member group is stacked with who researchers described to The Verge as celebrities in the field, drawn from institutions including Stanford, Harvard, Oxford, and Cambridge, with multiple Fields Medals and MacArthur “genius grants” among them. It will be hosted by Princeton, New Jersey’s Institute for Advanced Study (IAS), one of the world’s most revered centers of mathematical research and the former intellectual home of figures including Albert Einstein, John von Neumann, and J. Robert Oppenheimer.

“The other fundamental fact is that our overarching aim is to represent as well as we possibly can the interests of the mathematical community.”

OpenAI said the group, called the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), will operate independently, with the freedom to offer advice the company has not requested, publicly comment on its impact on mathematics, and make its advice public, though it did not provide details on what this may entail. It appears that the group will be granted early access to OpenAI’s research in order to fulfill its task. Members will not be paid by OpenAI and the group can change its membership as it sees fit, OpenAI said. “Its value depends on its members being able to exercise their own judgement and challenge ours,” the company said. “The group will advise on the review and communication of emerging results: they will help OpenAI assess their significance, advise on how to coordinate their dissemination, and advise on academic and professional standards of mathematical research. It will also advise on how our tools can support mathematical research and learning.”

For all the emphasis on independence, it remains unclear how much influence the group will actually have or why it was formed in the first place. Simon Machado, a researcher at ETH Zurich in Switzerland, said the whole thing seemed “shrouded in mystery” and he questioned how the nine members were selected. The group’s bare-bones website says it “came together after OpenAI approached some of its members about establishing an external advisory board,” but that, following discussions with the company, the mathematicians decided to launch an independent group instead and invite others to join. It’s not clear which members were initially approached by OpenAI or how the remaining members were selected.

In a blog post published Tuesday, advisory group member Martin Hairer elaborated on the group’s origins and the thinking behind it, responding to what he called a “torrent of misinformation” surrounding its formation. “It is obvious that AI has already had a profound impact on mathematical research and raises numerous questions of correct attribution of ideas, priority, human understanding of ideas, etc.,” he wrote, adding that there is no sense in the community “taking a hard ‘ostrich’ approach of simply ignoring the AI labs and refusing to talk to them on principle.”

While acknowledging that the group was formed in response to an approach from OpenAI, Hairer stressed that not all of its members had been contacted by the company and that the resulting organization is “genuinely independent of OpenAI and any other of the so-called ‘frontier’ AI labs.” Beyond “obvious confidentiality requirements,” he said members have not signed any restrictive agreements governing what they can say publicly, adding that they receive no financial compensation and are relying on the IAS for technical support.

“The other fundamental fact is that our overarching aim is to represent as well as we possibly can the interests of the mathematical community,” wrote Hairer, a professor of mathematics at Imperial College London and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL). While noting that the group is hardly a representative sample of the community, he said he is “absolutely certain that all nine of us take this extremely seriously and are acting in good faith.”

However the members were selected, the group currently comprises an elite cadre of academic mathematicians. The small size raises further questions about whether the group has the breadth of expertise required to evaluate everything coming its way, given the highly specialized skills and knowledge required to operate at the frontiers of mathematics.

Francesco Fournier-Facio, an incoming mathematics professor at Heriot-Watt University in Scotland, described himself as pretty “ambivalent” about the panel, saying that greater engagement with mathematicians “can only make things better.” But he questioned whether this group fully reflects the community whose work and livelihoods are being upended by OpenAI’s quest to rack up mathematical trophies. “It feels like an ivory tower,” he told The Verge.

Machado similarly questioned whether the group’s members fully understand, or can speak to, the concerns of the broader mathematical community when it comes to AI. “They’re amazing mathematicians, but I don’t know if they are the people I want to represent me in more political questions,” he said. For mathematicians in their and similarly elite positions, Machado said, “I think that the reality they are facing is very different from the reality that most mathematicians are facing right now.”

Whether the group can earn mathematicians’ trust will ultimately determine how effective it will be at containing the fallout from OpenAI’s recent parade of missteps in announcing results and, more importantly, soften the blow for whatever the company is planning to announce next. In his blog, Hairer said members would “be very naïve to believe that the AI labs won’t try to spin whatever we say in a way that suits their PR machine, which dwarfs anything we could possibly come up with.”

Nevertheless, Hairer argued it would be hypocritical not to engage now that OpenAI appears to be making an effort, particularly after so many criticized the company’s conduct and poor communications. The group has yet to settle on the advice it intends to provide, he said, but there is a clear problem it is responding to: “It is a fact that AI companies have in recent months been producing some high profile mathematical results and that their publication and dissemination has been falling far short of acceptable mathematical practice, whichever way that is defined.”

“We are currently facing the very specific challenge of advising OpenAI on how to coordinate the release of a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model.”

For now, Hairer said the group is gathering input through conversations with colleagues, a public feedback form, and discussion on Proofs and Prompts, a blog that has emerged as a key forum for mathematicians reckoning with AI’s impact on the field.

But the group’s biggest challenge likely lies ahead. When announcing the advisory group, OpenAI casually dropped the news that its new, unreleased model — the same that resolved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem — has now “resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.” It has previously said it is closing in on another Millennium Prize problem. On its website, the group said dealing with this logjam is its first priority: “We are currently facing the very specific challenge of advising OpenAI on how to coordinate the release of a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model.”

In part, the new effort at engaging mathematicians is an acknowledgement of the monumental PR disaster its attempt was, in which the company found itself fending off accusations of scooping researchers, failing to credit the human work its models built upon, and even stealing from those using its models. Those controversies led many mathematicians to wonder if the company understood — or even respected — the discipline and community it had barreled into.

After the last few months and with so much having been written about what mathematicians want, Kevin Buzzard, a mathematics professor at Imperial College London, wondered why OpenAI felt like it needed such an elite body to understand what the community wants. “It wasn’t proofs of hard theorems, it was better understanding of our subject,” he said. “It’s not entirely clear to me that you need a committee of brilliant people to hammer the point home.”

title: iPhone 18 Pro Face ID bug causing system to crash and reboot for some users
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max introduces a new smaller Face ID system, with the Infrared camera now hidden behind the screen, near where the time is shown in the status bar. It appears there may be a software glitch with that component in the shipping release of iOS 27. A number of reports from 18 Pro owners indicate that their device freezes and reboots after a failed Face ID attempt. more…
fullText:
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max introduces a new smaller Face ID system, with the Infrared camera now hidden behind the screen, near where the time is shown in the status bar.

It appears there may be a software glitch with that component in the shipping release of iOS 27. A number of reports from 18 Pro owners indicate that their device freezes and reboots after a failed Face ID attempt.

9to5Mac has reproduced the bug on at least one European iPhone 18 Pro model. The scope of the problem is unclear, as it does not seem to affect everyone. 

The issue appears to occur when using Face ID to unlock a protected app, like the Passwords app, private tabs in Safari, or other apps the user has chosen to lock behind biometric protection. It does not seem to trigger directly from the lock screen.

To try and reproduce for yourself, on an 18 Pro, when the device presents a Face ID challenge, cover your face with your hand to simulate an authentication failure on the first try. Then, tap the “Try Face ID Again” button in the alert that appears. If you are afflicted by the bug, the phone will lock up and stop responding to all touch input. After a few seconds, the phone panics and reboots back to the lock screen. 

In the Reddit thread of complaining users, one person says they contacted Apple support who apparently recommended a hardware swap. In our experience, this is probably a misdiagnosis and the problem will be fixable by a software update. 

There’s also a similar iOS 27 bug that can trigger system reboots on any iPhone model, which we also expect to be fixed by a forthcoming software patch.

We have reached out to Apple for comment on the matter and will let you know if we hear back.

title: Motorola’s wild-looking Signature 27 runs Qualcomm’s new Extreme chipset
snippet: You couldn’t accuse Motorola of designing a boring phone. | Image: Motorola Motorola is the first company to announce a phone running Qualcomm's top-end Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip. The Signature 27 looks set to be Motorola's most advanced flagship in some years, though we're still waiting for the full specs, price, and release date. Any prospective buyers will first have to get over the design, which seems guaranteed to earn mixed reception. The aluminum phone has a thin body, available in either black (sorry, "Pantone coal smoke") or green ("Pantone capulet olive"), with a woven tactical texture on one and a "feather-inspired" finish on the other. Either way, it slopes upwards into what Motorola calls a … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Dominic Preston

 

is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Motorola is the first company to announce a phone running Qualcomm’s top-end Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip. The Signature 27 looks set to be Motorola’s most advanced flagship in some years, though we’re still waiting for the full specs, price, and release date.

Any prospective buyers will first have to get over the design, which seems guaranteed to earn mixed reception. The aluminum phone has a thin body, available in either black (sorry, “Pantone coal smoke”) or green (“Pantone capulet olive”), with a woven tactical texture on one and a “feather-inspired” finish on the other. Either way, it slopes upwards into what Motorola calls a “camera plane,” with four lenses and a flash in an odd arch layout. It’s certainly unique.

Only a handful of the Signature 27’s specs have been confirmed, but they’re more appealing to me than the design. The B&O logo by the cameras gives away that Bang & Olufsen has helped design the audio, though the specifics are still unknown. There’s the promise of seven years of Android updates, still rare for Motorola. The cameras will include a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto and a 50-megapixel main camera — the latter is more exciting for using Sony’s LOFIC-enabled Lytia 910 sensor, also seen in this week’s Vivo X500 Pro Max, where it enables 17 stops of dynamic range. Hopefully Motorola’s phone matches that.

1/6Image: Motorola

Motorola says more details about the Signature 27 are on the way, with a global launch due before the end of the year. Unlike the first Motorola Signature, from earlier this year, that will include the US.

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

In this day and age, gas prices fluctuate quite a lot. If you want to have a better idea of how things are flowing, GasPulse is a great tool – giving you trends, historical prices, and an outlook to follow on your iPhone.

Top features

Using the weekly averages published by the Energy Information Administration, GasPulse shows you prices for each state or region. It’s not an app that’ll show you the cheapest gas station, but it shows you the trends with charts and a nice interface. It also has up to five years of historical prices.

Beyond that, it also offers an Outlook feature that gives you an idea of what to expect in the future. These are estimates, but it gives you a little bit of insight on whether or not things will go up or down. GasPulse also offers state-by-state comparisons, allowing you to see how things compare around you.

If you want price alerts, GasPulse also offers them for free for up to 6 areas, though it relies on iOS background refresh.

Lastly, GasPulse offers home screen and lock screen widgets, allowing you to keep an eye on things without opening the app. There’s also Siri support.

Download the app

GasPulse is available for free on the App Store for iPhone users running iOS 18 and later. There’s no requirement for a subscription, and it’s ad-free.

title: Motorola Signature 27 Is Coming to the US to Rival Samsung’s Galaxy Phones
snippet: After an overseas-only debut, Motorola’s new Signature 27 is coming to the US, with the high-end phone set to be released this year.
fullText:
Just when we thought Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro would be the last major flagship phone to be released in 2026 in the US, Motorola decided to step in by debuting the Signature 27 on Tuesday, during Qualcomm’s annual Snapdragon Summit. Unlike the original Signature, this one will be coming to US markets, and it looks like an aggressive entry into the high-end Android flagship phone market.

Motorola’s Signature 27 will include the newly announced Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, coupled with a partial list of high-end features that remind me of the recently departed OnePlus phone line. 

In addition to the early inclusion of Qualcomm’s chip, Motorola is touting a camera system that will include a 50-megapixel main camera along with a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto lens — the latter of which could be a boon for taking zoom photos from far distances, like at a concert. And there appear to be more cameras than Motorola has given details for, as the back of the phone shows four lenses, similar to Samsung’s quad-camera system on the Galaxy S26 Ultra.

For gamers — another audience that OnePlus had particularly focused on — the Signature 27 includes a cooling system that Motorola calls ArcticMesh. It combines a diamond-infused thermal gel, liquid metal, copper mesh and a 3D vapor chamber that’s 40% larger than the previous Signature phone — and should help it stay cool during intensive gaming and video recording.

Motorola’s Signature 27 has four cameras on the back, but so far we only know about the 50-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera.Motorola

The Signature 27 also matches Samsung’s Galaxy and Google’s Pixel lines with a seven-year commitment to software and security support, plus it will get an audio system developed in partnership with Bang & Olufsen. The Signature 27 is the first phone to get this audio system as part of a multiyear partnership with B&O, so it’s possible that down the road, the foldable Razr line will also benefit from this.

The Signature 27 will come in two colors with long names: “Pantone Coal Smoke in tactical weave” is a darker shade that features a woven texture for enhanced grip. “Pantone Capulet Olive in a brushed textile-inspired finish” is a green shade with a softer, tactile feel.

Motorola still has a lot of other details to unveil about the Signature 27, including its battery, charging speeds and display. But the first Signature phone the company debuted at CES 2026 in January included a 5,200-mAh silicon-carbon battery, 90-watt wired charging and a 6.8-inch display with a 165Hz refresh rate — all helpful reference points for what to expect in its successor. In Europe, the phone was priced at 999 euros (approximately $1,170 including tax) with 512GB of storage. 

Even if the Signature 27 were to recycle some of its predecessor’s specs — and somehow hold onto its pricing despite rising costs brought on by the ongoing RAM shortage — on paper, this could be a tempting draw for former OnePlus phone fans looking for a new alternative as well as a tempting rival to Samsung’s next Galaxy phone. 

We’ll find out more about the Motorola Signature 27 at a later date, with the phone set for release sometime before the end of the year.

title: iOS 27.2 reveals new features coming to Apple Music, CarPlay, more
snippet: iOS 27.2 beta 2 arrived today, and so far seems to have minimal user-facing changes. But code for iOS 27.2’s beta releases points to new features in the works for Apple Music, CarPlay Ultra, and more. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 beta 2 arrived today, and so far seems to have minimal user-facing changes. But code for iOS 27.2’s beta releases points to new features in the works for Apple Music, CarPlay Ultra, and more.

Whenever Apple releases new beta software, we tend to discover changes in two ways: through user-facing features active in the software, as well as underlying code changes that point to forthcoming changes.

With iOS 27.2, there were a variety of new features available for testing from day one, like the all-new Health app, user profiles in Apple TV, Siri AI expansions, and more.

But users skilled at examining the underlying code found even more changes in the works. 

For example, X user pdfu discovered that Apple Music will soon add live countdowns for new album releases.

Another discovery by pdfu in iOS 27.2 beta code involves the Shortcuts app.

Shortcuts’ new ‘Describe a Shortcut’ feature looks like it will soon gain support for including actions from third-party apps.

Describe a Shortcut could soon support actions from third-party developers.

Currently, the feature only supports Apple-developed actions. With a new feature flag in iOS 27.2 and macOS 27.2, the model can now choose actions from third-party apps.

To enable:

sudo mkdir -p… pic.twitter.com/sR6OJMwADy

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 17, 2026

Another noteworthy reveal from iOS 27.2 code involves CarPlay Ultra.

Aaron Perris discovered that code references a ‘Drive Mode Theme’ that changes things like gauge style and color, and even syncs ambient lighting in the vehicle.

iOS 27.2 beta 1 includes text that describes a "Drive Mode Theme" meant for CarPlay Ultra

"This will reset all customizations made to this theme, including gauge style, color, and wallpaper, to defaults."

"Ambient lighting will automatically sync with the color of your current… pic.twitter.com/7g2E5BeCB4

— Aaron (@aaronp613) September 17, 2026

CarPlay Ultra is still limited to only Aston Martin vehicles. But perhaps the addition of new theming features means Apple is about to expand support to another automaker.

We previously reported that iOS 27.2 will add a feature to more thoroughly wipe the data of your iPhone. Today’s beta 2 has more descriptive language on this addition—now called “Extended Erase”—as discovered by Aaron Perris.

Finally, Perris found evidence that Apple may be preparing a demo mode for users of its forthcoming ‘HomePad’ smart home device.

Which of iOS 27.2’s new and upcoming features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

title: Can Bambu Labs 3D Printer Success Translate to a Standalone Laser? I Believe It Can
snippet: While Bambu Labs has made laser cutters in the past, the R1 is the company’s first dedicated tool.
fullText:
If you’re into 3D printing and have been around for the last few years, the name Bambu Lab will be familiar to you. Its products often top best 3D printer lists, including ours, and the company has helped bring genuine plug-and-play standards to in-home 3D printing.

Today, Bambu Lab has announced the R1, a standalone CO2 laser engraver designed to integrate seamlessly into your existing ecosystem. The R1 is available today for a base price of $2,500. I’ve spent some time with it — though not enough for a full review — and so far it’s been a great experience.

	

			

	

									

						A standalone laser with Bambu finish					

									

						Bambu Lab R1					

							

While the R1 looks nothing like a 3D printer, it does have a design language that’s easily identifiable as Bambu Lab’s. The light gray plastic casing is well-fitted, and the interior metal frame feels solid when you move the machine. The LEDs in the back around the CO2 gas chamber highlight the interior and you can see the laser pulses through the rear glass as it works on your material.

Even the molding around the power button exudes a high-quality finish, making the R1 feel like a consumer product you would have in your home office rather than a workshop. The optional riser fits right into that aesthetic, too, and makes the laser-and-riser combo feel like one continuous piece.

The finishing touches, like this power button, show an effort to make things beautiful.

According to Bambu Lab’s press release, the company has brought what it’s learned from 3D printing to the R1, using a lot of its excellent acceleration algorithms and hardware to reduce ringing and other artifacts that occur when cutting or engraving at high speed. Bambu Lab has also used its vision encoders to make sure the cameras on the R1 accurately represent the material on the bed.

This is often an issue with larger lasers, as the fisheye lens can distort images at the edges, making the cuts off-center or overlap in weird ways. If you’re trying to cut around an existing image, this can lead to cutting failures that cost you time and money.

Why make a standalone laser cutter?

Cutting through 3mm plywood is a breeze with the R1.

Bambu Lab has already dabbled in laser cutting. The H2D and H2S both have laser configurations that work OK, but a two-in-one solution will always be a compromise. If you use the laser side of the H2D for too long, eventually the soot and buildup will compromise its ability to 3D print correctly. By creating the R1, Bambu Lab can potentially compete in a space that doesn’t look too kindly on two-in-one devices.

The R1 is a 55-watt CO2 laser, instead of the diode laser that was used in the H2D. The big difference between the two is the amount of materials you can work with. The CO2 laser can’t cut metal, or even etch it well (unless the metal is painted), but it can cut and engrave just about anything else.

I’ve only managed to play around with acrylic, wood and cardboard so far, but the R1 will etch on glass, cut through wood and clear acrylic without any issues. The list of what you can cut with a CO2 laser is long, and with the optional riser and conveyor system, you can go from a 600x300mm cutting area to a 600×3,000mm area, increasing the scope of your projects even more.

Being able to cut clear acrylic and etch on glass is a CO2 laser’s biggest asset, and the R1 does an excellent job. You can often see charring on clear acrylic when it’s not done right, but the settings for the R1 through its Bambu Suite software keep everything well in check. It even has a tracing feature that can take an image of the object on the bed and create a cutting sequence to cut around. It’s quite impressive.

First impressions

The CNET logo always looks good in red

Bambu Lab has a track record of making its first product a good one, and so far, the R1 meets that standard. From the testing I’ve done, this machine is competent, well-made and easily integrates with the great Bambu Lab infrastructure, using the Bambu Handy app and the Makerworld website to help you find projects.

As with all Bambu products, setup took minutes, and the R1 includes multiple calibration tools that make getting started a breeze. The company has long tried to lower the barrier to entry for 3D printing, and it is clearly doing the same with laser cutters. 

Xtool, WeCreat and Glowforge have long dominated the consumer and small business space for laser engraving. Some new competition from a proven crafting company can only be good for us all.

	

			

	

									

						A standalone laser with Bambu finish					

									

						Bambu Lab R1

title: CarPlay just got better, here’s everything new in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 has arrived, and with it a handful of improvements for CarPlay. Here’s everything new for CarPlay in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has arrived, and with it a handful of improvements for CarPlay. Here’s everything new for CarPlay in iOS 27.

Siri AI and new Siri app

Apple’s Siri overhaul is the tentpole addition to iOS 27. And the new ‘Siri AI’ capabilities on the iPhone are available in CarPlay too if you have a compatible iPhone.

Siri AI offers a new design that’s more like the pre-iOS 18 look, but with less color. It appears as a glowing orb at the bottom-center of the screen.

Siri in CarPlay is now much better at answering questions of any kind, similar to ChatGPT and Google Gemini. In my testing, it’s also able to retain the context of your current conversation better than ever before. Here are 100+ examples of what Siri AI can do.

In a nice touch, conversations you have in CarPlay are automatically synced to the Siri app on iPhone. You can browse the full Siri history in the app, and there’s a car icon marking conversations you had via CarPlay.

Video app support

Apple added video in the car with iOS 26, but it was limited to AirPlay streaming. But with iOS 27 developers can now make dedicated video apps for CarPlay, so that users can browse videos right on their CarPlay display.

From Apple’s WWDC video that’s targeted toward developers:

With iOS 27 you can create apps to browse and play videos in new cars that support the video in car feature. If your app supports AirPlay video streaming, no changes are needed. People can already watch videos from your app on their CarPlay display when they aren’t driving. To do so, they simply select the car’s display when playing the video on iPhone. Now you can take it to the next level and let people browse their favorite videos from iPhone right on their CarPlay display.

Automakers need to sign on to support the feature, so unfortunately it won’t be available automatically in every car.

New design updates and wallpapers

iOS 27 has a handful of design-related updates for CarPlay too. 

As seen above, media apps feature a new MiniPlayer in CarPlay. Available in the top-right corner of the app, the MiniPlayer provides artwork and player controls—a nice upgrade with more utility than the previous waveform icon offered.

You can now do audio scrubbing on the Now Playing screen when listening to music, audiobooks, or podcasts. There’s a larger progress indicator that’s similar to the iPhone design, making it easy to grab and drag.

App icons have been refreshed with updated Liquid Glass designs in iOS 27, and those new icons extend to CarPlay.

Finally, there are new CarPlay wallpapers available now that resemble what’s included across iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate.

Which new CarPlay features in iOS 27 are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more
snippet: Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October. more…
fullText:
Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October.

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Software

Google’s main pitch is that Googlebooks should be the laptop of choice for those with Android phones:

Today, we often switch between starting tasks on our phones and finishing them on our laptops. To make that experience better for Android users, we teamed up with the best laptop makers in the industry to deliver top-tier hardware alongside Google’s software experience that connects effortlessly with your phone.

Following phones and watches, Material 3 Expressive is coming to desktops. Quick Settings and notifications, which are nearly identical in design to what you’d find on Pixel, can be found in the top-right corner, while you have the time and date at the left. The bottom dock is center-aligned with the ‘G’ opening your app drawer. 

	

Upon signing in to a Googlebook, your Android phone’s settings, saved passwords, Wi-Fi, and messages will appear. Cross-device continuity includes Android 17’s “Continue On” capability and Cast My Apps if you don’t want to install the Android application on your laptop.

Additionally, Google touts a first-class Files app that can show what documents and photos are available on your phone. One good use of on-device AI is automatically generating file descriptions that aid search.

Gemini Intelligence is led by Magic Pointer and the wiggle gesture to bring up Gemini and enter a prompt, like adding dates to your Calendar. There’s also Rambler, like on the Pixel 11 series, to dictate a stream of consciousness, while Create My Widget is billed as letting you “customize your desktop by describing what you need in plain language.”

You get a “desktop-class” Chrome browser with support for extensions, the Gemini side panel, vertical tabs, and more. Most features found on Mac and Windows are available here.

The application story is a combination of Android and the web, with Google noting how 70% of time spent on laptops is in a browser. The company ultimately thinks it is up to developers to choose whether an Android app or the web is better for their application. There is a growing number of desktop-class Android apps, and the Play Store will highlight them with a new badge. 

On the gaming front, 20,000 mobile and PC titles will run on Googlebooks. They are optimized for keyboard, mouse, and touchscreen, with Google’s existing Play Games Level Up program resulting in monthly title launches. For everything else, Google offers a year of Nvidia GeForce Now.

For developers, Google very notably created an Antigravity app for Googlebooks that offers a native UI and interacts with the Linux environment. You can also install the Linux version of Antigravity if you wish, along with Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. For Android app development, Antigravity allows you to deploy directly to the Googlebook.

Under the hood, Google is integrating the multi-window performance and full browser capabilities of ChromeOS with a native Android stack that offers power and battery efficiency.

On the security front, Google touts the same security architecture as ChromeOS. There’s a Google Titan security chip and on-device malware detection. Additionally, a Level 5 security-certified hypervisor powered by pKVM isolation allows for the isolated Linux environment with full terminal access. This lets you “safely run any Linux developer tools, pull code repositories, access networks and the ports, or execute autonomous agents.”

Googlebooks get 10 years of automatic updates with quarterly feature drops similar to Pixel.

Hardware

On the hardware front, there are five flagship Googlebooks at launch, with Google mandating several key specs across the lineup. All devices are powered by Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with NPUs (40+ TOPS). As such, Googlebook OS is optimized for ARM and x86, with MediaTek-powered devices coming in the future.

There’s a baseline of 16 GB of RAM with 32 GB variants available. All have a touchscreen with up to 2.8K LCD or OLED. Devices have up to six speakers with Dolby Atmos surround sound and “studio-quality, background noise-canceling” microphones.

Googlebooks are made from “premium materials” like aluminum, magnesium, or carbon fiber.

There are also backlit keyboards and large glass trackpads with haptic feedback and support for gestures. Google touts up to 14 hours of video playback and 16 hours of web browsing.

Finally, all devices have a Glowbar on the cover that lights up in the Google colors when you open and close the lid. When you plug in a charger, there’s a current charge level indicator and “playful” animation when you talk to Gemini. Notably (unlike Pixel Glow), third-party apps can access it to “build custom, interactive animations.”

title: Apple releases Xcode 27.1 beta, enabling iPhone Duo app development
snippet: Apple has released Xcode 27.1 beta 1 for developers. This version specifically enables app development that targets the new foldable iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Apple has released Xcode 27.1 beta 1 for developers. This version specifically enables app development that targets the new foldable iPhone Duo.

While iPhone Duo doesn’t launch until October, today’s Xcode release gives developers a chance to prepare for initial iPhone Duo support. 

Properly optimizing most apps for iPhone Duo will probably take more than a few weeks for most apps. However, Xcode 27.1 meets Apple’s promise to release dev tools before the end of September.

Apps built against Apple’s iOS 26 SDK will need to be updated for iOS 27 for basic iPhone Duo support.

Apps made for iOS 27.1 and later will take full advantage of the larger display. Still, there are a lot of sizing and layout considerations that developers need to consider when shipping proper app support.

While the device isn’t out yet, Xcode 27.1 beta also gives developers the chance to virtually experience their apps on the iPhone Duo simulator.

Xcode 27.1 beta is available to download from Apple’s developer webpage here.

The release follows the introduction of Xcode 27.2 beta earlier this week. Apple is shipping iOS 27.2 as the next software update for iPhones running iOS 27.0 with the exception of the iPhone Duo.

 It will run iOS 27.1, a version designed for the foldable device, before syncing up with the rest of the iPhone lineup in a later version.

iPhone Duo will be available for pre-order on October 16 and ships October 23. Pricing starts at $1999.

title: Apple Wallet driver’s licenses coming to three new states soon
snippet: Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board.

Utah, Kentucky, and North Carolina appear set to launch driver’s licenses in Apple Wallet soon

Digital IDs are becoming far more common than they were when Apple first added support in the Wallet app back in 2021. And today, 16 US states plus Puerto Rico support the feature on iPhone.

The latest additions, Virginia and Oklahoma, debuted just in the last month.

And it looks like three more states will be coming soon:

Utah

Kentucky

North Carolina

This summer evidence was discovered of both Utah and Virginia being added to Apple’s backend for driver’s license support. Virginia has since gone live, so it’s expected that Utah will launch as one of the next supported states.

Kentucky previously announced it will support Apple Wallet driver’s licenses after upgrading its digital ID system this summer. All indications are that the upgrade has been completed, so based on the state’s original plans, we should see licenses in Apple Wallet soon.

North Carolina recently announced the launch of its new digital driver’s license system. As part of the announcement, it confirmed licenses will be supported in Apple Wallet by early 2027.

Additional states might always surprise us and launch in Wallet before Utah, Kentucky, or North Carolina. We’ve seen a clear acceleration of states signing on to offer Wallet driver’s licenses.

But for now at least, the three states above appear the strongest candidates to debut soon.

For more info on states that have pledged Apple Wallet support, see our coverage here.

title: New Mac mini drops support for aftermarket storage upgrades
snippet: When Apple released the M4 Mac mini two years ago, teardowns quickly revealed a pleasant surprise: the internal SSD was not soldered to the logic board. This allowed for aftermarket storage upgrades, and we even showed you how to do it. With the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini updates, however, it appears the storage is soldered to the logic board once again. more…
fullText:
When Apple released the M4 Mac mini two years ago, teardowns quickly revealed a pleasant surprise: the internal SSD was not soldered to the logic board. This allowed for aftermarket storage upgrades, and we even showed you how to do it.

With the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini updates, however, it appears the storage is soldered to the logic board once again.

New Mac mini takes a step backward with soldered storage

In a blog post, the folks at Expand Mac mini revealed that the NAND is soldered to the logic board, similar to the M1 and M2 versions of the Mac mini. This means the SSD module is no longer removable.

Expand Mac mini sells storage upgrade modules for the M4 and M4 Pro versions of the Mac mini. As it stands right now, however, they say that “support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely.”

No slot means nothing to swap, and very little room left for us. In August we said we would extend our coverage once we had tested real hardware. This is the result, and not the one we hoped for.

We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely. If that changes, you will hear it here first.

For comparison’s sake, Expand Mac mini’s 1TB SSD expansion module for the M4 Mac mini costs $300. Apple charges $500 to upgrade the M6 Mac mini from 256GB to 1TB. Expand Mac mini’s 2TB module costs $420, while Apple charges $1,000 for the upgrade.

As for the Mac Studio, Apple’s repair guide still shows removable SSDs. We haven’t spotted any teardowns yet confirming that information.

title: Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more
snippet: Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now. more…
fullText:
Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now. 

New design in iOS 27

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone. 

American Express rewards

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

Reload debit cards

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

Bonus: Apple Pay at Walmart 

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.  

Walmart started rolling out Apple Pay (and broader contactless support) this week in Arkansas. The retailer says it launch for all stores in the United States by the end of this year. 

Wrap up

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

fullText:
Apple today announced that Tap to Pay on iPhone is now available in eight additional Latin American countries, with support from six payment platforms across the region. Here are the details.

Tap to Pay on iPhone expands to eight new countries

In an update published to its Latin America and the Caribbean Newsroom, Apple announced today an expansion of Tap to Pay on iPhone across Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, and Peru.

Tap to Pay on iPhone allows merchants to accept in-person contactless payments using only a compatible iPhone and supported payment app, without the need for additional card readers or payment terminals.

Here’s the list of countries and payment platforms gaining support today:

Argentina: Mercado Pago

Colombia: SumUp, Symbiotic

Costa Rica: Geopagos, Symbiotic, Visa Acceptance Solutions

Dominican Republic: Azul, Visa Acceptance Solutions

Guatemala: Geopagos, Symbiotic

Honduras: Geopagos, Symbiotic

Panama: Geopagos, Symbiotic

Peru: SumUp

Apple also noted that Tap to Pay on iPhone “is compatible with contactless debit and credit cards from major payment networks, including American Express, Mastercard, and Visa.”

Apple originally announced Tap to Pay on iPhone on February 8, 2022. It was initially announced for the United States, with Stripe as the first payment platform set to support it.

Since then, it has expanded to 59 countries and regions, with Apple’s current list naming more than 100 payment service providers worldwide, including today’s additions.

title: MediaTek’s flagship laptop chip is the Dimensity CX C10 Max, debuts in a Lenovo Googlebook
snippet: The initial batch of Googlebook laptops that debuted earlier today use either Intel or Qualcomm chipsets, but MediaTek has confirmed it will also be backing the platform with the debut of its flagship laptop chip, the Dimensity CX C10 Max, which will show up in an incoming Lenovo Googlebook. more…
fullText:
The initial batch of Googlebook laptops that debuted earlier today use either Intel or Qualcomm chipsets, but MediaTek has confirmed it will also be backing the platform with the debut of its flagship laptop chip, the Dimensity CX C10 Max, which will show up in an incoming Lenovo Googlebook.

Following Qualcomm’s push in recent years on the Snapdragon X lineup, MediaTek is introducing its CX line of “Compute Experiences” chips. The first release is the Dimensity CX C10 Max, a 3nm chip built on TSMC’s process with an octa-core All Big Core design – 1x Arm Cortex-X925, 3x Arm Cortex-X4, 4x Arm Cortex-A720 –, 11-core GPU, and a dedicated NPU for boosting AI performance – all without fans or battery woes.

MediaTek explains:

Built on TSMC’s advanced 3nm process, Dimensity CX C10 Max utilizes an All Big Core design with octa-core CPU, 11-core GPU, and MediaTek’s 8th-generation NPU in a highly efficient platform engineered to deliver stellar performance across multitasking, productivity, entertainment, intelligent assistance, and more. Its power-efficient architecture enables manufacturers to design thinner, lighter, and fanless devices with all-day battery life.

The C10 Max is said to deliver 55 TOPs of performance for AI tasks while also offering features such as Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0 (though not in Googlebooks), and more.

	

MediaTek says in an email to 9to5Google that the Dimensity CX C10 Max will make its debut in an upcoming Googlebook product from Lenovo. That’s not the initial Lenovo Googlebook (15-inch) which is powered by Intel. Presumably, it’s for Lenovo’s leaked tablet that’s using the Googlebook OS.

title: Google confirms Pixel phones were exploited in ‘targeted’ attack related to modem
snippet: Google has confirmed that a “limited” number of Pixel phones were attacked by a vulnerability related to the modem on the device. more…
fullText:
Google has confirmed that a “limited” number of Pixel phones were attacked by a vulnerability related to the modem on the device.

As part of the September 2026 security update, Google patched over 200 security vulnerabilities, but specifically calls out that one of those was actively exploited in the wild.

Note: There are indications that CVE-2026-58704 may be under limited, targeted exploitation.

The issue is related to the modem, with a bypass that requires no user interaction. CVE-2026-58704 is described as follows:

In Cellular Modem, there is a possible permission bypass due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

Exact details of how the vulnerability was exploited are unclear – as well as which models were affected – but CISA (via The Hacker News) says that it was exploited on Pixel phones, explaining that “Google Pixel devices contain an improper authorization vulnerability in the cellular modem.” Combined with Google’s announcement, this was used in the wild, apparently to hack “targeted” devices. CISA issued a notice that this is a “known exploited vulnerability,” explaining that “this type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.” TechCrunch notes that this is called a “zero-click” attack, adding that Google hadn’t replied to a request for comment around the vulnerability being exploited and who was exploiting it.

	

If you’re on a Pixel phone, updating to the September 2026 patch, rolling out now, fixes the issue.

title: watchOS 27.2 beta 2 brings the App Switcher back with a new gesture
snippet: If you’ve been missing the double-click of the Digital Crown that used to bring up the App Switcher on the Apple Watch before watchOS 27, it looks like the feature is making a comeback as of watchOS 27.2 beta 2. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
If you’ve been missing the double-click of the Digital Crown that used to bring up the App Switcher on the Apple Watch before watchOS 27, it looks like the feature is making a comeback as of watchOS 27.2 beta 2. Here are the details.

Apple working to bring watchOS App Switcher back

Earlier today, Apple rolled out watchOS 27.2 beta 2 for developers, less than a week after releasing beta 1.

Included in today’s beta is a tidbit that will likely please longtime Apple Watch users, including my colleague Zac Hall. Earlier this month, he wrote about how watchOS 27 had removed the ability to quickly switch between recently used apps by double-clicking the Digital Crown.

In his piece, he noted that there was no longer any way to quickly jump between recent apps, and wished Apple would restore the gesture before releasing watchOS 27, or in a future update.

While Apple didn’t bring back the App Switcher’s Digital Crown shortcut in today’s watchOS 27.2 beta 2, it did restore the App Switcher itself with a new gesture.

As spotted by the Apple Den Discord server and shared by user Bones on X, watchOS 27.2 beta 2 lets users press and hold the bottom of the screen while inside an app to bring up the App Switcher.

Apple has brought back the App Switcher!

On watchOS 26 and earlier, you could access the App Switcher by double-clicking the Digital Crown, then turning the Digital Crown to navigate through your recently used apps. You could also swipe left on an app and tap the "X" button to… pic.twitter.com/G5fa0TeTR9

— 𝓑𝓸𝓷𝓮𝓼 (@limpless_skelly) September 22, 2026

As Bones noted in their tweet, the App Switcher otherwise works much like it did before: after activating the App Switcher with a long press on the bottom of the screen, users can turn the Digital Crown to scroll through recently used apps, or swipe left on an app and tap the “X” button to remove it from the switcher.

While, like with any beta, there is no guarantee that this exact interaction will make it into the final release (likely to come next month), its addition in watchOS 27.2 beta 2 suggests that Apple is listening to user feedback and looking for a way to bring the App Switcher back.

title: iOS 27.2 beta 2 reveals new details about unnanounced iPhone anti-snatching feature
snippet: Apple continues to work on a feature that automatically locks an iPhone when it detects that the device has been snatched from its owner’s hand. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple continues to work on a feature that automatically locks an iPhone when it detects that the device has been snatched from its owner’s hand. Here are the details.

Apple still working on iPhone anti-snatching feature

Earlier this year, 9to5Mac first reported that Apple was working on a new iPhone security feature that can automatically lock the device when it detects that it has been snatched from the user’s hand.

While Apple has yet to officially announce the feature, new references included in iOS 27.2 beta 2 show the company is still actively developing it.

According to new code seen today by 9to5Mac, the feature, which is called “AutoLock” internally, can use the following signals to determine whether an iPhone may have been taken from its owner:

A sharp acceleration consistent with the phone being snatched;

A paired Apple Watch remaining unreachable for a certain period;

Loss of connectivity to a paired Apple Watch;

Prolonged loss of network connectivity;

The device remaining unlocked beyond a certain interval.

Additionally, new references include safeguards meant to prevent false positives, such as successful biometric authentication, certain foreground app activities that could otherwise be mistaken for signs that the device has been taken, and a backoff mechanism that can temporarily suppress further automatic locks after repeated lock events.

The code also suggests AutoLock uses a voting system in which a potential theft signal can request a lock, while safeguards such as biometrics, familiar locations, or certain app activities can veto it.

These new details add to the references already present in the code, including a location-based safeguard similar to Stolen Device Protection that accounts for whether the iPhone is in a familiar place.

It is worth noting that the feature is still under development and is not currently enabled or available as a user-facing option in iOS 27.2 beta 2. Rather, Apple has enabled the underlying AutoLock service in the background, while keeping the component that actually locks the iPhone disabled, possibly as a way to test the underlying behavior without actually triggering automatic locks.

This means that, for now, the new references only provide a look at Apple’s progress in developing the feature. Whether or when it will ultimately launch remains up to Apple.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m bumping to Carly Rae Jepsen’s new double album (it’s great!), wishing I had more kidneys so I could afford the new M5 Ultra Mac Studio, marveling at Astra’s ability to decrypt 100-year-old WWI cyphers, and counting down the days until I can play Control Resonant.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

I’ve been covering Google’s multifarious hardware endeavors for nearly 20 years, from the early days of Nexus phones through this week’s Googlebook unveiling, and I see a few important parallels. Google has always wanted to assert some measure of control over the user experience, but that amount has ebbed and flowed depending on where its product sits in the funnel. 

	

The early days of Android were about growth, which meant leveraging established players like LG, Samsung, Huawei, and others to build its hardware while promulgating a free and open-source operating system that quickly supplanted giants like Nokia and Microsoft.

Alongside Android, Google nurtured Chrome OS (which later became, confusingly, ChromeOS) as its laptop (and occasional desktop) operating system, that, like Android, became synonymous with cheap-and-cheerful hardware, particularly in schools. And while Google did the work to rid itself of that budget reputation on the phone side (though, arguably, Samsung did the bulk of the heavy lifting), it never really managed to do the same on ChromeOS despite numerous attempts to build premium hardware.

Now, ChromeOS is being replaced by Googlebook, and its main appeal is quite simple to understand: “Hey premium Android users, we see you. Here’s a product that can bring you Apple users’ ecosystem benefits while retaining the openness and diversity of Android.”

A few questions jump to mind when I hear that:

Yes, there are billions of Android users out there, but are enough of them clamoring for ecosystem unity to replace their existing laptops in order to entwine their lives even further with Google?

Is that ecosystem unity actually additive in the same way that Apple has proven with iOS and macOS, or will it be more like the way Microsoft has tried to harmonize Android and iOS devices with Windows?

Will the legacy of Google killing off seemingly healthy products turn people away from Googlebooks?

Is this objectively the worst time to launch a new hardware brand?

Also interesting is that Google’s own hardware is absent from this ecosystem launch. Like Chromebooks before them, Googlebooks will be made by familiar companies like Lenovo, Dell, Acer, and ASUS, with internals from Intel, Qualcomm, and soon AMD — another reminder that Google is playing a very particular role here, that of software and AI vendor.

That Gemini Intelligence integration, which has been teased from the start of the Googlebook announcement, is another differentiator not only from macOS and Windows, but also from Chromebooks. Google is positioning the Googlebook as the best place to interact with Gemini, whose increasingly agentic aspirations now tap into every corner of Google’s product lineup. But it’s also appealing to developers and vibe-coders alike with a native Antigravity app and 12 months of Google AI Pro, a subscription that comes with a substantial amount of coding credit.

So is a Googlebook for Android users who want to code? Is it for fans of ChromeOS who want more integration with their phones? Is it for the Android faithful, the diehards who have been waiting patiently for their turn in the ecosystem sun? 

We don’t have long to wait: Googlebooks hit the market early next month.

✉️ Inbox

The camera is my favorite part of smart glasses, but it just feels wrong now. Ben’s Weekender essay grapples with the realities of being a glasshole in 2026.

Roku adding new apps & subscription bundles, homescreen redesign expanding. Could Roku’s smart TV OS get any more bloated and ad-infested? Of course it could.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 saw a surge in popularity as soon as Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo. No doubt that’s why Samsung wanted to get ahead of the iPhone Duo’s release.
