Google ‘AI contribution pilot’ tests paying websites when they’re used in AI results. Any more money for publishers is a good thing, but I doubt this will end with more money for journalism over the long term.

Google goes in-depth, and a bit NSFW, on Noto 3D emoji as Android rollout expands. I love these so, so much.

Motorola confirms ‘Signature 27’ debut next week alongside new Snapdragon chips. It’s giving old-school Droid Razr in the best way possible. This will be the first ‘Signature’ phone to come to the US.

Motorola teases high-end ‘Signature 27’ with a wild-looking design

Clicks Communicator lands in December with 12GB RAM, two months of free data. We feature Clicks’ Kevin and Jeff in this week’s Sideload episode, and it was a really fun conversation.

Gmail adds ‘Copy code’ shortcut for 2FA on Android & iOS. This is super handy, and I feel like I’m going to use it all the time.

Here’s the OnePlus 16 that you probably won’t be able to buy [Video]. Womp, womp.

🤝 Cc: Kevin Michaluk

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Kevin Michaluk, Clicks co-founder and former BlackBerry superuser.

Who are you?

Kevin Michaluk aka @crackberrykevin / CBK

What do you do for work?

How It Started: Founder at CrackBerry.com & Mobile Nations (spent 15 years in tech media); How It’s Going: Founder & President at Clicks Technology.

What do you do for fun?

Depends on the season! This summer picked up golf again (my obsession in my teenage years) and pickleball for the first time. I spend so much time working that some physical activities out of the house/office and away from screens for a few hours a week feels like a necessity for my mental and physical health.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

More intentional than ever. I wrote the first book on Smartphone Addiction back in 2008 and have been more acutely aware than most of the detrimental effects on individuals and society that smartphones, social media and tech can have. That’s part of the reason we launched Clicks in 2024 and Communicator this year. We’re building purpose built tech that helps people restore some of that balance with tech by building tools that respect their time. It’s not about being overly restrictive, but building experiences that people love and ideally lead to a healthier relationship with their tech. 

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

Whoop – I’ve had an on again / off again with fitness trackers over the years and have literally used them all… but this past year have grown to really love and rely on my Whoop. I jive more with their use of recovery score and strain goals over step count goals or trying to close rings, and I like that they have accessories to wear the tracker in. Sleeping with a ring or band on my wrist annoys me and ruins my sleep – with Whoop I literally own several pairs of their “Whoop underwear” that I put the tracker in and wear to bed. And as a guy who loves wearing real watches, I just don’t like wearing a smartwatch on my wrist that could be better occupied by a mechanical watch. And even Whoop’s new AI Chat feature I use more than I thought I would… it’s come in real handy for when I’m traveling internationally and trying to map out the best sleep and workout schedules to help me balance the time zone changes.

Shopify – I mean, when you’re building a company and one of your biggest sales channels is DTC, it’s hard not to spend a LOT of time in Shopify. 

TOP SECRET – No, that’s not the name of the app… but ask me about it again in early 2027 and I’ll share the details on the newest app I’m using that I actually can’t live without. It’s changed my life – I can’t imagine not having it on my phone. I’m not allowed to talk about it right now, but as an early private beta user can’t wait for others to start using it too! 

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Clicks Communicator, obviously!

What’s a recent song or album you loved?

My song of the summer was literally Summer on the Inside by warner case. Puts me in a good mood whenever it comes on 😉 

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

Reacher… cuz.. Reacher.

What’s a recent book you loved?

Grow by Mike Fata. Written by a local and successful Winnipeg-based entrepreneur and friend of mine (who I like to golf and/or drink Chianti with!), and it’s just an easy and motivating read for founders, whether aspiring or already in the thick of it.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

Watched MayDay on a whim (had no expectations when I hit play) and laughed a bunch. Ryan Reynolds meets Top Gun vibes.

What’s a recent game you loved?

Building Clicks! I think of business as a Team Sport. Every day is like a new match – with a new challenge or opportunity presented and you play with your teammates to try and win the day. I love the people I work (err…play?!) with and while it is a lot of work, it’s also a ton of fun.  (Ed. I’ll allow it.)

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Hanging with my wife and dog… don’t ask me which I love more! 😃

Thank you, Kevin, for reminding me that you can always turn onions into lemonade.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

On the eve of Sorkin’s new movie, The Social Reckoning, it’s also a good idea to revisit The Social Network, a brilliant movie that boasts one of the best scores ever.

title: tvOS 27.2 adds new HomePod surround sound feature to Apple TV 4K
snippet: Apple TV users have long been able to set HomePods as speakers for audio output. But tvOS 27.2 looks poised to offer a big upgrade, with HomePod surround sound now available in the beta. more…
fullText:
Apple TV users have long been able to set HomePods as speakers for audio output. But tvOS 27.2 looks poised to offer a big upgrade, with HomePod surround sound now available in the beta.

tvOS 27.2 beta 2 supports using four HomePods at once as speakers

Earlier this month, it was discovered that HomePod 27 beta 8 included references to a forthcoming surround sound feature for Apple TV. 

Now as spotted by FlatpanelsHD, that feature has made an appearance in tvOS 27.2 beta 2.

We've examined tvOS 27.2 beta 2 and the rumored 4x HomePod wireless surround pairing with Apple TV 4K is now implemented, as shown below.

However, it's not yet fully baked, as there is currently no way to assign roles to each HomePod pair, i.e. front and rear speakers. It works… https://t.co/cufeJwx0PQ pic.twitter.com/IG3uqH32NU

— FlatpanelsHD (@Flatpanels) September 23, 2026

As seen in the screenshot above, the Apple TV 4K running tvOS 27.2 is configured to send audio to four HomePods total—two full-size models and two HomePod minis.

More details are shared by Rasmus Larsen on FlatpanelsHD’s website:

Via the Home app, you can now pair two sets of HomePods, four in total, wirelessly to Apple TV 4K. However, the feature is not yet fully baked, as you cannot assign roles to the four speakers, for example rear speakers – they play the same audio from the front and rear. It works with Atmos and surround sound from video sources, but menu and game audio only plays through the front speakers.

It’s been widely rumored for some time that Apple is working on a big overhaul and expansion of its Home product line. A new ‘HomePad’ device along with new Apple TV 4K and HomePod models are expected to launch in October.

Surround sound could be a great addition for HomePod and Apple TV users. But it’s also likely a good sign that Apple will indeed launch new Home products soon.

title: Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]
snippet: After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one.

I didn’t quite spend as much time with the software as my colleague Abner, so for a full set of impressions on these laptops running Googlebook OS, please read his extensive thoughts. This is a little more focused on the hardware side, with a sprinkle of software.

The good news right up top: My initial worries have almost completely been washed away, save a few minor complaints about two specific devices; there’s more here to like than I ever expected. Notice I said “almost” as there are still concerns in the back of my mind, but despite lots of, I guess, negativity surrounding and preceding this launch, the entire lineup of Googlebooks has exceeded my fairly low expectations.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

I do believe that this is largely due to my mixed experience with various Chromebooks across the entire price spectrum, combined with the ultimately lackluster or barebones “Desktop mode” that was added to Pixel devices over the past year.

This time, we have fewer SKUs to deal with, and of the five Googlebook devices, there appear to be fewer pinch points – save the pricing. These are not going to be cheap, with prices “starting at” $899 and, in most cases, are going to be more expensive. That is likely where a portion of you are going to stop reading and just dismiss these entirely. I can completely understand why.

Without glossing over or forgiving the frankly inflated asking price, I do believe this comes with one distinct benefit. There is less compromise in quality, which is something that worried me, given the mixed history of Chromebooks and the pitfalls of the cheapest model becoming the flag-bearer for the “default” experience.

I spent around 45 minutes prodding and poking the lineup, and there are two standouts.

Right off the bat, the Dell XPS and the HP Googlebook were the most impressive launch devices here. That said, each of the five laptops has its own merits.

ASUS’ Googlebook, Lenovo’s Googlebook 15, and Acer’s Googlebook 14 offer, in my opinion, are marginally lesser but still fairly decent takes on the first wave of hardware. The Lenovo in particular takes some design cues from previous Chromebooks and pairs with a bright HDR display. It was really easy to see despite lots of glare and jostling in the testing area.

I will state that I am personally not a fan of 2-in-1 laptops, but Googlebook OS, as it’s being styled, just turns the Acer model into arguably the best touchscreen laptop-tablet hybrid on the market. In fact, all of these laptops have excellent touchscreens that run at 120Hz. I was worried ahead of time that we’d get 60Hz screens, so it was very good to see a baseline of 120Hz.

Windows and ChromeOS have always struggled with touch inputs, while MacOS doesn’t allow for user interface control with your hands – or stylus. How many elite touchscreen experiences exist on a laptop? I wager until now, none. This is where Android, in my opinion, is being leveraged in the potentially best way possible. Swipes, taps, prods, it’s all just like using your phone or a tablet.

Just dipping back into a specific device in the lineup for a second, the matte display on the Acer Googlebook 14 was a great touch. It just eliminated glare almost entirely and reminded me of the recently released iPhone Duo. My only gripe was that it was covered in greasy fingerprints and smudges after a few minutes of usage.

Lenovo, ASUS, and Acer are utilizing Intel Core Ultra “Pantherlake” chips, while Dell and HP are going with the Snapdragon X Elite chipset. All come with at least 16GB of RAM for optimal performance. Some SKUs might offer up to 32GB of RAM, but my session made no mention of storage capacities, and there is no way to expand storage using external storage like a microSD card. There could be a really easy way to get people onside by offering these in future SKUs; for now, it’s business as usual.

More good news: The performance is excellent. Every Googlebook felt especially snappy. These are desktop-level chips running Android, which sort of is to be expected.

If anything, I was shocked at how responsive the experience was. It helps that each device has almost identical specifications. You can pick the laptop that suits your specific needs and still expect performance parity. Given my trepidation due to how Chromebooks have been treated by OEMs, this was very refreshing. It’s a good sign right at launch, but let’s hope Google holds more cards this time to almost force device makers to hit base specifications once cheaper models arrive.

The touchpads on all of the models are genuinely impressive. There’s some level of haptics, but MacBooks still reign supreme here. Every keyboard felt tight and responsive, and I liked stabbing away at the keys however briefly. None of the five models felt mushy or squishy under my fingers, and the layouts were instantly familiar to my battle-worn MacBook Pro battered fingertips. I didn’t have too long to test out the two unique keyboard G and odd Caps Lock keys, but they’ll no doubt take a while to get used to if you’re coming from Windows or Mac.

We saw ahead of launch that the lightbar is a key branding differentiator on the Googlebook. Sure, it looks nice, but it didn’t seem to do much beyond, well, look kind of cool. Google is planning on opening this LED strip up to developers in the coming months, so I’m sure we’ll get various takes on notifications, DND mode, and more that I probably haven’t thought of.

Correction: XPS laptops have been sold under the “Project Sputnik” banner with Ubuntu pre-installed in a partnership with Canonical that has been in place since 2012 and has become part of the Dell XPS Developer Edition series. Mostly focused on developers, the following incorrect statement has been removed, but is kept for posterity. Apologies for any confusion caused.

Something that I hope isn’t missed here is that the XPS Googlebook from Dell is the first such laptop from the company to come without Windows pre-installed. I think, given how mediocre the Dell Chromebook line was, this feels like a real statement of intent for a product line that is widely heralded as the best alternative to a MacBook. The company wouldn’t stake the XPS line on a mediocre product. It’s a gorgeous small-form-factor laptop, and one I really hope to spend some extended time with soon.

Can Android fill in the gap Chromebooks leave behind?

There are so many question marks over the Googlebook lineup, most notably who the platform is going to suit best or how it’ll fit into someone’s existing computing lineup. Some will ship with HDMI ports; there’s no room for a single SD card slot, or at least one that I remember spotting. I’d love to know what the experience is like using a secondary display or taking that experience elsewhere.

I feel like the software is much better than I had anticipated for a launch product. Yes, we’re missing a few top-level professional tools, but the full desktop Chrome browser might dispel some pre-launch detractors. I installed an extension I use every day, and it wanted to track my cashback while I was visiting a few of my favorite online shopping haunts. That reduced some of my initial fears of mobile Chrome on a laptop form factor.

What I cannot fault is the launch hardware. It is solid.

I went in with some preconceptions likely based on some of the leaks and, I’ll be honest, a mediocre unveil during the Android Show earlier this year. The devices have done a lot of the talking, which is an interesting prospect, as they already feel like a fluid expansion of Android into a new form factor.

Right now, I am likely not the target market. I need certain pieces of software, but ask yourself: do you have one key piece of software that is locking you into your current laptop or tablet? If that is the case, you probably were never looking at making a switch to a new desktop platform on launch day anyway.

My overriding early thought is that a Googlebook is an option for someone who has no allegiance to a desktop OS, but has a strong urge for their phone to expand into a bigger, more competent portable display. That might be a tiny portion of the market, but it could also be huge given that many people still use a phone for 95% of their day-to-day tasks. I don’t have a crystal ball or next week’s lottery numbers, but we have a new operating system to choose from, and I can’t be too negative about it. Any challengers to Windows, Mac, or Linux are good in my book. We just need things to start moving fast right out of the gate.

I think back to the early era of the smartphone. I imagined being able to take my phone, plug it into a screen, and have access to everything I need or use most. If that really worked, we’d all be using Samsung DeX, but we’re all still using separate laptops and desktops instead.

The modern smartphone is a hub for payments, photos, emails, entertainment, and the “right hand” of most people. Here’s what is different: The Googlebook takes your Android phone and turns it into a laptop. Whether you want it is ultimately up to you.

title: You can now claim your payout from Apple’s $250 million Siri settlement
snippet: The major class action lawsuit against Apple over Siri and Apple Intelligence delays continues to progress. Apple is expected to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit, and you can now submit your claim to get a chunk of that payout. Here’s how. more…
fullText:
The major class action lawsuit against Apple over Siri and Apple Intelligence delays continues to progress. Apple is expected to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit, and you can now submit your claim to get a chunk of that payout. Here’s how.

How to claim your payout from Apple’s Siri settlement

Verita Global, the Settlement Administrator behind the case, has set up the website where you can submit claim information.

The eligible class includes people in the United States who purchased an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025. That covers the window between when Apple announced the first Apple Intelligence features at WWDC and when it officially delayed the “more personalized” version of Siri.

Apple is paying $250 million to settle the lawsuit, while also admitting no wrongdoing. Legal fees and lawyers will take a chunk of the settlement. For iPhone users, the payout is expected to be $25 per eligible device. That number, however, could vary. If more users than expected file a claim, it could be less. If fewer claims are filed, the maximum payout is $95 per eligible device.

On the settlement website, you’ll be asked to submit your contact information as well as the serial number of the qualifying iPhone. You can then choose whether you’d like to be paid by check, PayPal, Venmo, or ACH. The deadline to submit a claim is December 21, 2026. 

The settlement website explains (via MacRumors): 

The Settlement will provide a cash payment if you purchased an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, or iPhone 16 Pro Max that you purchased between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025 in the United States.

You must fill out and submit a complete and accurate Claim Form below by December 21, 2026. If your Claim Form is incomplete, contains false information, or is not submitted by the deadline, your claim will be rejected and you will waive all rights to receive a payment under this Settlement. The information you provide will be treated as confidential and used for the purpose of this Settlement only.

While the settlement website is now live, it will still be more than a year until payouts are sent. The final approval hearing for payouts is September 29, 2027, and payments will begin at least 60 days after that. 

Are you submitting a claim to get your $25? Do you think this is a fair settlement? Let us know down in the comments.

title: U.S. government urges Supreme Court to reverse Apple contempt ruling over App Store commission
snippet: Several legal and business groups, in addition to the U.S. government, filed briefs with the Supreme Court this week in the Apple vs. Epic Games lawsuit, urging the justices to reverse at least part of the contempt ruling against Apple. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Several legal and business groups, in addition to the U.S. government, filed briefs with the Supreme Court this week in the Apple vs. Epic Games lawsuit, urging the justices to reverse at least part of the contempt ruling against Apple. Here are the details.

A bit of context

In late June, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear Apple’s argument that a civil contempt ruling against the company should be reversed in its fight against Epic Games.

In essence, when Apple was compelled to allow developers to direct users to external purchasing options, the company did so while imposing a 27% commission on those transactions. When Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, the district court found the company in civil contempt.

Apple has been allowing developers to link to external purchasing options without charging a commission ever since.

Since then, the company has been trying to reverse that ruling, arguing that the actual text of the injunction did not prohibit it from charging a commission, and that lower courts improperly relied on the “spirit of the injunction” to find the company in contempt.

For reference, the original order read:

Apple Inc. and its officers, agents, servants, employees, and any person in active concert or participation with them (“Apple”), are hereby permanently restrained and enjoined from prohibiting developers from (i) including in their apps and their metadata buttons, external links, or other calls to action that direct customers to purchasing mechanisms, in addition to In-App Purchasing and (ii) communicating with customers through points of contact obtained voluntarily from customers through account registration within the app.

Last week, Apple filed its official opening merits brief with the Supreme Court, arguing once again that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not clearly prohibit the company from charging a commission on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its briefing, Apple also argued that allowing the contempt finding to stand would increase the risk of judicial overreach when courts enforce injunctions, leaving companies uncertain about what conduct an order actually prohibits.

U.S. government and other groups weigh in

While Epic Games has until November 13 to file its response, the court this week received a number of amicus briefs (filings from outside interested parties) from the U.S. Department of Justice, through the Solicitor General’s office, along with several legal and business groups weighing in on Apple’s challenge.

In its amicus brief, the Department of Justice argues that “[c]ivil contempt is […] appropriate only if the defendant’s conduct is clearly covered by the injunction’s express terms,” which it says was not the case with Apple’s decision to charge a 27% commission.

It goes on to echo Apple’s argument that civil contempt is improper whenever there is a “fair ground of doubt” as to whether an injunction actually prohibited the conduct at issue, concluding that the Supreme Court “should reverse the contempt finding as to the 27% commission.”

In the same brief, however, the Department of Justice says the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over its “plain button” restriction, arguing that the injunction clearly required Apple to permit both buttons and links, while Apple’s implementation effectively allowed only links.

On the remaining issues, such as restrictions on where external purchase links could appear, the Department of Justice says the Supreme Court should set aside the existing rulings and send them back to the lower courts to be reconsidered under the “fair ground of doubt” standard.

In addition to the Department of Justice, the Supreme Court also received amicus briefs from:

The Chamber of Commerce of the United States

Chamber of Progress

Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers

International Center for Law and Economics (ICLE)

Computer & Communications Industry Association, NetChoice, and Software & Information Industry Association

Washington Legal Foundation (WLF)

In short, they all support the general argument that Apple could not properly be held in civil contempt for conduct that the injunction did not clearly prohibit, and that courts should enforce injunctions based on their actual terms rather than their perceived “spirit.”

The ICLE adds that “choosing a profitable way to comply is still compliance,” while the Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers cited past precedent to argue that having judges determine what commission Apple may charge “is precisely the type of ‘direct price administration’ that ‘antitrust courts normally avoid.’”

Currently, proceedings are underway in the district court to determine how much, if any, commission Apple may charge on linked-out purchases, while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling itself.

snippet: Google today is rolling out Android Canary 2609 with another update to Quick Settings that lets you require an unlock before making changes. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out Android Canary 2609 with another update to Quick Settings that lets you require an unlock before making changes.

ZP11.260821.010 with the September 2026 security patch is available for the Pixel 10a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 8a, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7, Pixel 6a, Pixel Fold, and Pixel Tablet.

Google notes that “support for Pixel 11 devices will be added with the next Canary release. Additionally, Google has dropped support for the Pixel 6 and 6 Pro.

As always, “Canary builds are highly experimental and are NOT recommended for general use.”

	

Require unlock for Quick Settings

Go to Settings > Display & touch > Lock screen for the new “Require unlock for Quick Settings” toggle that is off by default: “To prevent unauthorized changes, you must unlock your device to use Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Mobile Data, and Airplane Mode.”

When enabled, you can still open the Quick Settings panel from the lockscreen, but tapping on those key Tiles will prompt you to fingerprint or PIN unlock. The flashlight, rotation, dark theme, etc. don’t require authorization.

Audio streams Quick Settings Tile

Additionally, the “Voice broadcast” Tile moves from system apps to Connectivity.

Notification Intelligence 

Appearing on older devices (Pixel 8) with just the existing Notification cooldown feature.

title: Google goes in-depth, and a bit NSFW, on Noto 3D emoji as Android rollout expands
snippet: Google Design published a more detailed explanation of Noto 3D today as it expands beyond Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google Design published a more detailed explanation of Noto 3D today as it expands beyond Pixel devices.

Google explains that the design process for Noto 3D involved “drawing, sculpting, and debating every single character by hand so that dimension never came at the cost of soul.”

Noto 3D prioritizes “emotional clarity” over “treating emoji as miniature scans of the natural world.”

Our job was to preserve the vibe behind each symbol: using 3D to give the character a body, but illustration to give it a soul.

Research found that “highly anatomical details like irises or nostril depth actually slow down how fast our brains process emotion,” so the aim was to remove “extraneous detail and [keep] facial geometry minimal.” Additionally, “excessive props and texture destroy comprehension,” with “background features and accessories” becoming “visual static” at 18×18 pixels.

	

The design team ultimately decided that “every emoji gets at most three essential details to communicate what it is.”

In going from flat assets to three dimensions, Google asked: “What does the back of a smiley face look like?” NSFW (truly) joke aside, the team found examples like how the poodle emoji only had three legs.

Meanwhile, the same research found that “people empathize far more with complete silhouettes — especially when it comes to depicting real animals.” As such, Google moved away from floating heads. 

Seeing an animal’s stance, paws, and posture helps communicate intent. Upon learning this last year, we updated a few animal emoji, like the raccoon, to embrace its full mischievous self — and now in 3D.

Following the Pixel 11 launch, Noto 3D is now “rolling out across Google apps, Android, and select devices from partners including Nothing, Lenovo, Xiaomi, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, vivo, iQOO, HONOR, TECNO, Infinix, itel, [and] Motorola.” You can also browse the entire collection on Google’s dedicated page.

title: The tiny magnetic e-readers from Xteink that attach to your Pixel are on sale right now
snippet: Qi2 or MagSafe have always been one of the wildest but useful additions to phones like the Google Pixel or iPhone, and the best accessory might just be another display on its own. Xteink’s magnetic mini e-readers, like the X4 Pro, are on sale while stock lasts during its autumn sale. more…
fullText:
Qi2 or MagSafe have always been one of the wildest but useful additions to phones like the Google Pixel or iPhone, and the best accessory might just be another display on its own. Xteink’s magnetic mini e-readers, like the X4 Pro, are on sale while stock lasts during its autumn sale.

I don’t personally believe there is a perfect e-reader size, but there’s absolutely nothing wrong with having a tiny e-reader on hand when you want to knock out another chapter. The Xteink X4 Pro and Classic models fit that mold with a corner-to-corner size of just 4.3 inches. Both fall under 6mm thick, so they don’t sit too pronounced when stuck to the back of your phone.

An e-reader doesn’t need to be fancy, just good. At $109 and $89 for the Xteink Pro and Classic, respectively, these are certainly good options for many users.

Right now, though, both have dropped by a $10 discount during Xteink’s fall sale. That puts the Xteink X4 Pro at $99 and the X4 Classic model at $79. It’s not a massive discount, but it’s enough to make the Pro version more approachable. It has a couple of advantages, like a front light for night reading and a bigger battery.

	

An illuminated display makes a huge difference, especially if you tend to read during your commute or want to put your phone down before bed and don’t want to keep the lights on while you fight to stay awake through what just so happens to be the longest chapter in the book.

A bigger battery helps, too. But it isn’t a massive game-changer with these low-demand devices. The biggest thing is the magnetic back, which doesn’t require a case if you have something like the Pixel 11. It can stick to the back of your phone at all times, or just when you need it. The point is, it adds a paper-like screen to your device so you can read in a little more comfort.

Xteink’s fall sale is first-come, first-served, and it’s expected to end on September 30.

snippet: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is mostly known for its global dominance over petroleum production and oil reserves - not necessarily cars and auto manufacturing, and certainly not electric vehicle production. fullText:
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is mostly known for its global dominance over petroleum production and oil reserves — not necessarily cars and auto manufacturing, and certainly not electric vehicle production. So it was a little surprising on Monday when a Saudi startup called Ceer unveiled a pair of hyper-angular, spaceship-like EVs, with plans to launch an additional five models by 2030.

The Exobot (yes, that’s the real name) sedan and SUV are expected to go on sale in Saudi Arabia starting in 2027. The ultra-futuristic designs scream Tron, Blade Runner, and every other sci-fi movie you’ve seen — and then some. The gullwing doors are ripped straight from the Tesla Model X (which, of course, was ripped straight from the DeLorean and a range of other rare production cars). Wild and wedge-shaped, the Exobots seemed built explicitly to draw attention. Which, in an attention-based economy, is probably the right strategy.

1/10

The sedan Exobot has low-slung, supercar proportions with a steeply raked windshield that flows seamlessly into the hood. The front fascia features a razor-thin, full-width LED light bar nestled under a sharp, forward-jutting nose, giving it a mean, visor-like glare. The two-tone bodywork and ample windshield immediately had me thinking about the Ferrari Luce, the polarizing electric supercar released earlier this year.

The SUV boasts a blocky, military-meets-cyberpunk stance with high ground clearance and aggressive angles. The whole thing looks thick and armor-plated, with a flat roofline and a distinctive, tactical presence. I wouldn’t be surprised to see this thing bouncing along the Moon’s surface someday. Both were designed by Rob Melville, McLaren’s former design director. But according to Autocar, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had final say on the design.

1/8

Ceer is hoping to take advantage of all the upheaval in the global car market, driven largely by the flood of Chinese electric vehicle exports in Asia, Europe, and South America. The US appears on its way to becoming an automotive backwater, with its ahistorical embrace of internal combustion engines and steep tariffs designed to keep Chinese EVs at bay. Why not release a pair of bombastic Batmobiles as a way to distract from the originating country’s extreme oil dependency?

Ceer didn’t exactly emerge from nothing. Rather, it’s a joint venture between Saudi Arabia’s PIF sovereign wealth fund and Foxconn, the Taiwanese company most known for manufacturing the iPhone for Apple. The company will be funded by the kingdom’s vast oil wealth, but with the purpose of building a lineup of vehicles that run on electricity.

Even though it’s distinctly a project built to jump-start the kingdom’s auto industry, Ceer needed to venture outside its borders when hiring for its top roles. Jim DeLuca spent 37 at General Motors, ending up as executive VP for global manufacturing, before joining Ceer as CEO.

“We ⁠wanted to make sure the world could see what Saudi Arabia is capable of,” DeLuca told Reuters. 

The kingdom has had mixed luck when it comes to automotive projects. There were plans to build a Jaguar-Land Rover factory there over a decade ago, but to no avail. Toyota declined a deal with the Saudis in 2019. The Public Investment Fund owns a controlling stake in California-based Lucid Motors, which is now building a manufacturing facility in King Abdullah Economic City.

Ceer is taking a diversified approach to its vehicle lineup. While the first models will be electric, subsequent vehicles will be hybrid and combustion-engine, depending on market demands.

That said, starting a car company from scratch is daunting. Just ask Fisker, Lordstown, or Arrival — all of which went bankrupt. Even Lucid, with its support from PIF, is still struggling. We’ll have to see whether Ceer can buck that trend.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is mostly known for its global dominance over petroleum production and oil reserves — not necessarily cars and auto manufacturing, and certainly not electric vehicle production. So it was a little surprising on Monday when a Saudi startup called Ceer unveiled a pair of hyper-angular, spaceship-like EVs, with plans to launch an additional five models by 2030.

The Exobot (yes, that’s the real name) sedan and SUV are expected to go on sale in Saudi Arabia starting in 2027. The ultra-futuristic designs scream Tron, Blade Runner, and every other sci-fi movie you’ve seen — and then some. The gullwing doors are ripped straight from the Tesla Model X (which, of course, was ripped straight from the DeLorean and a range of other rare production cars). Wild and wedge-shaped, the Exobots seemed built explicitly to draw attention. Which, in an attention-based economy, is probably the right strategy.

title: Android Auto update lets you customize your Google Maps ‘driving avatar’ via car display
snippet: Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display.

The ability to change the classic blue arrow navigation icon in Google Maps itself is not new, but it’s only been available on car displays for about a year. In May 2025, Google Maps rolled out support for showing your chosen icon on Android Auto and CarPlay, but it needed to be set on the phone itself. 

Now, Google is rolling out an on-car picker for your Google Maps “driving avatar” on Android Auto.

The change is rather simple. Through Google Maps on Android Auto, a new “driving avatar” setting appears alongside settings for home/work and alerts. Tapping it gives you the option to pick your avatar and change it to the color of your choice. It’s the same functionality found on your phone, just now accessible directly via the car’s display.

	

This appears to be going live with a server-side update. Android Authority spotted the change with Android Auto 17.8.163744 and Google Maps 26.38.01.980791571 but, despite using those same versions, we’re not seeing the option just yet. Sound off in the comments below if you have it.

In our teardown of Android Auto 17.8, we also noticed that Google has removed the neat little “Jimothy” Easter egg which, as we predicted, was clearly never meant for a public-facing rollout.

title: Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Qualcomm today announced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 to power the next generation of Android smartphones. more…
fullText:
Qualcomm today announced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 to power the next generation of Android smartphones.

The big change this year is how there are a pair of chips. Qualcomm considers both to be “flagship” offerings that give “OEMs greater choice.” The Elite Gen 6 is seen as the follow-up to last year’s Elite Gen 5, while the Elite Extreme Gen 6 comes in a level higher.

Both are built on a 2nm process with an Oryon CPU that has two 5GHz Prime Cores and six 4GHz Performance cores. The 8 Elite Gen 6 offers 10% improved CPU performance and a 37% gain in power efficiency compared to the Gen 5. 

On the 8 Elite Extreme, CPU performance improves by 13% compared to last generation. A global VVC (H.266) codec on the Extreme allows for more power-efficient video. 

	

A “rearchitected” Adreno GPU offers 35% improved GPU performance and 40% power efficiency improvement over the Gen 5.

On the Extreme, there are AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores that allow for more advanced models to run. GPU performance improves 44% compared to last year. There’s also 18 MB of High Performance Memory that compared to last generation offers a 12% power improvement. For gaming, Adreno Neural Fusion uses the new GPU matrix cores for AI super-resolution and frame generation, which makes possible up to 40% power savings in supported games.

The Hexagon NPU features a new Element Accelerator for transformer workloads to benefit LLMs. There’s 14% improved NPU performance and 20% improved AI performance-per-watt with the 12 scalar + 8 vector + 1 tensor + 1 element configuration.

On the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, a 50% larger shared memory allows for 30B+ parameters Mixture of Experts (MoE) models. The aim is to reduce trips to external memory, with 35% improved NPU performance and 33% improved AI  performance-per-watt. 

The Spectra ISP features what Qualcomm calls Intelligent Pixel Control to understand scenes on a per-pixel level. On the Extreme, you have support for 8K60 video and 4K240 ultra HD slow-motion capture. 

Both chips are paired with the Qualcomm X105 5G modem that is “newly architected” for greater downlink (10% increase) and uplink speeds. Specifically, six antennas can capture multiple data streams at once. This supports 3GPP Release 19 5G Advanced.

Motorola today announced the Signature 27 with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. More on that here.

Note: Qualcomm paid for travel and accommodations for this launch event, but had no input on editorial content.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 missing one health-focused feature
snippet: Well, this is odd. The handwashing timer feature is currently absent from the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 hardware. more…
fullText:
Well, this is odd. The handwashing timer feature is currently absent from the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 hardware.

Handwashing detection and timer feature not currently supported by Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4

Handwashing detection is still a feature in watchOS 27. It also remains a category in Apple Health, including the iOS 27.2 version. Handwashing detection works on Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3, and it’s still included in the watchOS 27 guide.

However, Apple’s newest watches aren’t included in the supported hardware list. It’s unclear if that’s an omission or a hardware difference.

In theory, there’s no reason to even mention supported hardware if Apple planned to continue supporting the feature on its newest watches. 

Handwashing detection arrived in 2020 as part of watchOS 7. It’s likely this pandemic-era feature is just no longer supported by Apple’s 2026 hardware. Series 12 and Ultra 4 include the first overhauled processor for the first time in a few years. It features new Audio Intelligence features like Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Handwashing detection may have just been left out.

We’ll update our coverage if we learn more about the missing feature.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are both available now. You can read the 9to5Mac review here.

title: Apple Watch Series 12: My three favorite new features so far
snippet: I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 last week, and so far after a few days of testing there are three standout features for me. more…
fullText:
I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 last week, and so far after a few days of testing there are three standout features for me.

#1: S11 chip makes everything fast

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri has been sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

#2: New health features and complications

The new Health Sensing System should make Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the new health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:

Heart Rate

Daily Steps

Readiness

These let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. 

I’ve been testing heart rate and step complications, but my Watch needs more data before readiness is available. Overall though, these are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

#3: Faster charging

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:

Apple Watch Series 12: 15 minutes charge gets up to 12 hours battery life

Apple Watch Series 11: 15 minutes charge gets up to 8 hours battery life

I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off quickly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

For more Series 12 thoughts, check out my colleague Chance’s full review here.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now available starting at $399.

title: iOS 27 gives Apple Mail my most wished for feature upgrade
snippet: Apple’s Mail app in iOS 27 includes the feature upgrade that’s been at the top of my wishlist for years: search that “just works.” more…
fullText:
Apple’s Mail app in iOS 27 includes the feature upgrade that’s been at the top of my wishlist for years: search that “just works.”

iOS 27 overhauls search in Apple Mail to make it more relevant and accurate

Apple’s Mail app has long been plagued by lackluster search. 

I suspect that statement won’t be controversial at all among years-long users of the app. In fact, some might say “lackluster” is too kind a word to use.

But Apple says iOS 27 finally brings the Apple Mail search upgrade the app deserves.

From Apple’s website detailing iOS 27’s new features:

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

Here’s how this new ranking system in Mail will benefit users.

When you first open search in iOS 27’s Mail app, there’s a banner at the top that highlights “Expanded Search Results.” It explains: “Mail can look for more results based on what you mean, not just the words you type.”

Essentially, Apple is bringing search into the 21st century. Or you could say, it’s making search work the way it always should have.

I’ve used iOS 27 in beta for several months, and in my experience it’s definitely an upgrade over the old system. There hasn’t been a single time that I’ve tried searching for something and couldn’t find it. But understandably, your mileage may vary.

The improved search relies on proper indexing, so if your iPhone is still performing indexing (check the Settings app to see if it’s “Optimizing Search & Siri”), you may need to wait a bit before search works as well as it should.

What’s your take on Apple Mail’s search capabilities today? Have you tried the iOS 27 version yet? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google Keep update tweaks the homescreen widget on Android
snippet: Google Keep for Android has rolled out a small tweak to the “Note collection” widget that shows a feed on your homescreen. more…
fullText:
Google Keep for Android has rolled out a small tweak to the “Note collection” widget that shows a feed on your homescreen.

The Material You-era sidebar on the right with shortcuts to add a text note, list, audio, drawing, or photo has been removed. It has been replaced by a circular FAB (floating action button) — like on “Single note” — that opens a pop-up. 

Introducing a second tap for note creation, this menu matches the behavior of the smaller, pill-shaped “Quick capture” widget.

Old vs. new

	

As such, there’s now an edge-to-edge design and you get to see a bit more of each note. By comparison, the previous design left considerable empty space, especially if you went for a full-width homescreen layout. 

Version 5.26.365.x of Google Keep is rolling out via the Play Store.

This follows the rollout of Keep Live for Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers.

snippet: The weather is turning cooler, and it’s time for camping and football tailgates. BLAVOR’s 20000mAh Solar Power Bank is built for this time of year. It has four built-in cables so you can leave your bag at home, a solar panel for recharging, and a wireless pad on top for your iPhone and Apple Watch. Let’s take a look at it. more…
fullText:
The weather is turning cooler, and it’s time for camping and football tailgates. BLAVOR’s 20000mAh Solar Power Bank is built for this time of year. It has four built-in cables so you can leave your bag at home, a solar panel for recharging, and a wireless pad on top for your iPhone and Apple Watch. Let’s take a look at it.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Four built-in cables

This is what sold me on the concept overall. The unit has four cables built directly into the housing (two USB-C, one Lightning, one USB-A) plus three separate ports, so you can charge six devices at once without carrying a standalone cable, which makes packing a lot easier.

The USB-C port supports 20-watt fast charging, which BLAVOR says gets a typical iPhone to full in around 50 minutes (Pro vs Pro Max will obviously change). On the capacity side, 20000mAh works out to roughly 4 charges for an iPhone 17, 2.7 for an iPad mini, and 37 for an Apple Watch. Those are BLAVOR’s numbers, but the ballpark is right for a bank this size battery overall. A lot will depend on temperature, if you are using it while charging, etc.

Wireless charging, but no MagSafe

There’s a wireless charging area on top that works with both the iPhone and the Apple Watch, but it has no magnets. This is plain old-school Qi, not MagSafe or Qi2, so your iPhone sits on the surface rather than snapping to it. Set the bank down on a table, and your iPhone stays put. I won’t stay connected in a bag, etc Ideally in a future one, I’d love to see MagSAafe

BLAVOR only advertises the 20-watt figure for the wired USB-C port, so treat the wireless pad as a convenience charger, not your primary way to charge. If you want high speeds, use one of the four cables already attached to the battery.

Solar charging is a great addition, but it won’t let you charge the battery from empty to full. A panel this small cannot recharge a 20000mAh cell in a day of sun. What it can do is keep the bank from dying over a long trip and give you an emergency option when there’s no outlet nearby. I would think of it as more of a backup option.

BLAVOR packed seven extras with the battery: a flashlight with three modes, a camping light with three brightness levels, a compass, a thermometer, a carabiner, and actually rope. It’s rated IPX5, which means splash and rain-resistant.

Wrap up

This is not the battery you will use on the plane. This is a great option for camping, tailgating, etc. It’s a good, nice one with plenty of wired options and really handy for an emergency recharge via solar. Super unique concept, and it’s something I’ll keep in my camping bag, etc.

You can buy the BLAVOR Solar Power Bank from Amazon or directly from BLAVOR.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 introduce a new Theater Mode setting
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new Health Sensing System that dramatically improves heart rate data. The new system also includes a new Theater Mode setting that you may want to enable. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new Health Sensing System that dramatically improves heart rate data. The new system also includes a new Theater Mode setting that you may want to enable.

The new watches measure heart rate every five seconds, a big increase over the five-minute rate from prior models. 

As a result, the green light behind the watch is pretty much always flashing now. It’s not something you’ll notice when you’re wearing your watch tight. However, you may see the green light if your band is a bit loose.

For that reason, the new Apple Watches drop back to the five-minute interval in two modes: Theater Mode and Sleep Mode.

Sleep Mode dropping down to five-minute intervals makes sense for a few reasons. First, it helps extend battery life while you’re not active. Second, sleeping means the watch doesn’t need to detect physical activity in the same way.

Theater Mode is different. Toggled on and off from Control Center, Theater Mode is meant to prevent the watch display from lighting up.

By default, it also drops heart rate sensing from live to every five minutes. This is presumably to prevent the green light from being noticeable in a dark environment.

However, if you don’t think the light is visible and want the most detailed heart rate data, you can change a new Theater Mode setting.

In Settings > Heart on the watch, you can toggle on “In Theater Mode” under “Allow Continuous Measurements” to restore the more frequent measurements. 

For me, I’m not noticing the green light unless I intentionally peak under the watch, so I turned the toggle on for now.

If the option existed for Sleep Focus as well, I’d be happy to give it a shot and see how it affects battery life as well. The other option is to just not use the Sleep Focus, but then you give up wrist temperature collection and probably Readiness score compatibility.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are both available now. You can read the 9to5Mac review here.

title: New all-glass iPhone 20 Pro rumor reveals another design change
snippet: Apple’s major 20th-anniversary iPhone refresh is in the works for next year. A new rumor today reiterates expectations that the iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone 20 Pro Max will have even bigger screens than the current models. more…
fullText:
Apple’s major 20th-anniversary iPhone refresh is in the works for next year. A new rumor today reiterates expectations that the iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone 20 Pro Max will have even bigger screens than the current models.

The rumor comes from Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station, who has a track record of sharing accurate iPhone leaks. Here are the screen sizes of next year’s iPhone 20 Pro models, according to the latest leak:

iPhone 20 Pro: 6.41 inches

iPhone 20 Pro Max: 6.96 inches

For comparison, the iPhone 18 Pro features a 6.27-inch display measured diagonally, which Apple markets as 6.3 inches. The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.86-inch display, which Apple rounds to 6.9 inches in its marketing materials.

This means the iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone 20 Pro Max could have the biggest iPhone screens ever — save, of course, for the 7.6-inch inner display on the looming iPhone Duo.

Today’s rumor adds that Apple is testing a “borderless quad-curved design” with a hole-punch display design, featuring a smaller Dynamic Island. The design is widely expected to be made primarily from glass.

In August, Bloomberg reported that this 20th-anniversary iPhone is still on track for next year. Mark Gurman described the design as using glass on the front and the back, and that the material “will curve into the sides of the devices, with a metal band in the middle.”

title: M6 Mac mini review: Apple’s most versatile Mac continues to shine
snippet: Over the last several years, the Mac mini has become one of the most compelling Macs in Apple’s lineup. It combines impressive performance with a compact footprint, making it versatile enough for all kinds of workflows. I’ve spent the last week using the M6 Mac mini, and it pushes that formula even further. Here’s everything you need to know. Buy the M6 Mac mini: from $879.99 (Reg. $899) Buy the M5 Pro Mac mini: from $1,669.99 (Reg. $1,699) more…
fullText:
Over the last several years, the Mac mini has become one of the most compelling Macs in Apple’s lineup. It combines impressive performance with a compact footprint, making it versatile enough for all kinds of workflows.

I’ve spent the last week using the M6 Mac mini, and it pushes that formula even further. Here’s everything you need to know.

Buy the M6 Mac mini: from $879.99 (Reg. $899)

Buy the M5 Pro Mac mini: from $1,669.99 (Reg. $1,699)

Design

From the outside, the new Mac mini looks identical to its predecessor. Apple gave the Mac mini its first proper redesign in more than a decade in 2024, dramatically shrinking its footprint to just 5 by 5 inches. That same design persists today, and it’s still incredibly easy to love.

There’s something about having the small but powerful Mac mini on my desk that just makes me smile. The amount of power Apple has packed into this tiny footprint is nothing short of impressive.

It’s a delightful example of Apple’s design team at its best, without compromising performance or connectivity.

Connectivity

On the front, you’ll find two USB-C ports and a 3.5mm headphone jack. On the back of the M6 configuration, you’ll find three Thunderbolt 4 ports, while the M5 Pro version features three Thunderbolt 5 ports. There’s also an HDMI port on the back.

One nice change: 2.5Gb Ethernet is now standard on both the M6 and M5 Pro configurations. The M4 models started at gigabit Ethernet. 10Gb remains an optional upgrade.

The other two connectivity updates for the new Mac mini models include Wi-Fi 7 instead of Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6 instead of Bluetooth 5.3.

For external displays, both versions of the Mac mini support up to three displays, but specifics vary based on the chip:

M4

M6

1 display

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

2 displays

2× 6K/60 or 4K/144; or 8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + 5K/60

2× 6K/60 or 4K/165; or 8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + 5K/60

3 displays

2× 6K/60 or 4K/144 + 1× 5K/60

2× 6K/60 or 4K/165 + 1× 5K/60

Single TB port

Up to 2 displays

Up to 2 displays

DisplayPort

1.4

1.4

M4 Pro

M5 Pro

1 display

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

2 displays

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + (6K/60 or 4K/144)

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + (5K/120 or 4K/200)

3 displays

3× 6K/60 or 4K/144

3× 6K/60 or 4K/165

Single TB port

Up to 2 displays

Up to 3 displays

DisplayPort

2.1

2.1

Performance

My review unit is the M6 configuration of the Mac mini, so I’m going to focus on that for most of this review. The M5 Pro version is the same chip we’ve come to know and love since debuting in the MacBook Pro earlier this year.

Here are the specs of my review unit:

12-core CPU

12-core GPU

24GB unified memory

512GB storage

The M6 chip has two additional CPU cores compared to the M4 and M5 chips. It’s Apple’s first 2nm processor for the Mac. It’s also Apple’s first chip to use all three of its CPU core types: 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores.

The super cores prioritize maximum single-threaded performance, while performance cores are optimized for multithreaded workloads. The efficiency cores handle lighter background tasks.

Memory bandwidth has also increased significantly, from 120GB/s with the M4 to up to 170GB/s with the M6 (153GB/s on the 16GB configuration).

The M6 also features a new 12-core GPU, up from the 10-core GPU in the M4. Apple says graphics performance is up to 2x faster than the M4 Mac mini, including up to 2x faster ray-traced rendering in Blender. Each GPU core also includes a Neural Accelerator, helping the M6 deliver up to 4x faster AI performance than the M4 Mac mini.

I won’t pretend to regularly run local AI models or other on-device AI workflows, so I don’t have much real-world insight to offer here. But for people who do, Apple’s own testing suggests the gains are real.

Here’s Federico Viticci, whose AI opinion I trust, on the new Mac Studio: 

M5 Ultra Mac Studio Review: The Dream Mac for Local AI Agents

In Geekbench 7 testing, the M6 Mac mini scored 4,074 in single-core, 22,632 in multi-core, and 92,542 in the Metal GPU test. That puts it 24% ahead of the M4 in single-core performance, 48% ahead in multi-core performance, and 71% ahead in GPU performance.

Geekbench results, of course, aren’t necessarily indicative of real-world performance. Instead, they’re good for cross-reference comparisons to other Macs.

As you can see, the M6 also starts to encroach on M4 Pro territory, beating the 12-core M4 Pro in both single-core and multi-core performance, though the M4 Pro still has the edge in GPU performance.

Apple also says the M6 Mac mini offers up to 2x faster storage, and my benchmarking supports that. I consistently hit around 6,000-6,400 MB/s write speeds and 6,000-6,300 MB/s read speeds in Blackmagic Disk Speed Test. For comparison, 512GB M4 Mac mini configurations generally reached around 3,000 to 3,400 MB/s.

Pricing

When Apple debuted the redesigned Mac mini in 2024, we marveled at the price. It started at $599 with the M4 chip paired with 16GB of memory and 256GB of storage.

A lot has changed since then.

The Mac mini has become a go-to recommendation for people looking for dedicated machines to run AI agents and other AI workflows. We’ve entered what former Apple CEO Tim Cook has called a “100-year flood” in terms of memory prices, and there are no signs of that ending anytime soon.

In May, Apple stopped selling the 256GB storage configuration for the M4 Mac mini, making the base configuration 512GB. This raised the pricing floor from $599 to $799.

When Apple raised prices for most products over the summer, the 256GB Mac mini configuration returned, priced at $799 (up $200 compared to its launch price).

At the time, it was reasonable to think this was Apple insulating the Mac mini from any future increases (at least in the short term). Unfortunately, that wasn’t the case.

The M6 Mac mini starts at $899 for 256GB of storage and 16GB of memory. The M5 Pro configuration starts at $1,699, up $300 from the M4 Pro launch price and up $100 from the M4 Pro’s most recent price.

The thing that stands out to me, though, isn’t necessarily the $899 starting price. It’s that you still only get 256GB of storage. If the M6 Mac mini started with 512GB of storage, I don’t think there would be much room to complain about the price. Instead, upgrading to 512GB of storage costs an additional $200, pushing the price to $1,099.

So, the good news is the Mac mini is better than it’s ever been. The bad news is that it’s no longer the exceptional $599 value it was two years ago … it’s just a really good value instead.

9to5Mac’s Take

I love that we live in a world where the Mac mini is thriving. Apple’s smallest Mac, which has occasionally felt neglected, is having its well-deserved moment in the spotlight.

There’s a lot to love about the new Mac mini, including the faster performance and storage, all with the same great design. That combination of performance and design also makes it the most versatile Mac Apple sells, whether you’re using it as a desktop, an always-on server, a machine for running AI agents, or something else entirely.

Is it a little awkward that the Mac mini comes in M6 and M5 Pro configurations, as opposed to M6 and M6 Pro? On paper, sure, but practically I’m glad that Apple is focused on updating the Mac mini with whatever chips are ready at a given moment. That flexibility is one of the best things about the Apple Silicon era.

While the higher starting price changes the value equation, it doesn’t change my overall feelings about the Mac mini. It’s still an easy Mac to recommend for people who want a compact desktop Mac without spending substantially more for a Mac Studio.

title: Samsung Gallery rolling out Google Photos sync, here are the details you need to know
snippet: As teased, Samsung Gallery is now rolling out support for Google Photos sync, though there are a few details worth noting. more…
fullText:
As teased, Samsung Gallery is now rolling out support for Google Photos sync, though there are a few details worth noting.

Through app updates earlier this week, Samsung confirmed it was replacing the Microsoft OneDrive backup integration in its Gallery app with Google Photos sync. The change wasn’t live at the time, but works similarly to integrations found in the pre-installed Gallery apps on other phones from other Android brands such as OnePlus and Xiaomi.

Now, it’s actually starting to roll out.

Following updates to the Gallery Sync and Samsung Cloud apps, a Samsung Gallery update is also now rolling out to some users, which enables Google Photos integration – we’re not yet seeing the update on our end. Ice Universe shared screenshots of the settings.

	

Samsung Gallery v15.9.01.7 seems to be the trigger for activating sync, despite other apps actually facilitating the sync.

On a support page, Google offers more details on how Samsung Gallery > Google Photos sync works. It requires your Samsung device to be running Android 13 or newer, doesn’t support Workspace accounts, and there are some restrictions on what media you can see and what features work.

Google says that images and videos synced from Samsung Gallery won’t work with Memories and highlights, Live albums, or Search in Google Photos. Samsung Gallery also won’t show content backed up directly through Photos – only content synced from Samsung Gallery via a Samsung device shows up in the app.

Samsung has access to the media items that were originally backed up from Gallery Cloud Sync, but not to other items in Google Photos that were not backed up from a synced Samsung device.

If your device has all of the needed updates, you’ll find the option to enable Google Photos sync in Samsung Gallery via Menu > Settings > Sync > Sync photos and videos.

Samsung Gallery’s integration with OneDrive ends on September 30 for those still using it.

title: Comma’s hands-off driving tech under investigation after 2 fatal crashes
snippet: The investigation involves at least some crashes where it appears drivers were using "forked" versions of Comma's software.
fullText:
Comma.ai, the startup founded by hacker George Hotz, is facing a federal investigation after five reported crashes involving the company’s aftermarket hands-off driver assistance tech, two of which resulted in three deaths.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) said this week that the reported crashes involved Comma.ai devices failing to detect or respond to slow or stopped vehicles in the same road lane. Across four of the crashes, as many as 11 people were injured, some seriously.

Some of the crashes, including at least one of the fatal incidents, may have involved the use of “forked” or modified versions of Comma.ai’s software, according to the ODI.

Comma.ai could not immediately be reached for comment. Hotz, who distanced himself from the startup’s day-to-day operations in 2022, did not immediately return a request for comment.

Founded in 2015, Comma.ai makes devices that can be installed on a range of modern cars. The devices — and Comma.ai’s software, “openpilot” — can control a car’s Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Automated Lane Centering (ALC) systems to perform functions “similar to Tesla Autopilot and GM Super Cruise,” according to the startup’s website. The goal is to “make driving chill.”

Comma.ai’s website claims that “openpilot can steer, accelerate, and brake automatically for other vehicles within its lane.” Still, much like Tesla and GM, Comma.ai warns drivers that they “must always be capable to immediately retake manual control of the vehicle, by stepping on either pedal or by pressing the cancel button.” The company’s device uses a camera-based driver-monitoring system to watch for distracted or sleepy drivers.

One of the two fatal crashes appears to have happened in February 2026 in Ascension Parish, Louisiana. A 2022 Toyota RAV4, which was running FrogPilot, a third-party fork of openpilot, struck a stopped first responder vehicle.

Louisiana State Police released details of a crash in February that appear to match the report in the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s database. In that crash, the Toyota struck a “fully marked Gonzales Police Department unit, was unoccupied and positioned in the left lane with emergency lights activated while officers investigated a separate crash.” The state police said two rear-seat passengers of the Toyota died. 

The other fatal crash couldn’t be immediately identified by the report numbers cited by the ODI. 

Advanced driver assistance systems have historically struggled with stopped or slow vehicles, or other stationary objects. Tesla and Ford have faced similar investigations after their systems were involved in multiple crashes.  

Comma.ai’s own website states that the “performance” of openpilot Adaptive Cruise Control can be affected by “vehicles in the same lane that are not moving.” 

“When abrupt braking maneuvers are required,” the company writes, “openpilot is designed to be limited in the amount of deceleration and acceleration that it can produce.”

Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. title: What iOS 27.2 Could Bring to Your iPhone Later This Year
snippet: The beta includes updates to apps like Facetime and Podcasts, as well as Siri AI in more languages.
fullText:
About a week after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released the second developer beta of iOS 27.2 on Sept. 21. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, this early look at iOS 27.2 shows Siri AI expanding to other languages and a few upgrades in other apps, like Facetime.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, Apple has said the foldable iPhone Duo will launch on 27.1 next month, and all devices will be able to update to 27.2 sometime later.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.2, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short — it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, more features could end up landing on your iPhone when Apple releases iOS 27.2. 

Here are some features developers can try now in the second iOS 27.2 developer beta.

Siri AI in more languages

In iOS 27, Siri AI is only available in English. But the beta of iOS 27.2 expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in Facetime

In the iOS 27.2 beta, you can use your front and rear facing cameras at the same time in Facetime calls. This allows you to Facetime call with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame in order to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

	

			

An anti-snatching feature

According to 9to5Mac, code within the iOS 27.2 beta shows a feature called AutoLock. This is reportedly an anti-theft feature that can lock your device if it detects it’s been snatched out of your hand. For example, AutoLock could lock your iPhone if it detects a sharp acceleration, as if it was snatched out of your hands, or if your device has been unlocked for an extended period of time.

It’s important to note that this feature is not a user-facing option on your iPhone in this beta. Rather, 9to5Mac has reportedly seen internal code related to the feature. That means this feature may not be available when Apple releases iOS 27.2 in October.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in the iOS 27.2 beta. The beta introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of what podcasts are new and what podcasts you still have to finish. 

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In the beta of iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with. 

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in the iOS 27.2 beta is Multiview. Developers who subscribe to Apple TV can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racecourse while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

Updated Health app

Developers can see a redesigned Health app in the beta of iOS 27.2. However, the redesign is expected to launch sometime later this year, despite being featured in this beta.

Those are a few of the new features developers can try now with the second developer beta of iOS 27.2. There will likely be more betas before the OS is released to the public. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.2 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices in October.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

title: iPhone 18 Pro’s best Dynamic Island feature is one Apple barely mentioned
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro is here (read our review), and its Dynamic Island is better than ever. My personal favorite change is something Apple barely mentioned: an improved dual Live Activity mode. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro is here (read our review), and its Dynamic Island is better than ever. My personal favorite change is something Apple barely mentioned: an improved dual Live Activity mode.

Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro lets you see more information when running two Live Activities

Apple debuted the Dynamic Island in 2022 on the iPhone 14 Pro. And while software support for Live Activities has expanded a lot since then, the actual Dynamic Island hardware has stayed unchanged.

But with iPhone 18 Pro, Apple managed to shrink the Dynamic Island for the first time. 

By moving certain Face ID components under the display, iPhone 18 Pro adds slightly more usable screen real estate than previous iPhones had. 

More importantly though, the Dynamic Island can now display more Live Activity information than before.

In Apple’s announcement earlier this month, it spotlighted how three Live Activities can now run at a time—up from the previous limit of two.

That’s a nice upgrade, but the change I’ve found even more beneficial (and I’m not alone) is that your second Live Activity can be a lot more informative on iPhone 18 Pro.

That’s because if you’re only running two Live Activities, there’s more space available than before, and Apple uses that space to give the second Live Activity additional info.

So if you’re listening to media while running a timer—something I do all the time at the gym—now you’ll actually see the remaining time in the Dynamic Island. Before, it only showed a timer icon.

I look forward to seeing how apps make their Live Activities even more useful for iPhone 18 Pro users.

Do you have an iPhone 18 Pro? What do you think of the new Dynamic Island? Let us know in the comments.

title: Android Bench 2.0 focuses on long-horizon tasks, agent evaluations
snippet: Google’s development of Android Bench continues today with a version 2.0 that reflects how AI can handle more complex development tasks. more…
fullText:
Google’s development of Android Bench continues today with a version 2.0 that reflects how AI can handle more complex development tasks.

The first version “focused on incremental changes to existing repositories,” like bug fixes or smaller feature requests. Android Bench 2.0 targets “tasks of great complexity that take an engineer multiple days or even a week to complete,” such as adding new features, building apps from scratch, and converting cross-platform apps to Android.

This new focus required “more nuanced evaluation and scoring” that goes beyond pass or fail grading. Google is moving from binary to continuous scoring:

We calculate this completion rate through a combination of factors like functionality, visual fidelity, and avoiding regressions. We also apply objective scoring penalties for deviations from evaluation instructions or structural constraints.

Google has rated Gemini 3.7/3.8 Flash, OpenAI GPT-6, Anthropic Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8 Max. GPT-6 Astra is at the top of the benchmark with a 28% pass rate (compared to scores in the 90% range with the previous approach).

	

Google shared insights like how “porting cross-platform apps to Android remains an open challenge—no model hits a 100% pass rate, and frontier models reach at most a 80% completion rate.”

“…AI does a better job at writing new code rather than refactoring existing code. Refactors and migrations get trickier because success depends on architectural complexity rather than code volume.”

“Models show strong capabilities on well-established, deterministic transformations, such as converting Java to Kotlin, swapping Retrofit for Ktor, or introducing a ViewModel layer.”

“…models struggle when tasks require runtime validation (like missing dependency injection graphs), involve breaking framework changes, or run into knowledge gaps with unreleased libraries.”

With agent evaluations, Android Bench ran “agents from the corresponding model provider,” like Gemini 3.8 Flash on Google Antigravity and GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex. Google says “harness design positively impacts developer outcomes,” with Android Bench planning to include different model and agent combinations in the future.
