title: Review: Satechi’s Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock pairs perfectly with the new M6 Mac mini
snippet: Apple just released a new Mac mini late last month, equipped with the new M6 and M5 Pro chips. If you’re looking for a perfect Thunderbolt 5 dock to pair with your new Mac mini (or your current M4/M4 Pro model) – Satechi has a great offering for you. more…
fullText:
Apple just released a new Mac mini late last month, equipped with the new M6 and M5 Pro chips. If you’re looking for a perfect Thunderbolt 5 dock to pair with your new Mac mini (or your current M4/M4 Pro model) – Satechi has a great offering for you.

Satechi’s Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock is shaped just like a Mac mini, making it a perfect companion, whether you have it side by side or stacked. It brings 8 additional ports, an M.2 NVMe SSD bay, and supports up to 140W of host charging if you’re pairing it with a laptop instead.

With Thunderbolt 5, there’s up to 120Gbps of throughput, allowing you to run up to three 6K@60Hz or 4K@144Hz displays with M5 Pro through a single cable, or two with any other chipset.

Beyond its display capabilities, it offers two 10Gbps USB-C ports and two 10Gbps USB-A ports, a 2.5G Ethernet port, an SD card reader, and a microSD card reader – with each supporting UHS-II. There’s also an additional 3.5mm combo audio jack if you need a second one.

The best part for me is the fact that it has an M.2 NVMe SSD bay, and the bay is large enough to fit SSDs that have a built-in heatsink – which can’t be said for every product with an SSD bay. The SSD bay sits within the enclosure and doesn’t expand the footprint. You can fit an 8TB SSD in it, at up to 6000MB/s – and it supports 2230, 2242, 2260, and 2280 drive sizes.

9to5Mac’s Take

If you want the best dock that can take advantage of Thunderbolt 5 capabilities and look right at home with your Mac mini, the Satechi CubeDock is undeniably the best option. title: Valve’s open-source ‘Lepton’ brings Android games to the $1,059 Steam Frame
snippet: Valve has just released its Lepton tool as an open-source resource for bringing Android-native games to Linux and, in turn, Steam. more…
fullText:
Valve has just released its Lepton tool as an open-source resource for bringing Android-native games to Linux and, in turn, Steam.

On GitLab, Valve has released Lepton as an open-source repository, allowing developers to use the tool primarily for porting games to the Steam Frame. Valve explains:

Lepton is a tool for use with the Steam client which allows games which are exclusive to Android to run on the Linux operating system. Most users should use Lepton provided by the Steam Client itself.

…Lepton is intended to help game developers bring their VR Android games to the Steam Frame. Other usecases are possible, but were not the focus of development and may lack polish.

The Verge points out that some developers are already using Lepton to port Meta Quest games (the Quest runs Android) to the Steam Frame.

The Steam Frame officially made its debut earlier this week, with the Snapdragon-powered VR headset coming in at a cost of $1,059. A waitlist is now open.

title: Google Home just became a power user’s paradise
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m finding some peace playing Lumines Remastered, deciding whether to get my kids one of the new 4th-gen Yoto players, and trying to figure out why everyone is freaking out about this recent Tom Cruise interview. more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m finding some peace playing Lumines Remastered, deciding whether to get my kids one of the new 4th-gen Yoto players, and trying to figure out why everyone is freaking out about this recent Tom Cruise interview.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Over the past few months, I’ve been using MCP (Model Context Protocol) to connect with my bank, my to-do app (TickTick), my personal database (Obsidian), and anything else I can get my hands on. I find it intuitive to have a conversation with a chatbot about stacking tasks, performing a complex set of calculations, or just figuring out the answer to a difficult problem. 

	

Now Google is getting in on the MCP action with Home MCP, a way to connect coding agents like Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Hermes, and OpenClaw to Google’s Home ecosystem and the products connected to it.

Right now, the tool is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced subscribers in the US, but it’s an ambitious first step toward making it easier to interact with what is usually a digital rat’s nest of brands, categories, and compatibility layers. Google has already rolled out Gemini for Home in an attempt to make automation more straightforward, but I commend the company for dipping its toe into the DIY space and seeing what happens.

According to Google, MCP “gives your favorite AI agent real-world physical context—allowing it to analyze and answer questions about home activity, summarize camera footage across rooms, manage devices on your behalf, or even create your own smart home dashboards using everyday language.” I’m totally going to use it to teach my Nest Cam Outdoor that the cat who wanders onto my driveway every morning isn’t, in fact, a person. Wish me luck.

✉️ Inbox

GM just found the ‘sweet spot’ for supporting Android Auto & CarPlay. See, all it took was people loudly complaining for three years.

MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro goes official with 2nm process and performance gains.

Oppo confirms global Find X10 Pro Max launch powered by MediaTek’s latest flagship chip.

SwiftKey ‘AI voice’ is Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text for other Android phones, works offline. I have my doubts that this is any good — SwiftKey’s been awful for years — but I guess it’s good that this exists?

Google just shared these fun Pixel 11 blueprint wallpapers. These are really fun.

Samsung Gallery is adding Google Photos backup to replace OneDrive. Good, no one uses OneDrive anyway.

Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking powers Gemini Live, Gmail, & Keep. Google is the undisputed leader of text-to-speech, and Gemini 3.8 Live just extends its lead.

The new Boox e-ink devices get Android 16 out of the box, including Palma 3. The Palma 3 looks like an actual gadget, no longer a plastic toy like the previous ones, and I must have it.

Google confirms Pixel phones were exploited in ‘targeted’ attack related to modem. This is pretty concerning, especially because it was “zero-click,” but glad it’s been fixed.

Philips Hue Bridge Pro is now $139, with even bigger price hikes globally. Woof.

Today in software updates:

Today in bug fixes:

YouTube’s login-breaking bug is getting a fix on TVs and consoles.

Amazon fixes bug that caused problems with Fire TV app sideloading.

🍎 Roll call

It’s iPhone review season, and because this seems like an “S” year, the camera is rightfully getting the most attention. That’s why I watched basically every second of all the new iPhone 18 Pro reviews from channels like PetaPixel, Tyler Stalman, The Verge, and Matti Haapoja.

I’m still not sure what to think about the aperture control. Most reviews are saying that it has very little real-world utility, while others are claiming that it was the only way to offer an f/1.48 lens without sacrificing depth control (or overly relying on software bokeh). Either way, once Apple decides to offer a hardware feature it tends to stick around whether or not it’s any good (see Camera Control), so we’ll likely see a few more generations of this tech.

Sticking with the iPhone theme, two of my favorite podcasters convened this week to discuss the iPhone Duo and how it fares next to the multitude of Android competitors. 

(And if you enjoy the conversation with Stephen Radochia and want to hear more from him, he and I host a little podcast called Old’s Cool that looks at new tech from a vintage point of view.)

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Tired of getting recorded against your will by other meeting attendees? Kalypta from Deveillance reportedly makes you “inaudible to AI” by “reshaping audio in real time” on your local machine. What a crazy world we live in.

OpenAI’s “Project Lily” tasks real humans with reading ChatGPT transcripts in order to make inference better and more accurate. According to 404 Media, which broke the story, “OpenAI is hiring hundreds of contractors who read a massive stream of real users’ ChatGPT prompts, with the prompts sometimes including sensitive personal information.” 

Snap finally let people try its $2,200 Specs smart glasses, a bulky and unwieldy computer that it’s inviting developers to test. The gadget has a 4-hour battery and can run real apps like Spotify while relying on a proactive AI assistant to do everything else. 

🤑 Action Items

Over the past couple of days, I’ve been trying out a new launcher on my Fold 8, a launcher unlike anything I’ve used on Android before. That’s because it’s defined by its adherence to the UX found on iOS — specifically the upcoming iPhone Duo.

From the demented mind of Reddit’s u/wolftech029, Folio is a love letter (for better or worse) to the way Apple’s home screen drastically differs from the ones found on various Android phones. From predefined grids to Apple’s App Library to the Duo’s funky blur effect, Folio has it all. 

I’m not sure it’s going to stay on my phone for long, but its existence (and the speed at which it was vibe-coded) is a testament to Android’s versatility and openness.

title: iCloud storage notification glitch puts unremovable red badge on Settings app
snippet: There’s an annoying little iPhone notification glitch impacting some users on iOS 27. For those affected, the Settings app gets a red badge prompting an alert to ‘Activate iCloud Storage’. However, tapping on this alert simply navigates to the iCloud storage purchase screen and the alert does not go away after dismissing it. This glitched notification appears even when the user has plenty of available iCloud storage already, like if they are on a 2 TB family Apple One plan. more…
fullText:
There’s an annoying little iPhone notification glitch impacting some users on iOS 27. For those affected, the Settings app gets a red badge prompting an alert to ‘Activate iCloud Storage’. 

However, tapping on this alert simply navigates to the iCloud storage purchase screen and the alert does not go away after dismissing it. This glitched notification appears even when the user has plenty of available iCloud storage already, like if they are on a 2 TB family Apple One plan.

While Apple sometimes does use the Settings app as a way to promote offers (like Apple TV trials) and remind users about AppleCare warranties, this particular notification appears to simply be a mistake rather than some underhand way to shove an iCloud upsell in front of customers.

The notification appears on devices running the release version of iOS 27 and iOS 27.2, as well as iOS 26.7. 

Some users have reported that signing out of their Apple Account on their device and logging back in causes the alert to go away. But hopefully Apple can also resolve this quickly with a backend change.

Update: Apple Support recommends logging out and back into your Media & Purchases account on the device. Go to Settings -> [name] -> Media & Purchases -> Sign Out, then sign back in.

title: Meta admits Muse’s likeness to OpenClaw isn’t a coincidence
snippet: Meta says Muse was built from scratch, but acknowledges the AI assistant was "heavily inspired" by OpenClaw — down to some of its workspace filenames and content.
fullText:
Early adopters of Meta’s Muse have been speculating that the reason the AI works so well is because it’s OpenClaw under the hood, wrapped in a more consumer-friendly package. Meta now says those comparisons aren’t entirely off-base. According to an X post by Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs (MSL), Muse was “definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw.”

However, he clarified that Muse itself was “built from scratch.” 

Friedman, the former GitHub CEO who joined Meta last year alongside Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang, said that the team at Meta had fallen in love with OpenClaw and wanted Muse to be “something like OpenClaw” that could be scaled to billions of people.

Because OpenClaw is an open source project, it wouldn’t be surprising that Meta looked to it for inspiration, especially given its breakout success, which prompted OpenAI to snatch up its creator earlier this year. However, it speaks to Meta’s well-known playbook that involves taking promising products, then copying their best features — something it did most notoriously with Snapchat’s invention of the stories format.

Friedman’s statement on X was made in response to a post that had gone viral among the AI crowd, where Ansh Nanda, an AI app co-founder, claimed that “Muse is LITERALLY OpenClaw for normies.”

Nanda’s X post had included a conversation with Muse, where the AI agent said that the similarity between its own system files and those belonging to OpenClaw was not just “a coincidence” but rather “a match.”

Soon, this thread (and X more broadly) began blowing up as others shared their own comparisons and findings. For instance, one person pointed out that Muse also had a SOUL.md file, the plain text configuration file (written in a simple formatting language called Markdown) that defines an AI agent’s personality, communication style and tone, values, behavioral boundaries, and expertise.

A third noted that the files weren’t just named the same between the two assistants; their content was almost entirely the same.

Following his X post, Friedman also responded to a question about why Muse had copied the exact file names that made up the AI agent’s workspace and had “nearly identical content” for the SOUL.md file. Instead of disputing these claims, Friedman simply replied that “we thought that Peter [Steinberger, OpenClaw’s creator] got those things exactly right.”

“We built Muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw. After I used OpenClaw in January, I bought hundreds of Mac minis for the MSL team, and lots of us fell in love with using OpenClaw (and other personal agents), Friedman said on X. (TechCrunch has corrected Friedman’s punctuation for readability.)

“@steipete [Peter Steinberger] is a genius, and his harness was pioneering from the jump. I think a lot of people were inspired by it. Our goal with Muse was to build something like OpenClaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people,” he wrote.

The Muse app has been something of a hit so far, having recently hit No. 1 on the U.S. App Store. Data indicates that it’s now outpacing ChatGPT’s launch when the platforms and market availability are compared directly.

Reached for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed to Friedman’s statement, saying the company had nothing more to add beyond that.

title: A Chrome bug is slowing extension load times to a snail’s pace on macOS, Google is aware
snippet: Google Chrome extensions are reportedly taking too long to load on macOS devices, when they should reasonably only take a couple of seconds, due to a bug in the latest updates. Google is aware of the issue. more…
fullText:
Google Chrome extensions are reportedly taking too long to load on macOS devices, when they should reasonably only take a couple of seconds, due to a bug in the latest updates. Google is aware of the issue.

The report comes courtesy of PiunikaWeb, which noted a thread entry on the Chromium issue tracker divulging the issue. The issue seems to affect macOS instances of Google Chrome, rather than Windows or mobile versions. The affected extensions are reportedly taking up to 60 seconds to load, when extensions should open instantly. 

Users began reporting extensions lag in Google Chrome last week, and one of the main third-party tools it seems to affect is password managers like 1Password. The credential management app offers an extremely handy Chrome extension for password autofill across any site that requires you to remember your reasonably complex password. According to the company, it’s aware that a Google Chrome update seems to be slowing extension performance.

Hey Don! There is a known issue in Google Chrome itself right now that can cause extension popups to take much longer than usual to open, and we’d like to figure out if that’s what you’re running into here.

When 1Password is slow or won’t open, do you notice the same thing with…

— 1Password (@1Password) September 16, 2026

It doesn’t seem to only affect 1Password. Some replies indicate other extensions are being affected by the bug, though it doesn’t appear to be consistent.

	

What seems to be causing this disparity in extension load times is mismanaged process priority on Google Chrome’s end, though that hasn’t been verified by Google. Specifically, this seems to happen on macOS 26, and for whatever reason, Google Chrome deems certain extensions a low-priority operation, effectively pushing them to the background while it diverts resources to other tasks. The result is a much longer load time for users.

Google is aware of the issue, posting a reply to the official community page. Here’s what Google’s team says:

We’re continuing to investigate this issue as a priority, and I’ve also asked the team to consider all options including if we can roll the experiment out any further. We’ll make sure to share further updates on this thread as we have them.

Some users have noted that, in the meantime, enabling the PMLoadingPageVoter flag fixes the issue. It’s worth noting that enabling/disabling flags in Google Chrome carries some risk, so please only do so with that in mind.

title: Apple Fitness+ team hit by layoffs, as ‘major changes’ reportedly loom
snippet: Apple is assessing the future of Apple Fitness+, according to a new Bloomberg report. The company has reportedly laid off a “handful of employees” working on the service, a move viewed as just the beginning of bigger changes still to come. more…
fullText:
Apple is assessing the future of Apple Fitness+, according to a new Bloomberg report. The company has reportedly laid off a “handful of employees” working on the service, a move viewed as just the beginning of bigger changes still to come.

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman says the layoffs affect people working on the audio features for Fitness+. That includes features like the guided Time to Walk and Time to Run audio sessions. Gurman notes, however, that new releases aren’t going away “completely,” but rather they will “drop in frequency.”

Apple Fitness+, however, is not “on the chopping block,” at least as of right now:

I don’t believe, as of this second, that the service is on the chopping block, but given the considerable costs, ever-present demand for new content and subscriber churn rates, it’s an easy place for Apple to look to make cuts. And that is starting now.

These layoffs are likely just the first shoe to drop for the future of Fitness+, though:

Still, this is widely seen within the Fitness+ organization as the beginning of more drastic cost-cutting measures and other major changes to the service in the months and years ahead.

Last November, Gurman reported that the future of Apple Fitness+ was “under review.” Leadership of the service shifted to services boss Eddy Cue and health boss Sumbul Desai. Cue has reportedly pressed Apple to “move faster and be more competitive” in health and fitness.

Gurman speculates that Apple will eventually integrate Fitness+ into the revamped Health app. I think he’s spot on with this. What about you? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Google Home app brings battery-efficient widget, reduces gray device tiles
snippet: Besides Home MCP, Google today is also rolling out Home app (especially for the homescreen widget) and Gemini for Home voice assistant updates. more…
fullText:
Besides Home MCP, Google today is also rolling out Home app (especially for the homescreen widget) and Gemini for Home voice assistant updates.

The Google Home widget has now been optimized to “pause background updates and polling whenever your phone’s screen is powered off, locked, or running a screensaver.” This helps save battery on your phone and connected cameras, while “ensuring your widgets refresh immediately the moment you unlock your phone.”

Meanwhile, Google has resolved an issue with device tiles for sensors, cameras, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. They could previously “appear grayed out after returning from device controller screens.” As such, you no longer have to reload the screen.

Other quality improvements include:

	

Smoother multi-account switching: If you have multiple accounts that you use with Google Home, switching between them is now more reliable with fewer “Home not found” errors and preference resets.

More reliable smart device setup: Addressed several setup and onboarding issues, including eliminating stalls during Wi-Fi pairing. This ensures a smoother, frustration-free onboarding journey when adding new smart devices to your home.

Smoother Google TV startup: Resolved a startup crash on Google TV devices, ensuring the Google Home experience launches reliably on your television.

More flexible in-app banners: Improved UI for triggering actions in announcement banners in the Google Home app.

Smoke alarm notifications: Rolling out improvements to smoke and carbon monoxide alarm notifications to show current device status in the Google Home app after an alarm has already been cleared.

On the camera front, there are three fixes:

Improved camera live stream tile reliability (Android): Resolved an issue where returning from the full-screen camera view back to the Favorites tab caused live stream tiles to temporarily turn black until manually scrolled. Live feeds now continue streaming seamlessly upon navigating back.

Smoother camera history scrolling across recording gaps (Android): Video timeline scrolling now smoothly scrolls past unrecorded or offline gaps without freezing.

Faster switching to live camera stream (iOS): Fixed an issue where tapping the “Live” button while watching recorded events failed to redirect smoothly into the live view, leaving playback paused.

Finally for September 16, 2026, Google has five Gemini for Home voice assistant updates:

Improved follow up question behavior: Minimized cases where Gemini asks unnecessary follow-up questions or ends conversations awkwardly.

Fixed TV streaming playback: Fixed an intermittent issue that prevented Gemini from launching TV streaming providers on smart displays.

Reduced Live Mode interruptions: Addressed an issue where some devices interrupted themselves during Live Mode.

Reduced Broadcast errors: Resolved an issue where there were error messages when attempting to broadcast. You can now more reliably broadcast across your whole Home.

Improved Playlist reliability: Fixed some issues where Gemini wasn’t able to identify and play personal playlists.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 might finally convince me to switch away from WHOOP
snippet: Earlier this year, I picked up a WHOOP for the very first time. As a longtime Apple Watch user I was looking forward to having a new way of tracking my health stats in a cleaner interface that the Apple Watch wasn’t offering. Now, with Apple Watch Series 12, I’m very convinced to switch back to the Apple Watch. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, I picked up a WHOOP for the very first time. As a longtime Apple Watch user I was looking forward to having a new way of tracking my health stats in a cleaner interface that the Apple Watch wasn’t offering. Now, with Apple Watch Series 12, I’m very convinced to switch back to the Apple Watch. Here’s why.

First things first, it’s worth noting that the Apple Watch Series 12 isn’t the only factor. There’s also the new Apple Health app in iOS 27.

The new Apple Health app has a much better interface. It offers your stats in a much cleaner manner. It’s very easy to understand all the data, which for me was the main thing breaking the Apple Watch.

Apple Health isn’t the only reason why I didn’t use the Apple Watch, though. It was also the fact that the Apple Watch didn’t collect data as frequently as the WHOOP did. The Apple Watch Series 12 now collects your heart rate once every 5 seconds, compared to every 5 minutes on previous models. This is still less than the WHOOP’s every 1 second, but so long as you’re not an athlete, I think every 5 seconds is fine.

Series 12 also introduced the new Readiness app on the Apple Watch, which gives you a 1-to-10 health score based on your HRV and other factors. This is akin to the recovery score the WHOOP calculated, which is one of the things that I like tracking, because even though Apple Watch always offered a sleep score, it wasn’t always the most useful piece of data. If you slept for a long time, you’d generally get a high score, regardless of whether other sleep factors weren’t quite great.

Wrap up

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max’s battery is so big Apple had to add this new feature to iOS 27
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers a huge jump in battery life, partly because the battery itself is physically larger. In a new support document published today, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has such a big battery that it has additional shipping requirements. more…
fullText:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers a huge jump in battery life, partly because the battery itself is physically larger.

In a new support document published today, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has such a big battery that it has additional shipping requirements.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: New battery feature

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a battery capacity over 20 watt-hours (Wh). As it turns out, most countries and regions have additional shipping requirements for products “with a single-cell battery over 20 Wh.”

To accommodate these requirements, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses an “innovative battery-firmware solution.” That firmware will limit the battery capacity of the device to below 20 Wh until it’s activated by the user:

To address these requirements, iPhone 18 Pro Max uses an innovative battery-firmware solution that limits battery capacity to below 20 Wh from the time it’s manufactured through its transport from the factory. When you activate your iPhone, the limit is removed and the battery’s full charging capacity is available.

The shipping requirements, however, also apply to other scenarios like shipping the iPhone 18 Pro Max for repair, trading it in, returning it, selling it, or gifting it to someone else.

For this, Apple has added a new “Prepare to Ship” feature in the Settings app. This will discharge your device’s battery below 20 Wh and set a charge limit to keep it below that threshold.

Your iPhone 18 Pro Max might need to discharge for Prepare to Ship to complete. While your iPhone battery discharges, it might become warmer than usual. This is expected. Your iPhone will cool down again when it’s ready to ship.

You can use your device as usual while your iPhone 18 Pro Max discharges. This might take only a few minutes, but if you start with a full charge, it can take up to a couple of hours. When the Prepare to Ship process is complete, the Settings app will display “Ready to Ship” with a red badge. If you erase your iPhone, you won’t be able to use it while the battery discharges.

The new option is in the Settings app. Open Settings, tap General, tap Transfer or Reset iPhone, then tap Prepare to Ship.

You can learn more in the full Apple support document.

title: Android 17 QPR1 changes some Pixel status bar icons
snippet: This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel. more…
fullText:
This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel.

The silent or mute icon goes from a crossed-out speaker to a bell.

This might be an accidental regression as Google switched from the bell to the speaker in Android 14. Notably, this change was not present during the Android 17 QPR1 Beta cycle and only went live with the stable OTA this week. 

The speaker icon is still live in 17 QPR2 Beta 5. (Meanwhile, the switcher at the top of the volume slider still uses the bell.)

	

Another icon change further complicates whether this tweak was intentional. The VPN icon is now much thicker and filled in, with this update also only appearing with the stable release.

We’ll know this was a mistake if Google changes it back in future releases, though any fix may not arrive until the sizable QPR2 update in December. Android 17 QPR1 is not yet available for the Pixel 11 series.

title: Android Auto update might fix cellular signal icon – is it back for you?
snippet: For months now, there have been reports of Android Auto’s status bar having a broken icon for cellular signal, but the latest updates seem to finally put an end to the debacle. more…
fullText:
For months now, there have been reports of Android Auto’s status bar having a broken icon for cellular signal, but the latest updates seem to finally put an end to the debacle.

The bottom/side bar on Android Auto shows your apps, the time, and your phone’s current battery and cellular signal status through icons. But, for around 4-5 months now, there have been reports of users seeing the cellular signal icon go missing at random, only to come back just as randomly for some. 

When it’s missing, it leaves a funny-looking gap in Android Auto.

Image via Reddit

With Android Auto 17.8, it seems Google may have finally addressed this problem more widely.

	

A number of users on Reddit all report that the latest update has suddenly fixed the cellular signal icon on Android Auto. That said, reports are limited to just a handful of users, one of which cleared their app cache following the update’s installation.

So, we’ll open this one to you. Has your cellular signal icon returned on Android Auto? Sound off in the comments and let us know.

title: Waymo’s latest expansion strategy: teenagers
snippet: Waymo is opening its robotaxi service to teenagers aged 13 to 17 in Nashville, its second city to offer rides to minors.
fullText:
Image Credits:Waymo	

	

						

10:36 AM PDT · September 22, 2026

											

			

Waymo will allow teenagers as young as 13 to use its robotaxi service in Nashville as the Alphabet-owned company looks to scale its business by reaching a new group of riders. 

Nashville is the second city to offer Waymo teen accounts; the company kicked off its teen account program in Phoenix last year. And more cities are likely to follow, according to the company.

A Waymo spokesperson told TechCrunch that its expansion to Nashville will be the “first of many” teen launches across multiple markets that use the Waymo app in the coming months. The spokesperson said it will offer teen accounts in cities where its operations are mature and local regulations allow it.

Nashville is a relatively new market for Waymo, although it has support from local leaders to offer the service to teens. The company launched its service in a 50-square-mile area of Nashville in April 2026, and earlier this month, its robotaxis became available on the Lyft app. 

Waymo’s ridership has skyrocketed over the past two years — a trajectory largely driven by the rapid succession of new markets. Paid robotaxi trips grew tenfold from 50,000 per week in May 2024 to more than half-a-million per week earlier this year. Over that same time span, Waymo has launched robotaxi services in a dozen cities. In the past month alone, the company opened robotaxi services in Denver, Las Vegas, San Diego, and Tampa.

The company’s introduction of teen accounts provides another means of growth — this one targeted at a demographic that relies on parents or public transit to get to school, work, or activities.

There are few limits to the service. The teen account must be connected to a parent or guardian, but once activated, teens can hail autonomous rides anywhere in Waymo’s service area in Nashville — and bring their friends along. Waymo told TechCrunch that teen account holders can bring up to three guests ages 13 to 17. The company didn’t share how these ages would be verified. 

That kind of access could certainly invite chaos — it’s not hard to imagine four 16-year-old kids unleashed in a robotaxi. But it may also be part of the appeal for parents who would rather their kids pile into a Waymo than in a vehicle driven by a teenager.

title: Xbox’s Latest Restructuring Puts Call of Duty Developer Activision in Charge of Halo
snippet: The two games once shared a rivalry as Xbox’s biggest FPS titles.
fullText:
Longtime Halo fans have only ever known two studios to develop the Halo franchise: Bungie and 343 Industries, which was later renamed Halo Studios. Microsoft has now thrown a curveball by entrusting the next iteration of the iconic FPS to Activision. 

On Tuesday, a statement titled Continuing Our Reset was sent to global Team Xbox employees, announcing a larger restructuring that included eliminating 268 roles from Halo Studios, other “first party” studios, and XGS management and central functions. The statement said it will create a dedicated, separate team to develop the next Halo game, distinct from its Call of Duty operations, and that a smaller team at Halo Studios will remain focused on supporting the current community and existing games.

It’s been some time since the Halo series switched hands. The final Halo game developed by Bungie was Halo: Reach in 2010, and Halo Studios has helmed the project ever since, up to and including the studio’s now-final release, Halo: Campaign Evolved, which received critical acclaim upon its launch earlier in 2026.

It also isn’t the first time Activision has assisted in a property that Bungie originally made. The two studios famously worked on Bungie’s Destiny franchise from 2010 until a rather messy public split in 2019, before Activision was acquired by Microsoft in 2022. Activision helped develop Bungie by bringing in external studios like Vicarious Visions and High Moon Studios to support PC and accelerate the development of new content.

This current “reset” marks a complete pivot in Xbox’s strategy and is part of Microsoft’s cost-cutting restructuring efforts, which the company began after Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said the business “is not healthy.” In July, the company announced 3,200 layoffs over the next year due to a struggling business and stagnant growth in Game Pass.

The end of an era

Activision is now the developer of Xbox’s two biggest FPS franchises, Call of Duty and Halo, a reality that no one playing either franchise in 2009 would’ve believed if you’d told them back then. The two games shared a rather intense rivalry during the 2000s that has softened over time, with Battlefield largely replacing Halo in the broader gaming lexicon as Call of Duty’s biggest rival.

“This feels like the end of an era,” said CNET senior writer Zachary McAuliffe. “Halo is a franchise that is largely synonymous with Xbox as a brand, so Microsoft handing the franchise to Activision feels like the company cutting off its nose to spite its face. It’s ironic because Call of Duty, Activision’s largest franchise, was Halo’s main gaming rivalry. Now that Activision controls Halo, it feels like Call of Duty won that rivalry.”

McAuliffe also points out that with Activision in control, it may subject Halo to some Activision habits, like annualized releases much like we see with Call of Duty games, and with a story-focused game like Halo, that may stifle creativity and cause the games to “feel flat.” A future like that would almost certainly cause Halo to lose its identity and become just a Call of Duty clone set in space. 

There aren’t any details about the next Halo game yet, except that it’ll be made by Activision.

The big Xbox restructure continues

Tuesday’s move is likely to be a massive deal in the gaming world because it outlines a radical, fundamental restructuring of Xbox’s first-party studios, including drastic changes to some of the most iconic franchises and developers in the industry.

Activision is also taking control of World’s Edge and Rare, developers of Age of Empires and Sea of Thieves, respectively. Bethesda is taking Obsidian under its wing, the developer of the next Fallout game. Candy Crush developer King is taking control of Microsoft Casual Games to combine the casual games segment under one roof. Finally, Playground and Turn 10 are being merged into a single studio, combining Forza and Fable under one roof. 

According to the announcement, Double Fine, Compulsion and Undead Labs have returned to being independent studios. Ninja Theory had two agreements fall through and is now being closed down for good, with its final release, Senua, still slated for 2027.

With these changes, Microsoft’s restructuring efforts aren’t yet over. “The actions completed since July, inclusive of the studio divestitures, bring us roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring,” the statement read.

title: Out of Pocket: Detailing our everyday carry
snippet: I love building a “kit,” a “pack,” a bag with enough stuff in it to make sure I am ready for every eventuality. I’m not talking about a survival kit per se, just some things that mean I am basically ready for any modern situation. more…
fullText:
I love building a “kit,” a “pack,” a bag with enough stuff in it to make sure I am ready for every eventuality. I’m not talking about a survival kit per se, just some things that mean I am basically ready for any modern situation.

EDC or Every Day Carry is basically part of my personality at this stage. It started with smartphones, moved on to earbuds, and steadily, like many of you, I accrued an assortment of gadgets, products, and things I found myself dragging with me everywhere.

I am constantly on the lookout for the next thing to enhance my EDC. I’m not alone in this; Andrew is in the same boat. We’re product people first and foremost, but practicality has to be a component before it becomes a bigger part of daily lives.

We figured that we’d share some of that intimate knowledge, driven by building packs for trade shows, travel, and just, well, hanging around.

	

So, this is Out of Pocket, our new series diving into what makes our EDC tick. Expect more deep dives into the kinds of things that are adjacent to your smartphone, the things that you carry every day, or brand new products that might pique your interest. After all, we all have our own specific EDC essentials. Here are a few of ours to hopefully get your own creative juices flowing…

My current kit (Damien)

The Sidebag – TomToc T33 (3.5L)

My search for the perfect sidebag has been, I’ll be honest, arduous. Day-to-day, I’m not much of a backpack guy, so a sling or a sidebag is the perfect accessory for all the little things I feel like I need. I already own a Bellroy Venture Ready sling, and while it’s awesome. It is just a little bit too small for a real EDC kit.

TomToc’s T33 sidebag is exponentially better with more pockets, exceptional internal organization, and interior sections. You could fit a small-ish water bottle or drink in the middle section, but netted segments mean I can throw in paracetamol or lip balm for easy access. There’s enough room for a really small tablet or notebook and documents in the back portion.

There’s a key carabiner so I can throw in my house keys and keychain right at the front. It’s stretchy enough to open a door and have the key snap back into the front pocket.

One of my must-haves on a sling is a body-facing “secret” pocket. When I’m traveling, my passport goes here so it’s accessible, but also harder for someone to try and slip their hand in – not that this has been a problem.

One of the most important things for me is that it’s waterproof. While it’s hot right now in England, we’re due a downpour. I like that all my stuff inside is safe and dry. The zippers are smooth, with waterproof seams, and there are lots of carabiner anchor points too, so you can attach a hat or a water bottle. It hits all the right notes, and I’ve abused it thoroughly, and it just wipes clean.

It’s super cheap for what it offers at under $45. My only gripe is that the color options aren’t all that extensive, but you could level that criticism at basically any sidebag. This is one that won’t break the bank.

Get the TomToc T33 sling

The Juice  – Anker Nano 5,000mAh power pack

Power banks are just so ubiquitous now that you can basically boil it down to what you want or need. Because I use the Pixel 11 Pro, I always want a Magsafe-compatible power bank around to slap to the back of the phone.

I had been using the Genki Energy Pack for almost a year now, and there were a number of reasons for that. Firstly, it looks awesome with the black and orange color scheme. Secondly, it’s Qi2 certified, so it does all the necessary handshake stuff required to get faster and more efficient charging speeds.

However, it’s blocky and bulky, so I switched it out recently for something a little lighter. I’m rocking the Anker Nano power bank now because it isn’t as bulky and has enough juice to give me a full charge on basically any phone I’m carrying.

There’s a tiny strip of LEDs that shows remaining battery level; it’s Qi2 certified, but that is limited to 15W. I use the solitary USB-C charging port if I need 20W and above, but most of the time it’s absolutely fine when you’re out and about. For what it’s worth, I carry a super short USB-C cable that’s like 10cm for that specific reason too.

I do think it’s a little pricey, but you can get it in different colours and mine has taken a beating over the year or slightly longer I’ve been using it. It’s just something that can slip on to the back of your phone without being huge or messing around with cables – which is something I appreciate.

Get the Anker Nano power bank

On-the-go entertainment – Boox Go 6 e-reader

I reviewed the Boox Go 6 e-reader almost two years ago, and since then, it has become a staple in my EDC setup. It’s just so small and inconspicuous that it basically lives in my sidebag.

As an e-reader, it’s nothing special. I’d even say it’s a little underpowered for what it offers, but the size and shape are what keep me coming back basically every single day. I basically leave it running the Kindle app or download some epub files, and it handles those absolutely fine. It is technically an Android tablet, so you can share files using Quick Share. I find this is great if you find something you want to read because you can just fire things over without messing with cables. Heck, I have hundreds of EPUBs that just work now, which is lovely. Even PDFs work just fine.

It’s under 300g with a magnetic flip case attached, so it’s not heavy by any stretch of the imagination. I have my eye on a few of the even smaller Magsafe e-readers, but at 6-inches this is like a pamphlet or an especially large coupon. Perfect for reading novels, documents, or even a downloaded webpage – not that I would recommend that!

A newer version has just been released that enables note-taking and various other improvements. I’m hoping to test drive that soon, but I have genuinely loved the compact design of the Go 6 and think I’d struggle to go back to a full-sized Kindle for that reason alone. It has come down in price to around $160, which isn’t cheap, but still not bad if you want something super small. That said, something even smaller might be better for just throwing into an even smaller sling bag…

Get the Boox Go 6 e-reader

Always available audio – USB-C earbuds

I simply hate not having some earbuds with me when I’m out of the house. I simply must be distracted with podcasts, YouTube Music, or if I want to take a call, I cannot live without a pair in my bag.

I usually have about 20 pairs of Bluetooth earbuds lying around my desk, but when the battery dies, they’re useless. I was so annoyed at a pair of buds dying mid-flight while traveling last year that I bought a random pair of USB-C earbuds from an airport vending machine to keep the music flowing. I think they’re from Xiaomi as there’s a little “Mi” logo embossed on the inline remote. I only paid like $16, but Belkin makes a pair that are $15 and reputable enough that I might pick up a pair as a spare.

Honestly, they sound fine. The threshold is that a pair of earbuds just needs to sound better than traffic or that dull airplane drone. These earbuds live in my bag as a last resort audio option, heck, they’re great to just share with someone if they’ve forgotten their own earbuds. They take up basically negligible space, too. When I’m done with them, I quickly wipe them with an alcohol pad, and they’re sterilized. Trust me, it’s worth having at least one backup option because the one time you need them, it’s a lifesaver. If you lose them, it’s not a big deal. Win-win in my book.

Get some cheap USB-C earbuds

Retro on the go – Gamesir Pocket Taco controller

If I’m taking a backpack, I usually try to make room for my Steam Deck or Switch 2, but if I’m going out for a few hours, I’ll usually stick to something much smaller. I love Gamesir’s range of controllers, but the Pocket Taco is one that, as a millennial gamer and Gameboy obsessive, I’m sticking with for now.

It clips onto your phone – don’t worry, it has rubber pads to stop scratches – and gives you real buttons to play games in portrait orientation like Nintendo intended back in the late 1980s. It really does feel like a DMG Game Boy in the best ways. Thankfully, there are more buttons that you can map so that you can play other emulators, not just Gameboy.

If you’re not a gamer, mobile or otherwise, this might not be for you, and that’s absolutely fine. For nerds of a certain “vintage,” you’ll probably love this as much as I do.

Get the Pocket Taco game controller

The extras – ‘stuff’ and ‘things’

We’re all humans, so we can’t just have cables and batteries in our bags. I carry a few other key things that are useful. Most of these are just cheap things that I’ve found are worth having.

After a trip to a city with questionable-quality streetlights, I picked up a little keychain torch that just attaches to my keys. Olight makes a ton of EDC lighting products, but I love the iMini 2 at just $20 because it can just go on my keys with the carabiner clip.

I just charge it every couple of months using the integrated USB-A plug at the back, and it lasts a lotng time despite the fact that it’s absolutely tiny. Detach to power on, then it magnetically snaps back into place, and the light turns off. Super useful if you don’t want to drain your smartphone’s battery, and it’s bright enough to light a small room. Sometimes I just use it to fine stuff I’ve dropped down the side of my car seats.

Get the Olight iMini 2 keychain flashlight

I have spilled tea and coffee on my clothes so many times that I started carrying around a Tide stain pen a while back, and it has saved many a shirt. It’s not going to get out huge stains, but it’s still nice to stop something from ruining your outfit. They’re around $15 for a 5-pack. I can’t recommend them highly enough because they’ve stopped so many of my shirts and t-shirts from getting completely ruined over the past few years.

On a similar note, I try to carry a microfiber cleaning cloth, alcohol cleaning pads, and napkins or tissues. Throw in some hand gel, lotion, a little sunscreen, and I’m covered for basically any eventuality.

My current kit (Andrew)

The backpack – Peak Design Travel Backpack 20L

Whether I step outside with a sling or my backpack is entirely down to whether I decide to tote my laptop along. I use a MacBook Air 13-inch, which has the smallest footprint one can reasonably expect a bag to fit. But even so, there is a true limit to the number of slings that can carry a small laptop. So if that’s coming with me, I’m taking the Peak Design Travel Backpack 20L.

The 20L variant has easily become my favorite backpack to lug around if I’m going with a heavier loadout. It weighs very little, and it’s completely unassuming. If there needs to be more on my back, it can expand slightly beyond that small capacity. But otherwise, I’m able to carry my laptop and a few essentials without worry.

The main compartment is great for just throwing random items in. When I’m using this bag, stuff doesn’t need to be organized as it would in a dedicated camera bag. I’m generally going to bring my tech pouch along, too. But that’s almost overkill because the top pocket has all of the same inner pockets for those little things I want to tag along.

It has all of the little creature comforts you’d want. Magnetic strap keepers, a pass-through for luggage handles, and an internal water bottle holder, so a giant container of liquid isn’t sloshing around way off balance. Overall, it’s simple but incredibly effective at what it does.

Get the Peak Design Travel 20L

The sidebag – Bellroy Lite Sling Mini

As for the sling, my rule states that I’ll swap to this if my laptop isn’t coming along. The Sling Lite Mini has the feel of an outdoor bag without so much of the look, so it flies under the radar more than a technical pack might. The outer material is strong and lightweight, but it doesn’t repel liquid as well as I’d hope it would. The internal pocket structure is simple, but efficient. The main pocket is plenty large enough for random items, and it’s complemented by a zipper pocket for thinner items. One of the gussets that let it expand is lined with a pocket I use to slip my Nomad titanium pen and handy USB ChargeKey. On the other side, I clip my knife and flashlight.

The best part about it being geared towards outdoor use is that it’s expandable. The gusseted construction keeps it compact, no matter how much you stuff in it. So even if it’s full, the shoulder strap pulls it tight so the overall profile is kept slim.

It’s tough and just easy to grab and go. I love this bag.

Neither is traditionally “cheap,” and Damien offers a great alternative with his TomToc sidebag. But at $79 for the sling and double that for the Travel Backpack, it’s a “buy it for life” sort of purchase.

Get the Bellroy Sling Lite Mini

The power – Baseus Qi2 25W

I generally don’t have the fear of running out of power with whatever phone I’m using. I wouldn’t say I’m an ultra-power user, but there are times when I just start to run out of steam on my Galaxy Fold 8 Ultra or Pixel 11. You can carry a slim charging brick, which I do anyway, or you can take a magnetic power bank.

I always carry the Baseus 10,000mAh Qi2.2 25W power bank with me. Because the Pixel has magnets on the back without the help of a case, I can always slap it on. If needed, I can plug the bank into something else via USB-C. Speeds aren’t really an issue, either, because it runs at 25W – right where the Pixel 10 Pro XL is rated, even if it doesn’t always charge that fast.

Baseus has slightly thinner options, but I prefer the charging speed I get with the 25W model. It just works when I need it, and it’s really not all that heavy.

Get the Baseus Qi2 power bank

The catalyst – Statik MagStak Pro USB-C cable

It’s kind of big, and it’s kind of bulky, but if I’m bringing a bag, I have little reason not to throw this in. Statik’s MagStack cable is a 100W magnetic cable that essentially coils itself back up every single time. It solves the issue of cables that are all over the place and are resistant to any coercion to get them back into shape.

I’ve been using the MagStack cable for the better part of a year, and it just refuses to lose it’s uniform appeal. I bring it with me whenever I can because it’s just easy to pack away, given you have the pocket space. Plus, I know it’s a high-speed cable, as opposed to all of my identical USB-C cables with varying levels of power delivery.

Get the Statik MagStack Pro cable

The wallet – Peak Design Mobile Slim

Yeah, maybe I am a Peak Design nerd. I can’t really help it. The design speaks to me on the photography side, as well as on the engineering side. I’ve been using the mobile slim wallet for what has to be three or four years. It’s almost time to replace it, because that once “Sun” yellow color has now darkened to a dijon.

It’s a standard slim pull-tab wallet. I hold a few cards in there, including a Google Find My Device tracker, unlike my European counterpart, who seems adamant that carrying a physical ID is no longer a normal part of society. Until Google Wallet can add my license without any potential governmental hiccups, I’m carrying a MagSafe wallet with me.

Get the Peak Design Mobile Wallet

The flat light – Olight ArkPro Ultra

I don’t know what it is about flashlights, but they come in clutch way more than you’d think. The ArcPro Ultra is technically a “flat” light, but it’s still sort of beefy. That doesn’t stop me from throwing it in my pocket or bags whenever I go out, even if it’s in the middle of the day and there’s no conceivable need to carry a torch.

Still, I’ve used it too many times to start leaving it behind. The battery essentially never dies, and I can beam up to 1,700 lumens with a simple double-tap. Plus, the slider to switch between UV, spotlight, and floodlight acts as a fantastic fidget toy.

Get the Olight ArcPro Ultra

title: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro vs. 17 Pro: What the Extra $100 Brings to the Newer Pro iPhone
snippet: While the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro look similar, there are a lot of changes on the inside.
fullText:
Though the new iPhone Duo might’ve captured a lot of headlines for its foldable design, the iPhone 18 Pro remains Apple’s standard-bearer due to its top-of-the-line camera, superb features and excellent battery life. One of the more impressive new features this year is the camera’s variable aperture, which lets you control exposure. 

But while the iPhone 18 Pro has a lot going for it, it really isn’t too different from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro. The design, features and internal specs have very minor differences. If you really care about having variable aperture, perhaps the iPhone 18 Pro is the better choice. But if you care more about saving money, the 17 Pro, which retails for about $100 less, might be the wiser option. 

Here’s a closer look at how last year’s flagship compares to this year’s.

The Dynamic Island is smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (right) than on last year’s 17 Pro Max.Patrick Holland/CNET

Design and display

When you look at the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 17 Pro side-by-side, there really isn’t a whole lot to differentiate them. They have the exact same dimensions of 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches, and both have 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR LTPO OLED displays. You can even use the same phone cases for the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro.

The iPhone 18 Pro is ever so slightly heavier — 7.44 ounces compared to the iPhone 17 Pro’s 7.27 ounces — likely due to the variable aperture’s polymer blades. Another change is that the Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro is slightly smaller, plus it supports up to three Live Activities at a time. On the inside, the 18 Pro has a redesigned vapor cooling chamber, which could be important if you intend to use the phone for more intensive tasks like gaming or lengthy video capture — the newer phone should be able to stay cooler for longer than the 17 Pro. 

Unfortunately for those who love the color orange, you won’t find an iPhone 18 Pro in that shade. Still, the colors for the 18 Pro are quite lovely. The iPhone 18 Pro ships in glacier blue, burgundy red, black and silver. The iPhone 17 Pro comes in cosmic orange, deep blue and silver. 

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is able to show three Live Activities at once.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Camera features

Both the iPhone 17 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro feature a triple 48-megapixel rear camera array. The key difference, however, is that the iPhone 18 Pro has variable aperture, which allows you to control light exposure at the hardware level. You can switch between four aperture presets (f1.48, f1.8, f2.8, and f4.0 f-stops) to adjust the amount of light that hits the sensor. This allows for greater depth of field in close-up shots and improved low-light photography, among other things.

Aside from that, the front-facing camera remains largely unchanged. Both have an 18-megapixel selfie camera with a Center Stage feature that automatically frames the people in the shot, plus it can switch between horizontal and vertical orientations without having to rotate the phone.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available in black (pictured) along with burgandy, glacier and silver.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Performance and battery life

The iPhone 18 Pro ships with the brand-new A20 Pro chip, which is an upgrade over the 17 Pro’s A19 Pro chip. The processor is Apple’s first to use a 2-nanometer process, which means the chip is denser — possibly allowing Apple to make room for a bigger battery. We still have more testing to do, but in our initial tests, we’ve found that the A20 chip is quite the beast, never stumbling on videos or games. 

If you still want an orange iPhone, the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max are currently your only option.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

As for battery life, we have so far found it to be the same on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro, with both phones lasting for close to 24 hours before needing to be recharged. The 18 Pro is one of the fastest-charging phones we’ve tested, with it charging from 0% to 82% in 30 minutes. That’s substantially faster than the 17 Pro, which recharged to 69% in the same test.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by CleanMyMac by MacPaw. With the release of macOS 27 Golden Gate, use CleanMyMac first to free up space, optimize your system, and ensure your new Mac runs at 100% on day one. Learn more.

macOS 27 Golden Gate is a huge upgrade over macOS 26 Tahoe, and not just because of the smarter design decisions. Just like iOS 27 for iPhone, the Mac adds a Liquid Glass appearance slider. This lets you dramatically change the look of your Mac across the system.

The slider

Liquid Glass is Apple’s design language that started with iOS 26 and macOS 26 Tahoe. Initially, Liquid Glass started with a single look. Apple later added a setting to make Liquid Glass less clear.

Starting with iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, Liquid Glass is no longer limited to just two styles. Instead, Apple has introduced an appearance slider. This lets you make Liquid Glass much more clear than before. You can also give Liquid Glass a more opaque look that still looks modern.

macOS 27 Golden Gate defaults to a medium setting. The system also invites you to adjust the slider during initial setup. You can also adjust the slider later in System Settings > Appearance.

The Liquid Glass slider provides a live preview of what to expect from each setting. Three notches suggest most clear, medium, and most opaque. However, you can assign it to any level in between notches as well.

The Dock

The Dock is the most prominent component that changes appearance based on the Liquid Glass slider setting.

It can range from showing your desktop wallpaper in clear definition to being a more opaque and defined material.

Here’s a closer look:

macOS desktop widgets can be full color, dim, or change automatically. The Liquid Glass slider changes how the dim widget appearance looks as well.

Apple Music and Podcasts

Apps like Apple Music and Podcasts that have system Now Playing bars have a very different look based on the Liquid Glass slider position.

Here’s the Now Playing bar Podcasts, for example:

And here’s Music: 

More

The slider also applies to sidebars, toolbars, and toolbar buttons. This changes the look of Photos, Safari, and other apps with window chrome.

The one thing about the Liquid Glass slider in macOS 27 Golden Gate is that a single slider controls all Liquid Glass appearances across the system. That means you get one look for the Dock, widgets, and window chrome. 

What’s your preference? More clear, more opaque, or somewhere in the middle? Personally, I really love how nice and mature the more opaque option looks on my Mac. Still, it can be fun to experiment with more clear, and I’m glad macOS 27 Golden Gate gives everyone the option to decide.

Share your thoughts in the comments!

title: Apple Notes adds a power user feature in iOS 27 that’s rare in other apps
snippet: Apple Notes in iOS 27 adds a variety of new features, including one that power users are sure to appreciate: section links. more…
fullText:
Apple Notes in iOS 27 adds a variety of new features, including one that power users are sure to appreciate: section links.

Apple Notes lets you link to specific sections of your note in iOS 27

There’s no shortage of third-party notes apps on the App Store. You can find everything from barebones note-takers to powerhouse productivity suites.

Apple Notes has long excelled at offering a minimalist, user-friendly interface while also providing tools that power users love.

And in iOS 27, Notes has an exciting new addition in the latter category: section links.

Whenever you select some text inside a note in iOS 27 and open the edit menu, tapping ‘Add Link’ will reveal a new option: Link to Section.

Inside this menu, you’ll find a full list of all the headings and subheadings in your note. Tap one, and Notes will create a link to that specific section. You can choose to use the section title as the link’s text, or your own custom text.

Section links are great for navigating long notes, as they make it quick and easy to jump to a specific area.

With section links you can create a full-blown table of contents at the top of your note, or just use them sparingly for sections you revisit a lot.

Most iPhone owners probably won’t ever use the feature. But for power users who value more flexibility in their notes app, section links in Apple Notes are a welcome new addition.

How will you use Apple Notes’ section links in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

title: Nest Doorbell has been triggering Gemini’s American accent, no matter what language you speak; fix coming
snippet: Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect. more…
fullText:
Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect.

According to one user on Reddit, Gemini has been responding to them in American accent only when its referencing their Nest Doorbell. That’s nothing out of the ordinary on the surface, but this user’s complaint revolves entirely around the fact that they’re French, speak French, and live in France. Even still, the Nest Doorbell seems to trigger Gemini’s US English.

It isn’t just affecting one user, or one device. A commenter expressed the same concern in the Netherlands, and another in the UK. For the user in the Netherlands, their Bosch washing machine alerts default to US English instead of Dutch. It sounds like every other interaction with Gemini happens in the language of choice, but certain appliances bring out a different Gemini voice altogether.

According to a response by an official Google account, the issue is being worked on. No fix has been rolled out, but Gemini will likely stop responding in its American accent soon enough, unless you specifically want that.

	

It might have been be a bug developed after the September Google Home update with changes to Gemini for Home. Spoken notifications seem to work as intended, but for whatever reason, Gemini chooses to give the user context in an American accent instead of the language or accent set in preferences. the only change note that refers to Gemini is one that improves follow up question behavior. Beyond that, there’s nothing pointing towards an obvious cause.

Something is clearly broken along the pipeline of information, but it’s manifesting in one of the most hilarious ways.

It’s a strange one, but Google is aware of the issue and claims to be working on it.

title: I’ve Been Waiting for a Coffee Maker With No Plastic in the Brew Path. Caraway Just Delivered
snippet: Caraway launched its first appliance today, and we got our hands on it early.
fullText:
Over the last two or so years, I’ve been slowly swapping out the plastic in my kitchen for better alternatives to avoid as many microplastics as possible. I use glass Pyrex for storage, bamboo utensils for cooking, a wooden cutting board for all of my slicing and dicing, glass dishes and reusable, stainless steel water bottles. But there was still one thing I knew for a fact contained plastic: my coffee maker. 

Although I haven’t removed every single piece of plastic from my kitchen, I was extra cognizant of my coffee maker because every time it’s used, boiling water goes over the plastic and into the coffee. No, I don’t put my morning beverages under a microscope, but I feel like there’s a good chance that microplastics are leached during this process. And it seemed unavoidable, because every single drip coffee maker I’ve used has had plastic either in the basket where the coffee grounds are placed or on the carafe lid.

So when I learned that Caraway was entering the appliance scene with a drip coffee machine that has absolutely no plastic in the brew path, I had a sneaking feeling that it would end up being my favorite coffee machine ever. Two weeks into having it in my kitchen, I can say I was right. 

	

			

Trying out Caraway’s new coffee maker

I was already familiar with Caraway through the brand’s ceramic-coated cookware, so I wasn’t surprised to find an exceptionally sharp-looking appliance when I opened the box. Aesthetically pleasing kitchenware is what the brand is known for after all. The design, the color, the quality of the build — all of it made a great first impression. Even the removable cord is thoughtfully designed, but I had to make sure it functioned as well as it looked.

The brew basket is stainless steel, and it comes with a reusable stainless steel coffee filter, too. The glass coffee carafe holds up to 10 cups, and although there’s silicone around the lid, the part that comes into contact with your hot coffee is stainless steel. All of those pieces are dishwasher safe.  

The coffee only comes into contact with stainless steel.Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

There is only one knob on the coffee maker, which helps it keep its sleek look. It controls the brew, clean and start/stop options. After the coffee is finished brewing, it stays warm in the carafe for up to an hour and a half.

You can twist the knob for brew or clean and push it for start or stop.Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

No plastic, no rogue grounds 

After using it multiple times, it has consistently made great coffee with no grounds in it, so the reusable coffee filter was a success, too. 

Although it’s simple in design, there are nice details throughout, such as a matte finish, a tall, glass carafe and the blue light that illuminates when you pour water into the reservoir.

If you like to schedule your coffee ahead of time, though, you won’t be able to do so with this appliance. There are no extra buttons for scheduling or digital screens, which is partly why this appliance looks so chic. 

After the coffee is finished brewing, the stainless steel filter can be rinsed out and reused next time.Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

I’m loving this coffee machine for many reasons, but the biggest one is that it solves a problem I’ve been focused on for a while. As we continue to learn more about microplastics and their potential impact on our health, I’m becoming more cautious about how often my food and drinks come into contact with plastic. 

Before this launch, if I wanted to avoid plastic when making coffee, a pour-over was the main option I saw. Caraway’s new coffee maker not only keeps plastic out of the brew path but also offers the convenience of a drip coffee maker — and looks great doing so.

The Caraway Coffee Maker is now available for $495 in cream, stone, midnight and clay colors.

title: Apple retires the Apple Park Visitor Center’s unique AR experience
snippet: Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.” That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park. more…
fullText:
Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.”

That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park.

When Apple opened the Apple Park Visitor Center to the public in 2017, here’s how the company touted the AR experience:

Inviting guests to explore Apple Park in an immersive and engaging way, a 3-D model of the campus is brought to life by augmented reality technology.

Visitors can learn about the world’s largest naturally ventilated building and view one of the largest on-site solar energy installations in the world. Visitors can also choose to lift the entire roof off the building to peek inside to the collaborative office pod layout.

Until this change, the Apple Park Visitor was divided into three sections: the AR exhibit, a traditional-style Apple Store, and a cafe.

Source: RedNote

Now, Apple has retired the AR exhibit and transformed that space into an extension of the more traditional Apple Store. As spotted by MacRumors, this includes Avenues along the wall showcasing accessories and redesigned display tables featuring Apple products.

The rest of the Apple Park Visitor Center, including the cafe, remains unchanged.

9to5Mac’s Take

The AR experience at the Apple Park Visitor Center was unique, but after nine years it was starting to feel like that space could be better utilized in other ways. 

I wish Apple had tried something other than converting it into a traditional retail store, but at least the cafe remains as a unique fixture of the Apple Park Visitor Center.

title: The Quantified Scientist tests the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart rate sensor
snippet: In a new video, The Quantified Scientist’s Rob ter Horst compares the new Apple Watch Series 12’s heart rate sensor against a Polar H10 ECG chest strap. Here’s what he found. more…
fullText:
In a new video, The Quantified Scientist’s Rob ter Horst compares the new Apple Watch Series 12’s heart rate sensor against a Polar H10 ECG chest strap. Here’s what he found.

Revamped heart sensor delivers

For the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple completely revamped the device’s heart sensor, which now measures heart rate every five seconds even when the user isn’t active.

In our review of Apple Watch Series 12, which you can read here, we found that the added data can provide more detailed insights into how everyday activities and moments throughout the day affect heart rate, such as hauling groceries, doing yard work, drinking an afternoon cup of coffee, or dealing with a stressful moment at work.

That said, Rob ter Horst from The Quantified Scientist YouTube channel published an in-depth look (via MacMagazine) at the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart rate sensor during indoor cycling, running, and weightlifting, and compared its readings with those from a Polar H10 ECG chest strap.

All in all, the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart sensor performed very well, particularly during indoor cycling, where its readings were nearly identical to the Polar H10 data.

During a running session, the Series 12 also performed well, with a 0.98 correlation with the chest strap (versus a near-perfect correlation of 1.0 during indoor cycling), though ter Horst noted some minor deviations at higher heart rates.

During weightlifting, which ter Horst notes is traditionally one of the hardest activities for wrist-based heart rate sensors, the Series 12 posted the lowest correlation of the three exercises tested, at 0.97. Even so, ter Horst said the result was “quite good” compared with the competition, placing the Series 12 above 85% of devices he has tested for weightlifting.

Compared with his longer-term testing of the Apple Watch Series 11, ter Horst said the new Apple Watch Series 12 delivered broadly similar heart rate accuracy overall, with the older model actually performing slightly better during running in his tests. It could be the case, ter Horst notes, that Apple is still tweaking its algorithms for the new sensor.

Finally, ter Horst also tested the Apple Watch Series 12’s step counter. He manually counted roughly 5,000 steps and found the Series 12 was generally spot-on or only slightly overcounted.

title: Apple Photos in iOS 27 gets camera roll feature it’s long needed
snippet: iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’ more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 Photos app contains only photos and videos you shot in Camera app

Apple’s Photos app has steadily expanded its feature set over the years. In addition to being home to the photos and videos your iPhone captures, it also includes content that’s been shared with you, Memories, screenshots, saved media, and a lot more.

The Photos app used to offer a ‘Camera Roll’ feature that was similar to what the ‘Recents’ album does today. It included images you captured as well as ones you saved.

But what’s been missing for a long time is a feature that actually just shows photos and videos that you’ve taken—in other words, something that could more accurately be called your ‘camera roll.’

iOS 27 delivers that long-missing feature, and it’s called ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 is a new Photos collection that does exactly what it sounds like. It includes only media that’s been captured by your Camera app.

So photos and videos that you shot on your iPhone are collected there. But you won’t see screenshots, images your friends sent you, or any other types of content.

In addition to the dedicated ‘Captured by Me’ collection, you can also use a ‘Captured by Me’ filter in your main Photos library.

Whichever way you use the feature, ‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 fills an important gap in Apple Photos’ feature set.
